conditions.name: Active liver disease or unexplained persistently raised transaminases
Acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids or other psychotropic medicines
Acute ulcerative colitis, antibiotic-associated colitis or diarrhoea caused by poisoning
Acute, unstable or decompensated heart failure
Asthma/urticaria/rhinitis triggered by aspirin or NSAIDs
Child with possibly compromised breathing (neuromuscular disorder, severe cardiac or respiratory condition, chest infection, multiple trauma or extensive surgery)
Children after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea
Connective tissue disorder (e.g. Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)
Crush injuries / extensive cell destruction (e.g. severe burns)
Current or past substance use disorder (including alcohol misuse)
Epilepsy not adequately controlled by treatment
Haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction
Heart valve disease (congenital or acquired) / risk of heart valve regurgitation
Hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency
Hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption
History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor
History of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (trimethoprim and/or sulfonamides)
Known skin photosensitivity, or phototherapy / photodiagnostic procedure
Low cardiac filling pressure (including acute MI with low filling pressure)
Methaemoglobin reductase deficiency or haemoglobin M
Peptic ulcer or GI bleeding (active or history)
Previous jaundice or liver injury caused by co-amoxiclav
Previous serious adverse reaction to a quinolone or fluoroquinolone
Protein C or protein S deficiency
Pulmonary hypertension secondary to sickle cell anaemia
Renal impairment (any severity; source gives no numeric threshold)
Respiratory failure / conditions causing tissue hypoxia
Severe acute or chronic infection (e.g. TB, HIV)
Severe illness (e.g. sepsis), malnutrition or chronic alcoholism (glutathione deficiency)
Severe renal failure not treated by dialysis
Severe renal impairment / renal impairment with oliguria
Severe renal impairment or renal failure (source gives no numeric threshold)
Stomatitis, mouth ulcers or active GI ulcer disease
Tendon disorder related to quinolone use
Using hormonal contraception (pill, implant, injection, patch, hormonal IUD)
Within 72 hours after major surgery with risk of severe bleeding
Woman attempting to conceive or under investigation for infertility
Woman of child-bearing potential not using effective contraception

formulations.label: Tablets
formulations.strengths: 5 mg (SmPC used; other strengths have their own SmPCs)

src.q: Each tablet contains 5 mg of amlodipine (as amlodipine besilate)

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Hypertension; chronic stable angina; vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina.

src.q: Hypertension Chronic stable angina pectoris Vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the amlodipine 5 mg tablets SmPC.

items.t: Adults: start 5 mg once daily; may increase to a maximum of 10 mg once daily depending on response.

src.q: For both hypertension and angina the usual initial dose is 5 mg Amlodipine once daily which may be increased to a maximum dose of 10 mg depending on the individual patient's response.

items.t: Elderly: normal doses; increase the dose with care.

src.q: Normal dosage regimens are recommended in the elderly, but increase of the dosage should take place with care

items.t: No amlodipine dose adjustment is needed when given with thiazide diuretics, beta blockers or ACE inhibitors.

src.q: No dose adjustment of amlodipine is required upon concomitant administration of thiazide diuretics, beta blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.

items.t: Hypertension, 6 to 17 years: 2.5 mg once daily; increase to 5 mg once daily if blood pressure goal not reached after 4 weeks. Doses above 5 mg daily have not been studied in children.

src.q: The recommended antihypertensive oral dose in paediatric patients aged 6-17 years is 2.5 mg once daily as a starting dose, up-titrated to 5 mg once daily if blood pressure goal is not achieved after 4 weeks.
Doses in excess of 5 mg daily have not been studied in paediatric patients

items.t: Under 6 years: no data available.

src.q: Children under 6 years old No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amlodipine, other dihydropyridines or any excipient.

src.q: hypersensitivity to the active substance, dihydropyridine derivatives or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Severe hypotension; shock (including cardiogenic shock).

src.q: severe hypotension shock (including cardiogenic shock)

items.t: Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (e.g. high-grade aortic stenosis).

src.q: obstruction of the outflow tract of the left ventricle (e.g. high-grade aortic stenosis)

items.t: Haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction.

src.q: haemodynamically unstable heart failure after acute myocardial infarction

items.t: Heart failure: use with caution. In severe heart failure (NYHA III-IV) more pulmonary oedema was reported with amlodipine than placebo; calcium-channel blockers may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality in congestive heart failure.

src.q: Patients with heart failure should be treated with caution.
Calcium channel blockers, including amlodipine, should be used with caution in patients with congestive heart failure, as they may increase the risk of future cardiovascular events and mortality.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: half-life prolonged and exposure higher; start at the lower end of the dose range and use caution when starting and when increasing the dose.

src.q: Amlodipine should therefore be initiated at the lower end of the dosing range and caution should be used, both on initial treatment and when increasing the dose.

items.t: Safety and efficacy in hypertensive crisis not established.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of amlodipine in hypertensive crisis has not been established.

items.t: Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, erythromycin, azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, diltiazem, verapamil): amlodipine exposure may rise markedly, with more risk of hypotension (more so in the elderly). Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Concomitant use of amlodipine with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, azole antifungals, macrolides like erythromycin or clarithromycin, verapamil or diltiazem) may give rise to significant increase in amlodipine exposure
Clinical monitoring and dose adjustment may thus be required.

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, St John's wort): amlodipine levels may change. Monitor blood pressure and consider dose adjustment during and after the combination.

src.q: blood pressure should be monitored and dose regulation considered both during and after concomitant medication particularly with strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g. rifampicin, hypericum perforatum).

items.t: Simvastatin: limit simvastatin to 20 mg daily in patients taking amlodipine (amlodipine 10 mg raised simvastatin exposure by 77%). MHRA: the 20 mg maximum applies with amlodipine 5 mg and 10 mg.

src.q: Limit the dose of simvastatin in patients on amlodipine to 20 mg daily.
The maximum recommended dose of simvastatin co-administered with amlodipine or diltiazem is now 20 mg per day.
the recommendation for a maximum daily dose of simvastatin of 20 mg applies with amlodipine at doses of both 10 mg and 5 mg.

items.t: Other antihypertensives: additive blood pressure lowering.

src.q: The blood pressure lowering effects of amlodipine adds to the blood pressure-lowering effects of other medicinal products with antihypertensive properties.

items.t: Grapefruit or grapefruit juice: not recommended (may increase blood pressure lowering).

src.q: Administration of amlodipine with grapefruit or grapefruit juice is not recommended

items.t: Tacrolimus: risk of raised tacrolimus levels; monitor tacrolimus levels and adjust its dose. Ciclosporin (renal transplant): consider monitoring ciclosporin levels and reducing its dose as needed.

src.q: administration of amlodipine in a patient treated with tacrolimus requires monitoring of tacrolimus blood levels and dose adjustment of tacrolimus when appropriate.
Consideration should be given for monitoring ciclosporin levels in renal transplant patients on amlodipine

items.t: Atorvastatin, digoxin and warfarin: amlodipine did not affect their pharmacokinetics in interaction studies.

src.q: amlodipine did not affect the pharmacokinetics of atorvastatin, digoxin or warfarin

items.t: Dantrolene infusion / malignant hyperthermia: avoid calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine in patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia and in its management (risk of hyperkalaemia; ventricular fibrillation and collapse seen in animals with verapamil plus IV dantrolene).

src.q: it is recommended that the co-administration of calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine be avoided in patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia and in the management of malignant hyperthermia
In animals, lethal ventricular fibrillation and cardiovascular collapse are observed in association with hyperkalaemia after administration of verapamil and intravenous dantrolene.

items.t: mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, temsirolimus, everolimus): amlodipine is a weak CYP3A inhibitor and may increase their exposure.

src.q: mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus, temsirolimus, and everolimus are CYP3A substrates.
With concomitant use of mTOR inhibitors, amlodipine may increase exposure of mTOR inhibitors.

items.t: Normal dose in renal impairment (plasma levels do not correlate with degree of renal impairment). Not dialysable.

src.q: Changes in amlodipine plasma concentrations are not correlated with degree of renal impairment, therefore the normal dosage is recommended.
Amlodipine is not dialysable.

items.t: Mild to moderate hepatic impairment: no established dose; choose the dose cautiously and start at the lower end of the range.

src.q: Dosage recommendations have not been established in patients with mild to moderate hepatic impairment, therefore dose selection should be cautious and should start at the lower end of the dosing range

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: not studied; start at the lowest dose and titrate slowly. Careful monitoring may be needed.

src.q: Amlodipine should be initiated at the lowest dose and titrated slowly in patients with severe hepatic impairment.
Slow dose titration and careful monitoring may be required in patients with severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: SmPC: safety in human pregnancy not established. Use only when there is no safer alternative and the disease itself carries greater risk for mother and fetus.

src.q: The safety of amlodipine in human pregnancy has not been established.
Use in pregnancy is only recommended when there is no safer alternative and when the disease itself carries greater risk for the mother and foetus.

items.t: BUMPS (calcium-channel blockers leaflet): no clear risks from calcium-channel blockers in pregnancy; nifedipine is the one commonly used. Others are less used and recommended only when benefit outweighs possible risk. No extra monitoring for major birth defects is needed.

src.q: There are no clear risks of taking a calcium channel blocker in pregnancy.

The other calcium channel blockers are less commonly used, and while not thought to cause problems, will only be recommended if the benefits of treating a potentially serious or lifestyle-impacting condition outweigh any possible risks.
No extra monitoring for major birth defects is required following use of a calcium channel blocker.

items.t: SmPC: amlodipine passes into breast milk (infant dose estimated at 3-7% of maternal dose, maximum 15%). Weigh the benefit of breastfeeding against the benefit of treatment.

src.q: Amlodipine is excreted in human milk.

A decision on whether to continue/discontinue breast-feeding or to continue/discontinue therapy with amlodipine should be made taking into account the benefit of breast-feeding to the child and the benefit of amlodipine therapy to the mother.

items.t: SPS: use with caution; nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine. As a precaution, watch the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain). Advice applies to full-term, healthy infants.

src.q: It can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but nifedipine is the preferred dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for hypotension which may manifest as drowsiness, lethargy, looking pale , poor feeding and inadequate weight gain.
Recommendations apply to full term and healthy infants only.

items.t: Reversible changes in the head of spermatozoa have been reported with calcium-channel blockers; clinical data on fertility are insufficient.

src.q: Reversible biochemical changes in the head of spermatozoa have been reported in some patients treated by calcium channel blockers.
Clinical data are insufficient regarding the potential effect of amlodipine on fertility.

items.t: Very common: oedema. Common: somnolence, dizziness, headache, palpitations, flushing, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspepsia, altered bowel habit, ankle swelling, muscle cramps, visual disturbance, dyspnoea, fatigue, asthenia.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions during treatment are somnolence, dizziness, headache, palpitations, flushing, abdominal pain, nausea, ankle swelling, oedema and fatigue.
General disorders and administration site conditions Very common Oedema Common Fatigue, asthenia

items.t: Very rare: angioedema, erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome; toxic epidermal necrolysis (frequency not known).

src.q: Very rare Hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic enzymes increased*
Very rare Pancreatitis, gastritis, gingival hyperplasia
Very rare Leukocytopenia, thrombocytopenia
Very rare Myocardial infarction

items.t: Overdose: marked, possibly prolonged hypotension up to fatal shock; non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema may appear 24-48 hours after ingestion. Dialysis unlikely to help.

src.q: Marked and probably prolonged systemic hypotension up to and including shock with fatal outcome have been reported.
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema has rarely been reported as a consequence of amlodipine overdose that may manifest with a delayed onset (24-48 hours post-ingestion) and require ventilatory support.

items.t: With CYP3A4 inducers: monitor blood pressure during and after the combination.

src.q: blood pressure should be monitored and dose regulation considered both during and after concomitant medication

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: slow titration and careful monitoring may be needed.

src.q: Slow dose titration and careful monitoring may be required in patients with severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: With tacrolimus: monitor tacrolimus blood levels.

src.q: requires monitoring of tacrolimus blood levels

items.t: Oral, once daily. Food does not affect absorption.

src.q: The bioavailability of amlodipine is not affected by food intake.

items.t: Dizziness, headache, tiredness or nausea can affect driving; take care especially at the start of treatment.

src.q: If patients taking amlodipine suffer from dizziness, headache, fatigue or nausea the ability to react may be impaired.
Caution is recommended especially at the start of treatment.

items.t: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.

src.q: Administration of amlodipine with grapefruit or grapefruit juice is not recommended

items.t: Ankle swelling and oedema are common.

src.q: Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders Common Ankle swelling, muscle cramps
Amoxicillin trihydrate equivalent to 500mg Amoxycillin per capsule.

Contains sodium benzoate Contains sorbitol

items.t: Adults and children: acute bacterial sinusitis, acute streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis/COPD, community-acquired pneumonia, acute otitis media, acute cystitis, acute pyelonephritis, asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy, typhoid/paratyphoid fever, dental abscess with spreading cellulitis, prosthetic joint infections, H. pylori eradication, Lyme disease.

src.q: Amoxicillin is indicated for the treatment of the following infections in adults and children

Acute bacterial sinusitis Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis (AECB)/acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) Community acquired pneumonia Acute otitis media Acute cystitis Acute pyelonephritis
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy Typhoid and paratyphoid fevers Dental abscess with spreading cellulitis Prosthetic joint infections Helicobacter pylori eradication Lyme disease

items.t: Prophylaxis of endocarditis.

src.q: Amoxicillin is also indicated for the prophylaxis of endocarditis.

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand-specific prescribing restriction found in the amoxicillin SmPCs accessed. SmPCs advise considering official guidance on appropriate antibacterial use.

items.t: Acute bacterial sinusitis, asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy, acute pyelonephritis, dental abscess with spreading cellulitis, acute cystitis: 250 mg to 500 mg every 8 hours, or 750 mg to 1 g every 12 hours; severe infections 750 mg to 1 g every 8 hours. Acute cystitis may be treated with 3 g twice daily for one day.

src.q: 250 mg to 500 mg every 8 hours or 750 mg to 1 g every 12 hours For severe infections 750 mg to 1 g every 8 hours Acute cystitis may be treated with 3g twice daily for one day
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy Acute pyelonephritis Dental abscess with spreading cellulitis Acute cystitis

items.t: Acute otitis media, acute streptococcal tonsillitis/pharyngitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis: 500 mg every 8 hours or 750 mg to 1 g every 12 hours; severe infections 750 mg to 1 g every 8 hours for 10 days.

src.q: Acute otitis media 500 mg every 8 hours, 750 mg to 1 g every 12 hours Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis For severe infections 750 mg to 1 g every 8 hours for 10 days

items.t: Community-acquired pneumonia: 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours.

src.q: Community acquired pneumonia 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours

items.t: Typhoid and paratyphoid fever: 500 mg to 2 g every 8 hours.

src.q: Typhoid and paratyphoid fever 500 mg to 2 g every 8 hours

items.t: Prosthetic joint infections: 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours.

src.q: Prosthetic joint infections 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours

items.t: Prophylaxis of endocarditis: 2 g orally as a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure.

src.q: Prophylaxis of endocarditis 2 g orally, single dose 30 to 60 minutes before procedure

items.t: H. pylori eradication: 750 mg to 1 g twice daily with a proton pump inhibitor and another antibiotic (e.g. clarithromycin or metronidazole) for 7 days.

src.q: 750 mg to 1 g twice daily in combination with a proton pump inhibitor (e.g. omeprazole, lansoprazole) and another antibiotic (e.g. clarithromycin, metronidazole) for 7 days

items.t: Lyme disease, early stage: 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours (maximum 4 g/day in divided doses) for 14 days (10 to 21 days).

src.q: Early stage: 500 mg to 1 g every 8 hours up to a maximum of 4 g/day in divided doses for 14 days (10 to 21 days)

items.t: Lyme disease, late stage (systemic involvement): 500 mg to 2 g every 8 hours (maximum 6 g/day in divided doses) for 10 to 30 days.

src.q: Late stage (systemic involvement): 500 mg to 2 g every 8 hours up to a maximum of 6 g/day in divided doses for 10 to 30 days

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment considered necessary. Duration should generally be as short as possible and set by infection type and response.

src.q: Elderly No dose adjustment is considered necessary.
should generally be as short as possible

items.t: Children < 40 kg, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia, acute cystitis, acute pyelonephritis, dental abscess: 20 to 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses.

src.q: Acute bacterial sinusitis 20 to 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses* Acute otitis media Community acquired pneumonia Acute cystitis Acute pyelonephritis Dental abscess with spreading cellulitis

items.t: Children < 40 kg, acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis: 40 to 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses. Twice-daily regimens only when the dose is in the upper range.

src.q: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis and pharyngitis 40 to 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses*
Twice daily dosing regimens should only be considered when the dose is in the upper range.

items.t: Children < 40 kg, typhoid and paratyphoid fever: 100 mg/kg/day in three divided doses.

src.q: paratyphoid fever 100 mg/kg/day in three divided doses

items.t: Children < 40 kg, prophylaxis of endocarditis: 50 mg/kg orally as a single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure.

src.q: Prophylaxis of endocarditis 50 mg/kg orally, single dose 30 to 60 minutes before procedure

items.t: Children < 40 kg, Lyme disease: early stage 25 to 50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 10 to 21 days; late stage (systemic involvement) 100 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 10 to 30 days.

src.q: Early stage: 25 to 50 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 10 to 21 days
Late stage (systemic involvement): 100 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 10 to 30 days

items.t: Children weighing 40 kg or more take the adult dose.

src.q: Children weighing 40 kg or more should be prescribed the adult dosage.

items.t: Paediatric suspension is recommended for children under six months of age.

src.q: Amoxicillin Paediatric Suspension is recommended for children under six months of age.

items.t: Very young children (including preterm newborns) in the first week of life: dosing interval should not be more frequent than twice daily (immature renal elimination).

src.q: For very young children (including preterm newborns) in the first week of life the interval of administration should not exceed twice daily administration

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amoxicillin, to any penicillin or to any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to any of the penicillins or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: History of a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) to another beta-lactam (e.g. a cephalosporin, carbapenem or monobactam).

src.q: History of a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) to another beta-lactam agent (e.g. a cephalosporin, carbapenem or monobactam).

items.t: Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) on amoxicillin requires stopping it and contraindicates any later use.

src.q: This reaction requires amoxicillin discontinuation and contra-indicates any subsequent administration.

items.t: Ask carefully about previous hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactams before starting. Serious, occasionally fatal reactions are more likely with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity and in atopic people. Stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: careful enquiry should be made concerning previous hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactam agents
These reactions are more likely to occur in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity and in atopic individuals.
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin therapy must be discontinued and appropriate alternative therapy instituted.

items.t: Avoid if infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is suspected: morbilliform rash.

src.q: Amoxicillin should be avoided if infectious mononucleosis is suspected since the occurrence of a morbilliform rash has been associated with this condition following the use of amoxicillin.

items.t: Convulsions may occur with impaired renal function, high doses or predisposing factors (history of seizures, treated epilepsy, meningeal disorders).

src.q: Convulsions may occur in patients with impaired renal function or in those receiving high doses or in patients with predisposing factors (e.g. history of seizures, treated epilepsy or meningeal disorders

items.t: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES), mainly in children: protracted vomiting 1-4 hours after a dose without skin or respiratory allergy signs; severe cases can progress to shock.

src.q: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES) has been reported mainly in children receiving amoxicillin
There have been severe cases including progression to shock.

items.t: Hypersensitivity can progress to Kounis syndrome (allergic reaction that can cause myocardial infarction); chest pain with an allergic reaction may be a presenting symptom.

src.q: Hypersensitivity reactions can also progress to Kounis syndrome, a serious allergic reaction that can result in myocardial infarction

items.t: Consider antibiotic-associated colitis in anyone with diarrhoea during or after treatment; if it occurs stop amoxicillin. Anti-peristaltic medicines are contraindicated in this situation.

src.q: Should antibiotic-associated colitis occur, amoxicillin should immediately be discontinued, a physician consulted and an appropriate therapy initiated.
Anti-peristaltic medicinal products are contra-indicated in this situation.

items.t: Renal impairment: adjust dose to degree of impairment (see Renal).

src.q: In patients with renal impairment, the dose should be adjusted according to the degree of impairment

items.t: High doses: keep adequate fluid intake and urine output to reduce the risk of crystalluria; check patency of bladder catheters.

src.q: During the administration of high doses of amoxicillin, it is advisable to maintain adequate fluid intake and urinary output in order to reduce the possibility of amoxicillin crystalluria.

items.t: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can follow treatment of Lyme disease; it is common and usually self-limiting.

src.q: Patients should be reassured that this is a common and usually self-limiting consequence of antibiotic treatment of Lyme disease.

items.t: Not suitable for some infections unless the pathogen is known or very likely to be susceptible, particularly UTIs and severe ear, nose and throat infections.

src.q: This particularly applies when considering the treatment of patients with urinary tract infections and severe infections of the ear, nose and throat.

items.t: Urine glucose: use enzymatic glucose oxidase methods (false positives with chemical methods). May distort oestriol assays in pregnancy.

src.q: It is recommended that when testing for the presence of glucose in urine during amoxicillin treatment, enzymatic glucose oxidase methods should be used.
The presence of amoxicillin may distort assay results for oestriol in pregnant women.

items.t: Suspension contains sorbitol: patients with rare hereditary fructose intolerance should not take it. Contains sodium benzoate, which may increase the risk of jaundice in newborn babies.

src.q: This medicinal product contains sorbitol. Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.
May increase the risk of jaundice in newborn babies.

items.t: Warfarin / acenocoumarol (oral anticoagulants): raised INR reported. If used together, carefully monitor prothrombin time/INR when amoxicillin is added or stopped; anticoagulant dose may need adjusting.

src.q: in the literature there are cases of increased international normalised ratio in patients maintained on acenocoumarol or warfarin and prescribed a course of amoxicillin
If co-administration is necessary, the prothrombin time or international normalised ratio should be carefully monitored with the addition or withdrawal of amoxicillin.

items.t: Methotrexate: penicillins may reduce methotrexate excretion and increase toxicity. SPS: for short penicillin courses (up to 10 days) consider using with caution and monitor for toxicity (sore throat, bruising, bleeding).

src.q: Penicillins may reduce the excretion of methotrexate causing a potential increase in toxicity.
If the duration of penicillin is short (up to 10 days), consider using with caution and advise to monitor for signs of toxicity.

items.t: Probenecid: concomitant use not recommended (raises and prolongs amoxicillin levels).

src.q: Probenecid Concomitant use of probenecid is not recommended.

items.t: Allopurinol: increased likelihood of allergic skin reactions.

src.q: Concurrent administration of allopurinol during treatment with amoxicillin can increase the likelihood of allergic skin reactions.

items.t: Tetracyclines and other bacteriostatic drugs may interfere with amoxicillin's bactericidal effect.

src.q: Tetracyclines and other bacteriostatic drugs may interfere with the bactericidal effects of amoxicillin.

items.t: Oral typhoid vaccine is inactivated by antibacterials.

src.q: The oral typhoid vaccine is inactivated by antibacterials.

items.t: GFR > 30 ml/min: no adjustment.

src.q: greater than 30 No adjustment necessary No adjustment necessary

items.t: GFR 10 to 30 ml/min: adults and children ≥ 40 kg maximum 500 mg twice daily; children < 40 kg 15 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg twice daily).

src.q: 10 to 30 Maximum 500 mg twice daily 15 mg/kg given twice daily (maximum 500 mg twice daily)

items.t: GFR < 10 ml/min: adults and children ≥ 40 kg maximum 500 mg/day; children < 40 kg 15 mg/kg as a single dose (maximum 500 mg). For children < 40 kg parenteral therapy is preferred in most cases.

src.q: less than 10 Maximum 500 mg/day 15 mg/kg given as a single dose (maximum 500 mg)
In the majority of cases, parenteral therapy is preferred.

items.t: Haemodialysis: adults/children > 40 kg 500 mg every 24 h, plus one extra 500 mg dose before and another 500 mg dose after dialysis. Children < 40 kg 15 mg/kg/day once daily (maximum 500 mg), plus 15 mg/kg before and after dialysis. Peritoneal dialysis: maximum 500 mg/day.

src.q: Haemodialysis Adults and children over 40 kg 500 mg every 24 h Prior to haemodialysis one additional dose of 500 mg should be administered.
Children under 40 kg 15 mg/kg/day given as a single daily dose (maximum 500 mg).
In patients receiving peritoneal dialysis Amoxicillin maximum 500 mg/day.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: dose with caution and monitor hepatic function at regular intervals.

src.q: Hepatic impairment Dose with caution and monitor hepatic function at regular intervals

items.t: SmPC: limited human data do not indicate an increased risk of congenital malformations; may be used when potential benefits outweigh potential risks.

src.q: Limited data on the use of amoxicillin during pregnancy in humans do not indicate an increased risk of congenital malformations.
Amoxicillin may be used in pregnancy when the potential benefits outweigh the potential risks associated with treatment.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): amoxicillin can be taken in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concerns that penicillin use will harm the baby; no extra monitoring for major birth defects needed.

src.q: Amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, and penicillin V can be taken in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
There are no concerns that use of a penicillin antibiotic in pregnancy will harm your baby.

items.t: SmPC: excreted in breast milk in small amounts (possible sensitisation, diarrhoea and mucosal fungal infection in the infant); use only after benefit/risk assessment.

src.q: Amoxicillin is excreted into breast milk in small quantities with the possible risk of sensitisation.
Amoxicillin should only be used during breast-feeding after benefit/risk assessment by the physician in charge.

items.t: SPS: all penicillins can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring; amoxicillin is a preferred choice. Monitor the infant for GI disturbance, oral candida, hypersensitivity (rash, breathing problems), nausea, irritability and drowsiness.

src.q: All penicillin antibiotics can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring.
the broad-spectrum penicillins, such as amoxicillin and ampicillin, are the preferred choices
As a precaution, monitor for gastro-intestinal disturbances, oral candida infection, hypersensitivity reactions (including rashes or breathing problems), nausea, irritability, and drowsiness.

items.t: No human fertility data; animal reproductive studies showed no effect on fertility.

src.q: There are no data on the effects of amoxicillin on fertility in humans. Reproductive studies in animals have shown no effects on fertility.

items.t: Common: diarrhoea, nausea, skin rash. Uncommon: vomiting, urticaria, pruritus.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are diarrhoea, nausea and skin rash.
*Common Diarrhoea and nausea *Uncommon Vomiting
*Common Skin rash *Uncommon Urticaria and pruritus

items.t: Severe allergic reactions (angioedema, anaphylaxis, serum sickness, hypersensitivity vasculitis): stop amoxicillin and start appropriate alternative therapy.

src.q: Severe allergic reactions, including angioneurotic oedema, anaphylaxis, serum sickness and hypersensitivity vasculitis
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin therapy must be discontinued and appropriate alternative therapy instituted.

items.t: Severe skin reactions (erythema multiforme, SJS, TEN, bullous/exfoliative dermatitis, AGEP, DRESS). AGEP requires stopping and contraindicates future use.

src.q: Skin reactions such as erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, bullous and exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)
This reaction requires amoxicillin discontinuation and contra-indicates any subsequent administration.

items.t: Antibiotic-associated colitis (including pseudomembranous colitis): stop immediately and seek medical review.

src.q: Should antibiotic-associated colitis occur, amoxicillin should immediately be discontinued, a physician consulted and an appropriate therapy initiated.

items.t: Very rare: hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice; reversible leucopenia (including severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis), thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia; convulsions; interstitial nephritis; crystalluria (including acute renal injury).

src.q: Very rare Hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice.
Reversible leucopenia (including severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis), reversible thrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia.
Very rare Interstitial nephritis Not known Crystalluria (including acute renal injury)

items.t: Prolonged therapy: periodic assessment of renal, hepatic and haematopoietic function is advisable.

src.q: Periodic assessment of organ system functions; including renal, hepatic and haematopoietic function is advisable during prolonged therapy.

items.t: With oral anticoagulants: monitor prothrombin time/INR when amoxicillin is started or stopped.

src.q: Appropriate monitoring should be undertaken when anticoagulants are prescribed concomitantly.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: monitor hepatic function at regular intervals.

src.q: Hepatically impaired patients should be dosed with caution and hepatic function monitored at regular intervals.

items.t: Stop if an allergic reaction, AGEP or antibiotic-associated colitis occurs.

src.q: If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin therapy must be discontinued
This reaction requires amoxicillin discontinuation

items.t: Oral. Absorption is not affected by food.

src.q: Absorption of amoxicillin is unimpaired by food.

items.t: Capsules: swallow with water without opening. Not suitable for patients who cannot swallow capsules; other oral forms are available.

src.q: Swallow with water without opening capsule.
Capsules are not suitable for the treatment of patients who cannot swallow capsules

items.t: Suspension: reconstitute before use (84 ml water for 100 ml); after reconstitution store at 2-8 °C in a refrigerator for up to 7 days.

src.q: 84ml to reconstitute 100ml of 125/5ml Amoxicillin Sugar Free Suspension
Reconstituted Suspension: Store up to 7 days at 2°C - 8°C in a refrigerator.

items.t: Report any rash, swelling, breathing difficulty or chest pain with allergy symptoms straight away; treatment must be stopped.

src.q: Presenting symptoms of such reactions can include chest pain occurring in association with an allergic reaction to amoxicillin

items.t: Report diarrhoea during or after the course (possible antibiotic-associated colitis).

src.q: it is important to consider this diagnosis in patients who present with diarrhoea during, or subsequent to, the administration of any antibiotics

items.t: Side effects such as dizziness, allergic reactions or convulsions may affect driving or using machines.

src.q: undesirable effects may occur (e.g. allergic reactions, dizziness, convulsions), which may influence the ability to drive and use machines

formulations.label: Film-coated tablets
formulations.strengths: 10 mg (the strength covered by the 10 mg film-coated tablet SmPC used here)

src.q: Each film-coated tablet contains 10 mg atorvastatin (as atorvastatin calcium trihydrate).

formulations.label: Chewable tablets
formulations.strengths: 10 mg (the strength covered by the 10 mg chewable tablet SmPC used here)
formulations.note: Same indications, doses and warnings as the film-coated tablets; can be chewed or swallowed whole. Contains aspartame (phenylalanine).

src.q: Each chewable tablet contains 10 mg atorvastatin (as atorvastatin calcium trihydrate).
Lipitor chewable tablets can be chewed or swallowed whole with a drink of water
Lipitor chewable tablet contains aspartame which is a source of phenylalanine. May be harmful for people with phenylketonuria.

items.t: Adjunct to diet to lower total-C, LDL-C, apolipoprotein B and triglycerides in primary hypercholesterolaemia (including heterozygous familial) or mixed hyperlipidaemia, in adults and children aged 10 years or older, when diet and other measures are not enough.

src.q: in adults, adolescents and children aged 10 years or older with primary hypercholesterolaemia including familial hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous variant) or combined (mixed) hyperlipidaemia

items.t: Adults with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, as an adjunct to other lipid-lowering treatment (e.g. LDL apheresis) or if such treatment is unavailable.

src.q: Lipitor is also indicated to reduce total-C and LDL-C in adults with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia

items.t: Prevention of cardiovascular events in adults estimated to be at high risk of a first cardiovascular event, alongside correction of other risk factors.

src.q: Prevention of cardiovascular events in adult patients estimated to have a high risk for a first cardiovascular event

items.t: Children: use only by physicians experienced in treating paediatric hyperlipidaemia, with regular re-evaluation.

src.q: Paediatric use should only be carried out by physicians experienced in the treatment of paediatric hyperlipidaemia

items.t: General: usual starting dose 10 mg once a day; adjust at intervals of 4 weeks or more; maximum 80 mg once a day. Patient should follow a cholesterol-lowering diet.

src.q: The usual starting dose is 10 mg once a day. Adjustment of dose should be made at intervals of 4 weeks or more. The maximum dose is 80 mg once a day.

items.t: Primary hypercholesterolaemia and mixed hyperlipidaemia: most patients are controlled on 10 mg once a day; maximum response usually within 4 weeks.

src.q: The majority of patients are controlled with Lipitor 10 mg once a day.

items.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (adults): start 10 mg daily, adjust every 4 weeks to 40 mg daily; then either increase to a maximum of 80 mg daily or combine 40 mg once daily with a bile acid sequestrant.

src.q: Patients should be started with Lipitor 10 mg daily. Doses should be individualised and adjusted every 4 weeks to 40 mg daily.
either the dose may be increased to a maximum of 80 mg daily or a bile acid sequestrant may be combined with 40 mg atorvastatin once daily

items.t: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: 10 to 80 mg daily (limited data), as an adjunct to other lipid-lowering treatment.

src.q: The dose of atorvastatin in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is 10 to 80 mg daily

items.t: Prevention of cardiovascular disease: 10 mg/day was used in primary prevention trials; higher doses may be needed to reach guideline cholesterol levels.

src.q: In the primary prevention trials the dose was 10 mg/day. Higher doses may be necessary in order to attain (LDL-) cholesterol levels according to current guidelines.

items.t: Maximum 20 mg/day with elbasvir/grazoprevir or letermovir; not recommended with letermovir plus ciclosporin.

src.q: the dose of atorvastatin should not exceed 20 mg/day
Use of atorvastatin is not recommended in patients taking letermovir co-administered with ciclosporin

items.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, 10 years and above: start 10 mg per day; may increase to 80 mg daily by response and tolerability, adjusting at intervals of 4 weeks or more.

src.q: For patients with Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia aged 10 years and above, the recommended starting dose of atorvastatin is 10 mg per day
The dose may be increased to 80 mg daily, according to the response and tolerability.

items.t: Not indicated below 10 years of age; no dose recommendation can be made (only limited data in ages 6 to 10).

src.q: Atorvastatin is not indicated in the treatment of patients below the age of 10 years.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to atorvastatin or any excipient.

src.q: with hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent serum transaminases above 3 times the upper limit of normal.

src.q: with active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases exceeding 3 times the upper limit of normal

items.t: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, and women of child-bearing potential not using appropriate contraception.

src.q: during pregnancy, while breast-feeding and in women of child-bearing potential not using appropriate contraceptive measures

items.t: With the hepatitis C antivirals glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.

src.q: treated with the hepatitis C antivirals glecaprevir/pibrentasvir

items.t: Muscle effects: can cause myalgia, myositis and myopathy that may progress to rhabdomyolysis. Prescribe with caution if there are pre-disposing factors for rhabdomyolysis.

src.q: may in rare occasions affect the skeletal muscle and cause myalgia, myositis, and myopathy that may progress to rhabdomyolysis
Atorvastatin should be prescribed with caution in patients with pre-disposing factors for rhabdomyolysis.

items.t: Measure CK before starting in: renal impairment, hypothyroidism, personal/family history of hereditary muscle disorders, previous muscle toxicity with a statin or fibrate, previous liver disease and/or substantial alcohol use; consider in people over 70. Do not start if baseline CK is above 5 times ULN.

src.q: A CK level should be measured before starting statin treatment in the following situations: - Renal impairment - Hypothyroidism
If CK levels are significantly elevated (> 5 times ULN) at baseline, treatment should not be started.

items.t: Use with caution in people who drink substantial quantities of alcohol and/or have a history of liver disease.

src.q: Lipitor should be used with caution in patients who consume substantial quantities of alcohol and/or have a history of liver disease.

items.t: After recent stroke or TIA, 80 mg was linked to more haemorrhagic stroke; in people with prior haemorrhagic stroke or lacunar infarct, the benefit-risk of 80 mg is uncertain and haemorrhagic stroke risk should be carefully considered.

src.q: For patients with prior haemorrhagic stroke or lacunar infarct, the balance of risks and benefits of atorvastatin 80 mg is uncertain

items.t: Systemic fusidic acid: atorvastatin must not be given with it or within 7 days of stopping it; stop the statin during fusidic acid treatment.

src.q: Atorvastatin must not be co-administered with systemic formulations of fusidic acid or within 7 days of stopping fusidic acid treatment.

items.t: Statins can raise blood glucose; people at risk of diabetes (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, BMI>30kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension) should be monitored. This is not a reason to stop the statin.

src.q: Patients at risk (fasting glucose 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L, BMI>30kg/m2, raised triglycerides, hypertension) should be monitored both clinically and biochemically according to national guidelines.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: statins may cause or worsen myasthenia gravis or ocular myasthenia; stop if symptoms get worse. MHRA: advise patients with myasthenia gravis to watch for worsening symptoms.

src.q: Lipitor should be discontinued in case of aggravation of symptoms.
advise patients with pre-existing myasthenia gravis to be alert to aggravation of symptoms while taking a statin

items.t: Interstitial lung disease has been reported; stop the statin if it is suspected.

src.q: If it is suspected a patient has developed interstitial lung disease, statin therapy should be discontinued.

items.t: Contains lactose: people with rare hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take it.

src.q: Lipitor contains lactose.

items.t: Chewable tablets contain aspartame, a source of phenylalanine: may be harmful for people with phenylketonuria.

src.q: Lipitor chewable tablet contains aspartame which is a source of phenylalanine. May be harmful for people with phenylketonuria.

items.t: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin): avoid if possible. If unavoidable, consider lower starting and maximum atorvastatin doses with clinical monitoring.

src.q: should be avoided if possible. In cases where co-administration of these medicinal products with atorvastatin cannot be avoided lower starting and maximum doses of atorvastatin should be considered

items.t: Clarithromycin: SPS advises avoiding it with atorvastatin; consider pausing atorvastatin for the course; if both must be used, maximum atorvastatin 20 mg daily. MHRA (2008 article) also says do not exceed 20 mg atorvastatin daily with clarithromycin.

src.q: Avoid the use of clarithromycin with atorvastatin and use a non-interacting antibiotic if possible.
Use a lower dose of atorvastatin (maximum 20mg daily) if concurrent administration is unavoidable.
Clarithromycin: do not exceed 20 mg atorvastatin daily

items.t: Warfarin / coumarin anticoagulants: check prothrombin time before starting atorvastatin and often enough early on; repeat if the atorvastatin dose is changed or stopped. MHRA: monitor INR before starting and regularly, especially with dose changes.

src.q: prothrombin time should be determined before starting atorvastatin in patients taking coumarin anticoagulants
Monitor INR before starting treatment and regularly during treatment, especially with dose changes

items.t: CYP3A4 inducers such as St John's Wort can reduce atorvastatin levels.

src.q: inducers of cytochrome P450 3A (e.g. efavirenz, rifampin, St. John's Wort) can lead to variable reductions in plasma concentrations of atorvastatin

items.t: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. erythromycin, diltiazem, verapamil, fluconazole): consider a lower maximum dose and monitor.

src.q: a lower maximum dose of atorvastatin should be considered and appropriate clinical monitoring of the patient is recommended when concomitantly used with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors

items.t: Amlodipine and magnesium/aluminium hydroxide antacid: small changes in atorvastatin exposure; no specific recommendation in the SmPC.

src.q: Amlodipine 10 mg, single dose 80 mg, SD 1.18 No specific recommendation.

items.t: Avoid large quantities of grapefruit juice.

src.q: Concomitant intake of large quantities of grapefruit juice and atorvastatin is not recommended.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Renal impairment is a reason to measure CK before starting.

src.q: Renal impairment No adjustment of dose is required
A CK level should be measured before starting statin treatment in the following situations: - Renal impairment

items.t: SPS (all statins): if eGFR is less than 30 mL/min/1.73m2, check the dose with a renal specialist.

src.q: If eGFR less than 30mL/min/1.73m2 check dose with renal specialist.

items.t: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; contraindicated in active liver disease.

src.q: Lipitor should be used with caution in patients with hepatic impairment
Lipitor is contraindicated in patients with active liver disease

items.t: SPS: statins are not recommended in unexplained active liver disease or unexplained ALT/AST above 3 x ULN. In stable/chronic liver disease they can be used with caution; consider a lower starting dose such as atorvastatin 20 mg daily with gradual increase.

src.q: Statins are not recommended in patients with: unexplained active liver disease or, unexplained elevations of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) that are greater than 3 x the upper limit of normal (ULN).
consider a lower dose of a high-intensity statin, such as atorvastatin 20 mg daily or rosuvastatin 10 mg daily, with gradual dose escalation

items.t: Contraindicated in pregnancy; do not use in women who are pregnant, trying to become pregnant or who suspect pregnancy. Suspend for the duration of pregnancy.

src.q: Lipitor is contraindicated during pregnancy
Treatment with Lipitor should be suspended for the duration of pregnancy

items.t: BUMPS: statins are usually avoided in pregnancy; as a precaution most women are advised to stop statins three months before trying to conceive and during pregnancy.

src.q: Statins are usually avoided in pregnancy if possible as there is not enough information to say they are safe for the baby.
As a precaution, most women are advised to stop taking statins for three months before trying to conceive, and during pregnancy.

items.t: SmPC: contraindicated during breastfeeding; women taking atorvastatin should not breastfeed.

src.q: Atorvastatin is contraindicated during breast-feeding

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): atorvastatin is a preferred statin and can be used with caution while breastfeeding, with infant monitoring (feeding, growth, weight gain; diarrhoea, constipation, irritability). Postponing therapy until after exclusive breastfeeding is preferred if possible.

src.q: Atorvastatin can be used with caution while breastfeeding, but infant monitoring is still required.
if possible, the preferred option would be to postpone lipid-lowering therapy until after the exclusive breastfeeding period

items.t: Women of child-bearing potential should use appropriate contraception during treatment.

src.q: Women of child-bearing potential should use appropriate contraceptive measures during treatment

items.t: No effect on male or female fertility in animal studies.

src.q: In animal studies atorvastatin had no effect on male or female fertility

items.t: Common: nasopharyngitis, allergic reactions, hyperglycaemia, headache, pharyngolaryngeal pain, epistaxis, constipation, flatulence, dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhoea, myalgia, arthralgia, pain in extremity, muscle spasms, joint swelling, back pain, abnormal liver function tests, raised CK.

src.q: Common: nasopharyngitis.
Common: constipation, flatulence, dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhoea.
Common: myalgia, arthralgia, pain in extremity, muscle spasms, joint swelling, back pain.
Common: liver function test abnormal, blood creatine kinase increased.

items.t: Rhabdomyolysis / myopathy: stop if CK is above 10 x ULN or rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed or suspected; stop if CK above 5 x ULN with muscle symptoms.

src.q: Atorvastatin must be discontinued if clinically significant elevation of CK levels (> 10 x ULN) occur, or if rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed or suspected.
If these levels are found to be significantly elevated (> 5 times ULN), treatment should be stopped.

items.t: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (very rare): persistent proximal weakness and raised CK despite stopping the statin.

src.q: There have been very rare reports of an immune mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) during or after treatment with some statins.

items.t: Liver injury: hepatitis (uncommon), cholestasis (rare), hepatic failure (very rare). If transaminases above 3 x ULN persist, reduce dose or stop.

src.q: Uncommon: hepatitis. Rare: cholestasis. Very rare: hepatic failure.
Should an increase in transaminases of greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) persist, reduction of dose or withdrawal of Lipitor is recommended

items.t: Rare severe skin reactions and angioedema (angioneurotic oedema, bullous dermatitis including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis); anaphylaxis very rare.

src.q: Rare: angioneurotic oedema, dermatitis bullous including erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis

items.t: Interstitial lung disease: stop the statin if suspected.

src.q: If it is suspected a patient has developed interstitial lung disease, statin therapy should be discontinued.

items.t: Liver function tests before starting and periodically thereafter.

src.q: Liver function tests should be performed before the initiation of treatment and periodically thereafter.

items.t: SPS before starting: ALT or AST, blood pressure, BMI, lipid profile (non-fasting), serum creatinine or eGFR, HbA1c. Consider CK if persistent muscle symptoms and TSH if thyroid symptoms.

src.q: Before starting Required Baseline ALT or AST Blood pressure Body mass index

items.t: SPS: ALT or AST and lipids between months 2 and 3; then consider annually (ALT/AST after the first year only if indicated).

src.q: Required Between months 2 and 3 ALT or AST
Annually ALT or AST · repeat after first year only if indicated

items.t: Measure CK if muscle pain, cramps or weakness occur; do not measure after strenuous exercise.

src.q: If such symptoms occur whilst a patient is receiving treatment with atorvastatin, their CK levels should be measured.

items.t: SPS: stop or do not start a statin if ALT or AST are greater than 3 times ULN, or if CK is greater than 5 times ULN.

src.q: Stop existing statin or do not initiate new statin if ALT or AST are greater than 3 times upper limit of normal (ULN).
Stop existing statin or do not initiate statin if creatine kinase (CK) greater than 5 times ULN.

items.t: Oral, once daily at any time of day, with or without food.

src.q: Each daily dose of atorvastatin is given all at once and may be given at any time of day with or without food.

items.t: Chewable tablets can be chewed or swallowed whole with water, at any time of day, with or without food.

src.q: Lipitor chewable tablets can be chewed or swallowed whole with a drink of water, and can be taken at any time of day, with or without food.

items.t: Report muscle pain, cramps or weakness promptly, especially with malaise or fever.

src.q: Patients must be asked to promptly report muscle pain, cramps, or weakness especially if accompanied by malaise or fever.

items.t: Avoid large quantities of grapefruit juice.

src.q: Concomitant intake of large quantities of grapefruit juice and atorvastatin is not recommended.

items.t: Women who could become pregnant should use contraception; stop and seek advice if pregnancy is planned or occurs.

src.q: Women of child-bearing potential should use appropriate contraceptive measures during treatment

formulations.label: Chewable tablets 1500 mg (calcium only, no vitamin D)
formulations.strengths: Calcium carbonate 1500 mg (600 mg elemental calcium) per tablet
formulations.note: This entry covers the calcium-only product. Calcium carbonate products that also contain colecalciferol (vitamin D3) are different medicines and are not covered here.

src.q: Calcium carbonate: 1500mg equivalent to 600mg of elemental calcium
1. Name of the medicinal product Adcal 1500mg Chewable Tablets

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Supplementary source of calcium when requirements are high, and correction of dietary calcium deficiency.

src.q: recommended as a supplementary source of calcium when normal requirements are high and in the correction of calcium deficiency in the diet

items.t: Adjunct to specific osteoporosis treatments.

src.q: They can be used in osteoporosis therapy as an adjunct to more specific conventional treatments.

items.t: Phosphate binder in renal failure.

src.q: Adcal chewable tablets can be used as a phosphate binding agent in the management of renal failure.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions in the calcium carbonate SmPC.

items.t: Adults and elderly: 2 chewable tablets per day (each tablet 600 mg elemental calcium), preferably one in the morning and one in the evening.

src.q: Dietary deficiency and as an adjunct in osteoporosis therapy; 2 chewable tablets per day, preferably one tablet each morning and evening.
equivalent to 600mg of elemental calcium

items.t: Dose adjusted for the individual patient according to serum phosphate.

src.q: For use in binding phosphate in the management of renal failure in patients on renal dialysis, the dose should be adjusted for the individual patient and is dependent on the serum phosphate level.

items.t: The SmPC gives the same dose for adults, elderly and children (2 chewable tablets per day) and states no lower age limit.

src.q: Adults, elderly and children Dietary deficiency and as an adjunct in osteoporosis therapy; 2 chewable tablets per day

items.t: Hypercalcaemia (e.g. from myeloma, bone metastases, other malignant bone disease, sarcoidosis).

src.q: Absolute contra-indications are hypercalcaemia resulting for example from myeloma, bone metastases or other malignant bone disease, sarcoidosis

items.t: Primary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin D overdosage.

src.q: primary hyperparathyroidism and vitamin D overdosage

items.t: Severe renal failure not treated by renal dialysis.

src.q: Severe renal failure untreated by renal dialysis.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to any tablet ingredient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to any of the tablet ingredients.

items.t: Relative contraindications: osteoporosis due to prolonged immobilisation, renal stones, severe hypercalciuria.

src.q: Relative contra-indications are osteoporosis due to prolonged immobilisation, renal stones, severe hypercalciuria.

items.t: Mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria: supervise carefully and check plasma calcium and urinary calcium excretion periodically.

src.q: Patients with mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria should be supervised carefully.
Periodic checks of plasma calcium levels and urinary calcium excretion should be made

items.t: History of renal stones: measure urinary calcium excretion to exclude hypercalciuria.

src.q: In patients with a history of renal stones urinary calcium excretion should be measured to exclude hypercalciuria.

items.t: Allow for calcium and vitamin D from other sources.

src.q: Allowances should be made for calcium and vitamin D supplements from other sources.

items.t: Should not be taken by people with hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicine.

items.t: Calcium reduces absorption of thyroxine (levothyroxine), quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin), tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride and iron. Calcium carbonate SmPC: allow at least 4 hours before taking the calcium.

src.q: Calcium salts may reduce the absorption of thyroxine, bisphosphonates, sodium fluoride, quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics or iron.
It is advisable to allow a minimum period of four hours before taking the calcium.

items.t: Levothyroxine SmPC: calcium salts and antacids may reduce levothyroxine absorption; separate by 4-5 hours.

src.q: Absorption of levothyroxine (thyroxine) possibly reduced by antacids, calcium salts
(administration should be separated by 4-5 hours)

items.t: Ciprofloxacin SmPC: give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after calcium-containing products.

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron)
ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine SmPC: antacids may reduce hydroxychloroquine absorption; keep a 4-hour interval.

src.q: antacids may reduce absorption of hydroxychloroquine so it is advised that a 4 hour interval be observed between hydroxychloroquine sulfate and antacid dosing

items.t: Iron: if both are needed, take at different times.

src.q: If Adcal and iron supplements are both required to be administered to the patient, they should be taken at different times

items.t: Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion: consider the risk of hypercalcaemia.

src.q: The risk of hypercalcaemia should be considered in patients taking thiazide diuretics since these drugs can reduce urinary calcium excretion.

items.t: Digitalis/cardiac glycosides: avoid hypercalcaemia; strict medical supervision and, if needed, ECG and calcium monitoring.

src.q: Hypercalcaemia must be avoided in digitalised patients.
Strict medical supervision is needed and, if necessary monitoring of ECG and calcium.

items.t: Systemic corticosteroids reduce calcium absorption.

src.q: Calcium absorption is reduced in patients receiving systemic corticosteroid therapy.

items.t: Foods containing oxalic acid, phosphate or phytinic acid may reduce calcium absorption.

src.q: Certain foods (e.g. those containing oxalic acid, phosphate or phytinic acid) may reduce the absorption of calcium

items.t: Contraindicated in severe renal failure not treated by dialysis.

src.q: Severe renal failure untreated by renal dialysis.

items.t: Mild to moderate renal failure: supervise carefully; check plasma calcium and urinary calcium periodically. (No eGFR/CrCl thresholds given.)

src.q: Patients with mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria should be supervised carefully.

items.t: On renal dialysis: can be used as a phosphate binder, dose by serum phosphate.

src.q: the dose should be adjusted for the individual patient and is dependent on the serum phosphate level

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment advice in the calcium carbonate SmPC.

items.t: Use in pregnancy under the direction of a physician. Calcium needs are higher; allow for calcium from other sources.

src.q: During pregnancy and lactation treatment with Adcal should be under the direction of a physician.
allowances should be made for availability of these agents from other sources

items.t: Calcium carbonate SmPC: use during lactation under the direction of a physician.

src.q: During pregnancy and lactation treatment with Adcal should be under the direction of a physician.

items.t: SPS: calcium carbonate can be used during breastfeeding at the doses used for heartburn and dyspepsia; no specific infant monitoring usually needed (calcium is a natural part of breast milk, poor oral bioavailability).

src.q: Calcium carbonate can be used during breastfeeding at recommended doses used for heartburn and dyspepsia
calcium is a natural component of breast milk

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception statements in the calcium carbonate SmPC.

items.t: No common or very common effects listed. Rarely: mild GI upset (constipation, flatulence, nausea, gastric pain, diarrhoea).

src.q: The use of calcium supplements has, rarely, given rise to mild gastro-intestinal disturbances, such as constipation, flatulence, nausea, gastric pain, diarrhoea.

items.t: Hypercalcaemia is not expected from overdose except with excessive vitamin D; treat by lowering serum calcium (high fluid intake, low calcium diet).

src.q: would not be expected to cause hypercalcaemia except in patients treated with excessive doses of vitamin D
Treatment should be aimed at lowering serum calcium levels through a high fluid intake and low calcium diet.

items.t: History of renal stones: measure urinary calcium excretion before treatment to exclude hypercalciuria.

src.q: In patients with a history of renal stones urinary calcium excretion should be measured to exclude hypercalciuria.

items.t: Long-term treatment: monitor serum and urinary calcium and kidney function. Mild to moderate renal failure or mild hypercalciuria: periodic plasma and urinary calcium.

src.q: With long-term treatment it is advisable to monitor serum and urinary calcium levels and kidney function

items.t: Reduce or stop treatment temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5 mmol/24 hours.

src.q: reduce or stop treatment temporarily if urinary calcium exceeds 7.5mmol/24 hours

items.t: Chew the tablets (do not swallow whole). Take just before, during or immediately after a meal.

src.q: The tablets should be chewed, not swallowed whole and taken just prior to, during or immediately following a meal.

items.t: Chew each tablet with a meal; usual dose one in the morning and one in the evening.

src.q: preferably one tablet each morning and evening

items.t: Take levothyroxine, quinolone antibiotics, tetracyclines, bisphosphonates or iron first and wait at least 4 hours before taking calcium.

src.q: It is advisable to allow a minimum period of four hours before taking the calcium.

items.t: Tell the prescriber about other calcium or vitamin D supplements.

src.q: Allowances should be made for calcium and vitamin D supplements from other sources.

formulations.note: Contains benzyl alcohol and sucrose (approx. 1.4 g per 5 mL). Use the graduated measuring spoon.

src.q: 5 mL suspension after reconstitution (1 measuring spoon) contains 250 mg ciprofloxacin.
Excipients with known effect: benzyl alcohol, sucrose.
Always use the graduated measuring spoon to obtain the dose for administering the suspension.
