items.t: Adults: lower respiratory tract infections due to Gram-negative bacteria (COPD exacerbations, cystic fibrosis/bronchiectasis infections, pneumonia), chronic suppurative otitis media, acute exacerbation of chronic sinusitis, uncomplicated acute cystitis, acute pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, bacterial prostatitis, gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis, epididymo-orchitis, PID, GI infections (e.g. travellers' diarrhoea), intra-abdominal infections, Gram-negative skin and soft tissue infections, malignant external otitis, bone and joint infections, meningococcal prophylaxis, inhalation anthrax; may be used in febrile neutropenia.

src.q: Lower respiratory tract infections due to Gram-negative bacteria o exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Acute pyelonephritis Complicated urinary tract infections Bacterial prostatitis Genital tract infections

Intra-abdominal infections Infections of the skin and soft tissue caused by Gram-negative bacteria Malignant external otitis Infections of the bones and joints Prophylaxis of invasive infections due to Neisseria meningitidis Inhalation anthrax

items.t: Children and adolescents: Pseudomonas broncho-pulmonary infection in cystic fibrosis, complicated UTI and acute pyelonephritis, inhalation anthrax; other severe infections when considered necessary.

src.q: Children and adolescents Broncho-pulmonary infections due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis Complicated urinary tract infections and acute pyelonephritis Inhalation anthrax

items.t: Only prescribe when other antibiotics commonly recommended for the infection are inappropriate (resistance, contraindication, side effects requiring stopping, or treatment failure). This applies to all indications (MHRA, January 2024).

src.q: this product must only be prescribed when other antibiotics that are commonly recommended for the infection are inappropriate. This applies to all indications listed below.
the UK indications for systemic fluoroquinolones have been updated so they must only be used in situations when other antibiotics, that are commonly recommended for the infection, are inappropriate

items.t: Do not prescribe for non-severe or self-limiting infections or non-bacterial conditions (e.g. non-bacterial chronic prostatitis).

src.q: fluoroquinolones should not be prescribed for non-severe or self-limiting infections, or non-bacterial conditions, for example non-bacterial (chronic) prostatitis

items.t: Children and adolescents: treatment should be initiated only by physicians experienced in cystic fibrosis and/or severe infections in children and adolescents.

src.q: Treatment should be initiated only by physicians who are experienced in the treatment of cystic fibrosis and/or severe infections in children and adolescents

items.t: Lower respiratory tract infections: 500 mg to 750 mg twice daily for 7 to 14 days.

src.q: Infections of the lower respiratory tract 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily 7 to 14 days

items.t: Acute exacerbation of chronic sinusitis; chronic suppurative otitis media: 500 mg to 750 mg twice daily for 7 to 14 days. Malignant external otitis: 750 mg twice daily for 28 days up to 3 months.

src.q: Chronic suppurative otitis media 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily 7 to 14 days
Malignant external otitis 750 mg twice daily 28 days up to 3 months

items.t: Uncomplicated cystitis: 250 mg to 500 mg twice daily for 3 days (pre-menopausal women: 500 mg single dose may be used). Complicated cystitis / uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. Complicated pyelonephritis: 500 mg to 750 mg twice daily for at least 10 days.

src.q: Uncomplicated cystitis 250 mg twice daily to 500 mg twice daily 3 days In pre-menopausal women, 500 mg single dose may be used
Complicated cystitis, Uncomplicated pyelonephritis 500 mg twice daily 7 days Complicated pyelonephritis 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily at least 10 days

items.t: Prostatitis: 500 mg to 750 mg twice daily for 2 to 4 weeks (acute) or 4 to 6 weeks (chronic).

src.q: Prostatitis 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily 2 to 4 weeks (acute) to 4 to 6 weeks (chronic)

items.t: Gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis: 500 mg single dose. Epididymo-orchitis and PID: 500 mg to 750 mg twice daily for at least 14 days.

src.q: Gonococcal uretritis and cervicitis 500 mg as a single dose 1 day (single dose)
Epididymo-orchitis and pelvic inflammatory diseases 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily at least 14 days

items.t: Bacterial diarrhoea (Shigella other than S. dysenteriae type 1, severe travellers' diarrhoea): 500 mg twice daily for 1 day; S. dysenteriae type 1: 5 days; Vibrio cholerae: 3 days; typhoid fever: 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. Intra-abdominal (Gram-negative): 500-750 mg twice daily for 5 to 14 days.

src.q: empirical treatment of severe travellers' diarrhoea 500 mg twice daily 1 day
Diarrhoea caused by Shigella dysenteriae type 1 500 mg twice daily 5 days Diarrhoea caused by Vibrio cholerae 500 mg twice daily 3 days Typhoid fever 500 mg twice daily 7 days
Intra-abdominal infections due to Gram-negative bacteria 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily 5 to 14 days

items.t: Skin and soft tissue infections: 500-750 mg twice daily for 7 to 14 days. Bone and joint infections: 500-750 mg twice daily, maximum 3 months.

src.q: Infections of the skin and soft tissue 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily 7 to 14 days Bone and joint infections 500 mg twice daily to 750 mg twice daily max. of 3 months

items.t: Meningococcal prophylaxis: 500 mg single dose. Inhalation anthrax (post-exposure prophylaxis and treatment, oral): 500 mg twice daily for 60 days from confirmed exposure. Febrile neutropenia: 500-750 mg twice daily with other antibacterials for the whole period of neutropenia.

src.q: meningitidis 500 mg as a single dose 1 day (single dose)
500 mg twice daily 60 days from the confirmation of Bacillus anthracis exposure
Therapy should be continued over the entire period of neutropenia

items.t: Elderly: dose according to infection severity and creatinine clearance.

src.q: Elderly patients should receive a dose selected according to the severity of the infection and the patient's creatinine clearance.

items.t: Cystic fibrosis: 20 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 750 mg per dose) for 10 to 14 days. Other severe infections: 20 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 750 mg per dose).

src.q: Cystic fibrosis 20 mg/kg body weight twice daily with a maximum of 750 mg per dose. 10 to 14 days
Other severe infections 20 mg/kg body weight twice daily with a maximum of 750 mg per dose.

items.t: Complicated UTI and pyelonephritis: 10 mg/kg to 20 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 750 mg per dose) for 10 to 21 days; consider only when other treatments cannot be used.

src.q: Complicated urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis 10 mg/kg body weight twice daily to 20 mg/kg body weight twice daily with a maximum of 750 mg per dose. 10 to 21 days
Ciprofloxacin treatment of urinary tract infections should be considered when other treatments cannot be used

items.t: Inhalation anthrax: 10 mg/kg to 15 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg per dose) for 60 days from confirmed exposure.

src.q: 10 mg/kg body weight twice daily to 15 mg/kg body weight twice daily with a maximum of 500 mg per dose. 60 days from the confirmation of Bacillus anthracis exposure

items.t: Arthropathy risk: start only after careful benefit/risk evaluation; arthropathy occurs commonly in children. CF trials included ages 5-17 (limited data 1-5 years). Dosing with renal/hepatic impairment not studied in children.

src.q: Treatment should be initiated only after a careful benefit/risk evaluation, due to possible adverse events related to joints and/or surrounding tissue
In children, arthropathy is reported to occur commonly
Dosing in children with impaired renal and/or hepatic function has not been studied.

items.t: Suspension contains benzyl alcohol: in children under 3 years do not use for longer than one week (gasping syndrome risk in young children and neonates).

src.q: In young children (less than 3 years old), Ciproxin oral suspension should therefore not be used for longer than one week.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin, other quinolones or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, to other quinolones or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Concomitant tizanidine.

src.q: Concomitant administration of ciprofloxacin and tizanidine

items.t: Prolonged, disabling and potentially irreversible serious reactions (musculoskeletal, nervous, psychiatric, senses) can occur regardless of age or risk factors. Stop at the first sign of any serious adverse reaction; patient should contact the prescriber.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin should be discontinued immediately at the first signs or symptoms of any serious adverse reaction and patients should be advised to contact their prescriber for advice
fluoroquinolones can cause long-lasting (up to months or years), disabling and potentially irreversible side effects, sometimes affecting multiple body systems and senses

items.t: Avoid in patients who had serious adverse reactions to a quinolone or fluoroquinolone before; only start if no alternative and after careful benefit/risk assessment.

src.q: The use of ciprofloxacin should be avoided in patients who have experienced serious adverse reactions in the past when using quinolone or fluoroquinolone containing products
avoid fluoroquinolone use in patients who have previously had serious adverse reactions with a quinolone antibiotic

items.t: Tendinitis/tendon rupture (often Achilles, can be bilateral) from 48 hours up to months after stopping. Higher risk: older patients (MHRA: over 60), renal impairment, solid organ transplant, corticosteroid use. Generally do not use with a history of quinolone-related tendon disease. Stop at first sign of tendinitis.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin should generally not be used in patients with a history of tendon disease/disorder related to quinolone treatment.
The risk of tendinitis and tendon rupture is increased in older patients, patients with renal impairment, patients with solid organ transplants, and those treated concurrently with corticosteroids.
prescribe fluoroquinolones with special caution for people older than 60 years and for those with renal impairment or solid-organ transplants, because they are at a higher risk of tendon injury

items.t: Aortic aneurysm/dissection and heart valve regurgitation: use only after careful benefit-risk assessment and considering alternatives if family history of aneurysm, congenital or existing valve disease, existing aneurysm/dissection, or predisposing conditions (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, Turner, Behcet's, hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, Takayasu/giant cell arteritis, known atherosclerosis, Sjögren's, infective endocarditis). Seek emergency care for sudden abdominal, chest or back pain.

src.q: fluoroquinolones should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and after consideration of other therapeutic options in patients with positive family history of aneurysm disease or congenital heart valve disease
connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Turner syndrome, Behcet's disease, hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis
fluoroquinolones should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and after consideration of other therapeutic options in patients at risk for aortic aneurysm and dissection
fluoroquinolones should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment and after consideration of other therapeutic options in the following patients at risk

items.t: QT prolongation: caution with congenital long QT, other QT-prolonging drugs, uncorrected hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, cardiac disease (heart failure, MI, bradycardia); elderly and women may be more sensitive.

src.q: Caution should be taken when using fluoroquinolones, including ciprofloxacin, in patients with known risk factors for prolongation of the QT interval
uncorrected electrolyte imbalance (e.g. hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) - cardiac disease (e.g. heart failure, myocardial infarction, bradycardia)
Elderly patients and women may be more sensitive to QTc-prolonging medications.

items.t: Seizures: can trigger seizures or lower seizure threshold; caution in CNS disorders predisposing to seizures; stop if seizures occur.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin should be used with caution in patients with CNS disorders which may be predisposed to seizure.
If seizures occur ciprofloxacin should be discontinued

items.t: Psychiatric reactions (including depression/psychosis progressing to suicidal thoughts) can occur after the first dose; stop if they occur. MHRA: can exacerbate existing psychiatric symptoms.

src.q: In rare cases, depression or psychosis can progress to suicidal ideations/thoughts culminating in attempted suicide or completed suicide.
note that fluoroquinolones can exacerbate existing psychiatric symptoms

items.t: Dysglycaemia (hypo- and hyperglycaemia, hypoglycaemic coma), usually in diabetics on oral hypoglycaemics or insulin: monitor blood glucose carefully.

src.q: Cases of hypoglycaemic coma have been reported. In diabetic patients, careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis: use with caution (symptoms can worsen).

src.q: Ciprofloxacin should be used with caution in patients with myasthenia gravis, because symptoms can be exacerbated

items.t: G6PD deficiency: haemolysis reported; avoid unless benefit outweighs risk, then monitor for haemolysis.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin should be avoided in these patients unless the potential benefit is considered to outweigh the possible risk.

items.t: Peripheral neuropathy: patients should report pain, burning, tingling, numbness or weakness before continuing.

src.q: Patients under treatment with ciprofloxacin should be advised to inform their doctor prior to continuing treatment if symptoms of neuropathy such as pain, burning, tingling, numbness, or weakness develop

items.t: Hepatic necrosis and life-threatening hepatic failure reported; stop if signs of liver disease.

src.q: Cases of hepatic necrosis and life-threatening hepatic failure have been reported with ciprofloxacin

items.t: Photosensitivity: avoid extensive sunlight/UV. Crystalluria: keep well hydrated, avoid excessive urine alkalinity. Vision problems: see an eye specialist immediately.

src.q: Patients taking ciprofloxacin should be advised to avoid direct exposure to either extensive sunlight or UV irradiation during treatment
Patients receiving ciprofloxacin should be well hydrated and excessive alkalinity of the urine should be avoided.

items.t: Not recommended for streptococcal infections (inadequate efficacy); not suitable as monotherapy for severe or Gram-positive/anaerobic infections.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin is not recommended for the treatment of streptococcal infections due to inadequate efficacy

items.t: Suspension: contains sucrose - hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase deficiency should not take it. Benzyl alcohol: large amounts only with caution, especially in liver or kidney impairment.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or saccharose-isomaltase deficiency, should not take Ciproxin 250 mg/5 mL.
large amounts of benzyl alcohol should only be administered with caution and if absolutely necessary, especially in subjects with liver or kidney impairment

items.t: Iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium (including mineral supplements), antacids, sucralfate, polymeric phosphate binders: reduced ciprofloxacin absorption. Give ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after them (does not apply to H2-blockers).

src.q: multivalent cation-containing drugs and mineral supplements (e.g. calcium, magnesium, aluminium, iron), polymeric phosphate binders (e.g. sevelamer or lanthanum carbonate), sucralfate or antacids
Consequently, ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations.

items.t: Corticosteroids: avoid concomitant use (increased tendinitis/tendon rupture risk); also may increase aortic aneurysm risk.

src.q: Therefore, concomitant use of corticosteroids should be avoided.
avoid coadministration of a corticosteroid with a fluoroquinolone since this could exacerbate fluoroquinolone-induced tendinitis and tendon rupture

items.t: Methotrexate: increased methotrexate levels and toxicity; concomitant use not recommended.

src.q: The concomitant use of ciprofloxacin with methotrexate is not recommended

items.t: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists: anticoagulant effect may increase; monitor INR frequently during and shortly after co-administration.

src.q: It is recommended that the INR should be monitored frequently during and shortly after co-administration of ciprofloxacin with a vitamin K antagonist

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, tricyclics, macrolides, antipsychotics): use with caution.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin, like other fluoroquinolones, should be used with caution in patients receiving drugs known to prolong the QT interval (e.g. Class IA and III anti-arrhythmics, tricyclic antidepressants, macrolides, antipsychotics)

items.t: Oral hypoglycaemic agents (e.g. glibenclamide) or insulin: dysglycaemia; monitor blood glucose.

src.q: usually in diabetic patients receiving concomitant treatment with an oral hypoglycaemic agent (e.g., glibenclamide) or with insulin

items.t: Sildenafil: exposure roughly doubles; use with caution weighing risks and benefits.

src.q: caution should be used prescribing ciprofloxacin concomitantly with sildenafil taking into consideration the risks and the benefits

items.t: Tizanidine: must not be given together (contraindicated). Theophylline: check levels and reduce dose. Clozapine, ropinirole, duloxetine, agomelatine, phenytoin, ciclosporin, zolpidem: monitor/adjust (CYP1A2 inhibition and others).

src.q: Tizanidine must not be administered together with ciprofloxacin
During the combination, serum theophylline concentrations should be checked and the theophylline dose reduced as necessary

items.t: Omeprazole: slight reduction in ciprofloxacin Cmax and AUC (no action stated).

src.q: Concomitant administration of ciprofloxacin and omeprazole containing medicinal products results in a slight reduction of Cmax and AUC of ciprofloxacin.

items.t: Dairy products or mineral-fortified drinks taken alone (e.g. milk, yoghurt, calcium-fortified juice) reduce absorption; avoid taking at the same time. Dietary calcium as part of a meal does not significantly affect absorption.

src.q: Dietary calcium as part of a meal does not significantly affect absorption.
with ciprofloxacin should be avoided because absorption of ciprofloxacin may be reduced

items.t: Creatinine clearance (ml/min/1.73 m2) > 60: usual dose.

src.q: > 60 < 124 See Usual Dosage.

items.t: Creatinine clearance 30-60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (serum creatinine 124-168 µmol/L): 250-500 mg every 12 h.

Tablet SmPC: creatinine clearance ≤ 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (serum creatinine ≥ 169 µmol/L): 250-500 mg every 24 h. Suspension SmPC: < 30 ml/min/1.73 m2: 250-500 mg every 24 h (so in the suspension SmPC a value of exactly 30 falls in the 30-60 band). Haemodialysis: 250-500 mg every 24 h after dialysis. Peritoneal dialysis: 250-500 mg every 24 h.

src.q: ≤30 ≥169 250-500 mg every 24 h Patients on haemodialysis > 169 250-500 mg every 24 h (after dialysis) Patients on peritoneal dialysis > 169 250-500 mg every 24 h

items.t: Renal impairment also raises tendon-injury risk (MHRA: prescribe with special caution).

src.q: prescribe fluoroquinolones with special caution for people older than 60 years and for those with renal impairment or solid-organ transplants

items.t: No dose adjustment required in impaired liver function. Hepatic necrosis/failure has been reported: stop if signs of liver disease (anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, tender abdomen).

src.q: In patients with impaired liver function no dose adjustment is required.
In the event of any signs and symptoms of hepatic disease (such as anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, or tender abdomen), treatment should be discontinued.

items.t: Tablet SmPC: data show no malformative or fetal/neonatal toxicity, but cartilage damage cannot be excluded (animal data); as a precaution it is preferable to avoid use in pregnancy.

src.q: The data that are available on administration of ciprofloxacin to pregnant women indicates no malformative or foeto/neonatal toxicity of ciprofloxacin.
As a precautionary measure, it is preferable to avoid the use of ciprofloxacin during pregnancy.

items.t: Suspension SmPC: not recommended in pregnancy (cartilage concern plus benzyl alcohol, which may accumulate and cause fetal toxicity).

src.q: Therefore, it is not recommended to use Ciproxin oral suspension during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): quinolones can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no good evidence of harm to the baby; a different antibiotic will usually be tried first. (Differs in emphasis from the SmPCs.)

src.q: Quinolone antibiotics can be used in pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
There is no good evidence that use of a quinolone antibiotic in pregnancy will harm your baby.
Yes, a different antibiotic will usually be tried first.

items.t: Tablet SmPC: excreted in breast milk; should not be used during breastfeeding (risk of articular damage).

src.q: Due to the potential risk of articular damage, ciprofloxacin should not be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: Suspension SmPC: not recommended during breastfeeding (articular damage risk and benzyl alcohol).

src.q: Ciproxin oral suspension is not recommended for use during breast-feeding.

reproductive.note: No human fertility, contraception or reproductive-potential statements found in section 4.6 of the ciprofloxacin SmPCs accessed. BUMPS states no evidence that quinolones used by the father harm the baby via sperm.

items.t: Most commonly reported: nausea and diarrhoea. In children, arthropathy is common.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are nausea and diarrhoea.
In children, arthropathy is reported to occur commonly

items.t: Tendinitis/tendon rupture, muscle or joint pain/swelling, peripheral neuropathy, CNS or psychiatric effects (including suicidal thoughts): stop immediately and contact the doctor.

src.q: patients should be advised to stop fluoroquinolone treatment at the first signs of a serious adverse reaction, such as tendinitis or tendon rupture, muscle pain, muscle weakness, joint pain, joint swelling, peripheral neuropathy and central nervous system effects

items.t: Aortic aneurysm/dissection: sudden severe abdominal, chest or back pain needs emergency assessment. Valve regurgitation: acute breathlessness, new palpitations, abdominal or leg oedema need immediate medical attention.

src.q: In case of sudden abdominal, chest or back pain, patients should be advised to immediately consult a physician in an emergency department.
Patients should be advised to seek immediate medical attention in case of acute dyspnoea, new onset of heart palpitations, or development of oedema of the abdomen or lower extremities.

items.t: Anaphylaxis (can follow a single dose): stop and treat. Severe/persistent diarrhoea (possible C. difficile colitis): stop immediately.

src.q: Hypersensitivity and allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis and anaphylactoid reactions, may occur following a single dose
In such cases, ciprofloxacin should immediately be discontinued, and an appropriate therapy initiated.

items.t: Seizures (including status epilepticus), QT prolongation/torsades de pointes, hepatic necrosis/failure, SJS/TEN, hypoglycaemic coma, bone marrow depression, renal failure.

src.q: Seizures (including status epilepticus)
Ventricular arrhythmia and torsades de pointes (reported predominantly in patients with risk factors for QT prolongation)
Liver necrosis (very rarely progressing to life-threatening hepatic failure)

items.t: Before prescribing: confirm other commonly recommended antibiotics are inappropriate; check for previous serious quinolone reactions, tendon history, aneurysm/valve risk factors, QT risk factors, age > 60, renal impairment, transplant, corticosteroid use.

src.q: the UK indications for systemic fluoroquinolones have been updated so they must only be used in situations when other antibiotics, that are commonly recommended for the infection, are inappropriate
avoid fluoroquinolone use in patients who have previously had serious adverse reactions with a quinolone antibiotic

items.t: SPS: no ECG monitoring needed if used alone without risk factors; monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment if non-modifiable patient/medicine risk factors.

src.q: Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment in people with non modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: Diabetes: careful blood glucose monitoring. Warfarin: frequent INR monitoring during and shortly after the course.

src.q: In diabetic patients, careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended.
It is recommended that the INR should be monitored frequently during and shortly after co-administration of ciprofloxacin with a vitamin K antagonist

items.t: Stop at the first signs of a serious adverse reaction (tendon, muscle, joint, nerve, psychiatric), seizures, liver disease signs or severe diarrhoea.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin should be discontinued immediately at the first signs or symptoms of any serious adverse reaction
At the first sign of tendinitis (e.g. painful swelling, inflammation) the treatment with ciprofloxacin should be discontinued

items.t: Tablets: swallow unchewed with fluid, with or without food. Do not take with dairy products (milk, yoghurt) or mineral-fortified juice.

src.q: Tablets are to be swallowed unchewed with fluid. They can be taken independent of mealtimes.
Ciprofloxacin tablets should not be taken with dairy products (e.g. milk, yoghurt) or mineral-fortified fruit-juice (e.g. calcium-fortified orange juice)

items.t: Suspension: can be taken with meals (including dairy as part of a meal) but not with dairy or mineral-fortified drinks taken alone; otherwise give 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after them. Use the measuring spoon; no additions to the mixed suspension. Missed dose: take unless less than 6 hours to the next dose; do not double. Reconstituted suspension lasts 14 days.

src.q: Ciprofloxacin oral suspension can be taken during meals containing dairy products or mineral-fortified drinks.
If less than 6 hours remain before the next dose, the missed dose should not be taken and treatment should be continued as prescribed with the next scheduled dose.
Shelf life of the reconstituted oral suspension 14 days

items.t: Separate from iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium products and antacids: ciprofloxacin 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after.

src.q: Consequently, ciprofloxacin should be administered either 1-2 hours before or at least 4 hours after these preparations.

items.t: Stop and contact your doctor immediately if tendon pain/swelling, joint pain or swelling, abnormal sensations (pins and needles, numbness, burning), weakness, severe tiredness, low mood, anxiety, memory or sleep problems, or changes in vision, taste, smell or hearing occur. Rest a painful tendon.

src.q: tendon pain or swelling - if this happens, rest the painful area until you can see your doctor
severe tiredness, depressed mood, anxiety, problems with your memory or severe problems sleeping changes in your vision, taste, smell or hearing

items.t: Tell friends/family you are taking it; if thoughts of suicide or self-harm occur, take no more doses and get help immediately.

src.q: if you develop thoughts of suicide or have attempted suicide, do not take any further doses of your fluoroquinolone, and talk to your doctor or another healthcare professional immediately

items.t: Seek emergency help for sudden severe abdominal, chest or back pain; urgent help for sudden breathlessness (especially lying flat), ankle/leg/abdominal swelling or new palpitations.

src.q: the importance of seeking immediate medical attention in case of sudden-onset severe abdominal, chest or back pain
a rapid onset of shortness of breath, especially when lying down flat in bed swelling of the ankles, feet, or abdomen new-onset heart palpitations

items.t: Avoid strong sunlight/UV; drink plenty of fluids; may impair driving (neurological effects). Tell future prescribers about any serious reaction so fluoroquinolones are avoided.

src.q: Due to its neurological effects, ciprofloxacin may affect reaction time. Thus, the ability to drive or to operate machinery may be impaired.
Tell your doctor if you have had any of the above effects at any point while taking a fluoroquinolone - this means you should avoid them in the future
Each film-coated tablet contains 500 mg of clarithromycin
The usual dose is 250 mg twice daily although this may be increased to 500mg twice daily in severe infections.

formulations.label: Oral suspension (granules)
formulations.note: Contains sucrose, aspartame and sodium benzoate.

src.q: Each 5 ml of the reconstituted suspension contains 125 mg clarithromycin.
Each 5 ml reconstituted suspension contains 3194 mg of sucrose, and 1 mg of aspartame.

formulations.label: Prolonged-release tablets
formulations.note: Contraindicated if creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min (dose cannot be reduced).

src.q: Each film-coated prolonged release tablet contains; Clarithromycin citrate equivalent to clarithromycin 500mg.
Xetinin 500 mg Tablets are contraindicated in patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Lower respiratory tract infections (acute and chronic bronchitis, pneumonia), upper respiratory tract infections (sinusitis, pharyngitis), skin and soft tissue infections of mild to moderate severity. Tablets: also H. pylori eradication in duodenal ulcer (with omeprazole or lansoprazole). Tablets are for adults and children 12 years and older.

src.q: Clarithromycin film-coated tablets are indicated in adults and children 12 years and older.
Lower respiratory tract infections for example, acute and chronic bronchitis, and pneumonia
Upper respiratory tract infections for example, sinusitis and pharyngitis.
Clarithromycin is also indicated in skin and soft tissue infections of mild to moderate severity
Clarithromycin in the presence of acid suppression effected by omeprazole or lansoprazole is also indicated for the eradication of H. pylori in patients with duodenal ulcers.

items.t: Prolonged-release 500 mg tablets: adults and children 12 years and older with lower and upper respiratory tract infections and mild to moderate skin and soft tissue infections.

src.q: Xetinin XL 500 mg Tablets are indicated in adults and children 12 years and older.
Xetinin XL 500 mg Tablets are also indicated in skin and soft tissue infections of mild to moderate severity

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand-specific prescribing restrictions found in the clarithromycin SmPCs accessed. SmPCs advise considering official guidance on appropriate antibacterial use.

items.t: Respiratory tract / skin and soft tissue infections: usually 250 mg twice daily, increased to 500 mg twice daily in severe infections; usual duration 6 to 14 days.

src.q: Adults: The usual dose is 250 mg twice daily although this may be increased to 500mg twice daily in severe infections. The usual duration of treatment is 6 to 14 days.
Children older than 12 years: As for adults.

items.t: H. pylori eradication (duodenal ulcer), triple therapy for 6 to 14 days: clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily with lansoprazole 30 mg twice daily plus amoxicillin 1000 mg twice daily or metronidazole 400 mg twice daily; or with omeprazole 40 mg daily plus amoxicillin 1000 mg twice daily or metronidazole 400 mg twice daily; or with omeprazole 20 mg daily plus amoxicillin 1000 mg twice daily.

src.q: Eradication of H. pylori in patients with duodenal ulcers (Adults) The usual duration of treatment is 6 to 14 days.
Triple Therapy Clarithromycin (500mg) twice daily and lansoprazole 30mg twice daily should be given with amoxicillin 1000mg twice daily.
Triple Therapy Clarithromycin (500mg) twice daily and omeprazole 40mg daily should be given with amoxycillin 1000mg twice daily or metronidazole 400mg twice daily.
Triple Therapy Clarithromycin (500mg) twice daily and omeprazole 20mg daily should be given with amoxycillin 1000mg twice daily.

items.t: Prolonged-release: one 500 mg tablet once daily with food; severe infections two 500 mg tablets once daily; usual duration 6 to 14 days.

src.q: The usual recommended dosage of Xetinin XL Tablets in adults is one 500mg modified-release tablet daily to be taken with food. In more severe infections, the dosage can be increased to two 500mg modified-release tablets daily. The usual duration of treatment is 6 to 14 days.

items.t: Elderly: as for adults.

src.q: Elderly: As for adults.

items.t: Children under 12 years should use the paediatric suspension; tablets (immediate- and prolonged-release) are not recommended under 12 years.

src.q: Use of Clarithromycin film-coated tablets are not recommended for children younger than 12 years.
Use of Xetinin XL Tablets is not recommended for children younger than 12 years.

items.t: Suspension, children (studied 6 months to 12 years): 7.5 mg/kg twice daily, maximum 500 mg twice daily, doses 12 hours apart, usually for 5 to 10 days. Weight bands: 8-11 kg 2.5 ml; 12-19 kg 5 ml; 20-29 kg 7.5 ml; 30-40 kg 10 ml, each twice daily. Under 8 kg: 0.3 ml/kg twice daily.

src.q: is based on a 7.5 mg/ kg twice a day (b.i.d.) dosing regime up to a maximum dose of 500 mg b.i.d.
*Children < 8 kg should be dosed on a per kg basis: 0.3ml/kg twice a day (approx. 7.5 mg/kg twice a day)
The usual duration of treatment is for 5 to 10 days depending on the pathogen involved and the severity of the condition.

items.t: Clinical trials of the paediatric suspension were in children 6 months to 12 years.

src.q: Clinical trials have been conducted using clarithromycin paediatric suspension in children 6 months to 12 years of age.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to clarithromycin, other macrolides or any excipient.

src.q: Clarithromycin is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the active substance clarithromycin, to other macrolide antibiotic drugs or to any of the excipients

items.t: With ergot alkaloids (ergotamine, dihydroergotamine), oral midazolam, lomitapide, ticagrelor, ivabradine, ranolazine, colchicine, and with astemizole, cisapride, domperidone, pimozide or terfenadine (QT prolongation/arrhythmias).

src.q: Concomitant administration of clarithromycin and any of the following drugs is contraindicated: astemizole, cisapride, domperidone, pimozide and terfenadine
Concomitant administration with ticagrelor, ivabradine or ranolazine is contraindicated.
Concomitant administration of clarithromycin and colchicine is contraindicated
Concomitant administration of clarithromycin and oral midazolam is contraindicated

items.t: With simvastatin or lovastatin (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis); suspend these statins during the course if clarithromycin cannot be avoided.

src.q: Concomitant use of clarithromycin with lovastatin or simvastatin is contraindicated
If treatment with clarithromycin cannot be avoided, therapy with lovastatin or simvastatin must be suspended during the course of treatment.

items.t: History of QT prolongation (congenital or documented acquired) or ventricular arrhythmia including torsades de pointes; electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia).

src.q: Clarithromycin should not be given to patients with history of QT prolongation (congenital or documented acquired QT prolongation) or ventricular cardiac arrhythmia, including torsades de pointes

the use of clarithromycin is contraindicated in patients taking any of astemizole, cisapride, domperidone, pimozide and terfenadine; in patients who have electrolyte disturbances such as hypomagnesaemia or hypokalaemia

items.t: Severe hepatic failure combined with renal impairment.

src.q: Clarithromycin should not be used in patients who suffer from severe hepatic failure in combination with renal impairment.
Clarithromycin is contraindicated in patients who suffer from severe hepatic failure in combination with renal impairment.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min.

src.q: Xetinin 500 mg Tablets are contraindicated in patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min.

items.t: Use with caution in coronary artery disease, severe cardiac insufficiency, conduction disturbances, clinically relevant bradycardia, and with other QT-prolonging medicines (other than those contraindicated).

src.q: Patients with coronary artery disease, severe cardiac insufficiency, conduction disturbances or clinically relevant bradycardia; Patients concomitantly taking other medicinal products associated with QT prolongation other than those which are contraindicated

items.t: Observational studies: rare short-term risk of arrhythmia, myocardial infarction and cardiovascular mortality with macrolides; balance against benefit.

src.q: Some observational studies have identified a rare short-term risk of arrhythmia, myocardial infarction and cardiovascular mortality associated with macrolides including clarithromycin.

items.t: Hepatic dysfunction (raised enzymes, hepatocellular/cholestatic hepatitis, fatal hepatic failure) reported. Caution in impaired hepatic function. Patients should stop and contact their doctor if anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus or tender abdomen develop.

src.q: caution should be exercised in administering this antibiotic to patients with impaired hepatic function
Patients should be advised to stop treatment and contact their doctor if signs and symptoms of hepatic disease develop, such as anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, or tender abdomen.

items.t: Caution in moderate to severe renal impairment.

src.q: Caution should also be exercised when administering clarithromycin to patients with moderate to severe renal impairment

items.t: Severe acute hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, SCAR such as AGEP, SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop immediately and treat urgently.

src.q: clarithromycin therapy should be discontinued immediately and appropriate treatment should be urgently initiated

items.t: C. difficile-associated diarrhoea can occur up to 2 months after treatment; consider stopping clarithromycin, test and treat; avoid anti-peristaltic drugs.

src.q: CDAD has been reported to occur over two months after the administration of antibacterial agents
Drugs inhibiting peristalsis should be avoided.

items.t: Pneumonia: sensitivity testing important (macrolide-resistant S. pneumoniae); in hospital-acquired pneumonia combine with other antibiotics. Skin infections: test sensitivity.

src.q: it is important that sensitivity testing be performed when prescribing clarithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia
In hospital-acquired pneumonia, clarithromycin should be used in combination with additional appropriate antibiotics.

items.t: Suspension excipients: 3194 mg sucrose per 5 ml (take into account in diabetes); hereditary fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take it; aspartame may be harmful in phenylketonuria.

src.q: This should be taken into account in patients with diabetes mellitus.
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance, glucose-galactose malabsorption or sucrase-isomaltase insufficiency should not take this medicinal product.
This may be harmful for people with phenylketonuria.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets contain lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Simvastatin (and lovastatin): contraindicated (myopathy, rhabdomyolysis). If clarithromycin is essential, stop simvastatin for the course.

src.q: Concomitant use of clarithromycin with lovastatin or simvastatin is contraindicated
If clarithromycin is essential to use, simvastatin must be stopped whilst the patient is taking the course of clarithromycin.

items.t: Atorvastatin: SmPC advises caution with other statins (lowest dose, monitor for myopathy). SPS: avoid and use a non-interacting antibiotic if possible; consider pausing atorvastatin for the course; if unavoidable use a maximum of 20 mg daily. MHRA: do not exceed 20 mg atorvastatin daily with clarithromycin.

src.q: Caution should be exercised when prescribing clarithromycin with statins.
Avoid the use of clarithromycin with atorvastatin and use a non-interacting antibiotic if possible.
Use a lower dose of atorvastatin (maximum 20mg daily) if concurrent administration is unavoidable.
Clarithromycin: do not exceed 20 mg atorvastatin daily

items.t: Warfarin: risk of serious haemorrhage and marked INR rise; monitor INR and prothrombin time frequently. Caution with DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban), especially if high bleeding risk.

src.q: There is a risk of serious haemorrhage and significant elevations in International Normalized Ratio (INR) and prothrombin time when clarithromycin is co-administered with warfarin
INR and prothrombin times should be frequently monitored while patients are receiving clarithromycin and oral anticoagulants concurrently.

items.t: Oral hypoglycaemic agents (e.g. sulfonylureas) and/or insulin: significant hypoglycaemia possible; monitor glucose carefully.

src.q: The concomitant use of clarithromycin and oral hypoglycaemic agents (such as sulfonylurias) and/or insulin can result in significant hypoglycaemia. Careful monitoring of glucose is recommended

items.t: Calcium-channel blockers metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g. amlodipine, verapamil, diltiazem): caution, risk of hypotension; levels of both may rise.

src.q: Caution is advised regarding the concomitant administration of clarithromycin and calcium channel blockers metabolized by CYP3A4 (e.g., verapamil, amlodipine, diltiazem) due to the risk of hypotension.

items.t: Sildenafil (and tadalafil, vardenafil): increased exposure; consider dose reduction.

src.q: Reduction of sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil dosages should be considered when these drugs are co-administered with clarithromycin.

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine: carefully weigh benefits and risks (increased cardiovascular events and mortality seen with azithromycin + hydroxychloroquine); use with caution, especially with cardiac risk factors.

src.q: careful consideration should be given to the balance of benefits and risks before prescribing clarithromycin for any patients taking hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine
if there is a clinical need to prescribe systemic macrolide antibiotics with hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine, use caution in patients with risk factors for cardiac events

items.t: Corticosteroids metabolised by CYP3A (systemic and inhaled): caution; monitor for systemic corticosteroid effects.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in concomitant use of clarithromycin with systemic and inhaled corticosteroids that are primarily metabolised by CYP3A

items.t: CYP3A inducers (e.g. rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort) may lower clarithromycin levels; use with caution.

src.q: Drugs that are inducers of CYP3A (e.g. rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St. John's wort) may induce the metabolism of clarithromycin.
Clarithromycin should be used with caution when administered concurrently with medications that induce the cytochrome CYP3A4 enzyme

items.t: Omeprazole: omeprazole levels increase with clarithromycin (no action stated; combination used for H. pylori).

src.q: The steady-state plasma concentrations of omeprazole were increased

items.t: Digoxin: monitor serum digoxin carefully. Theophylline/carbamazepine: dose reduction may be needed. Other CYP3A substrates with narrow margins: caution.

src.q: Serum digoxin concentrations should be carefully monitored while patients are receiving digoxin and clarithromycin simultaneously.
Dose reduction may need to be considered.

items.t: Oral contraceptives: warn that diarrhoea, vomiting or breakthrough bleeding may mean contraceptive failure.

src.q: Patients taking oral contraceptives should be warned that if diarrhoea, vomiting or breakthrough bleeding occur there is a possibility of contraceptive failure.

items.t: Immediate-release tablets: CrCl < 30 mL/min - halve the dose (250 mg once daily, or 250 mg twice daily in more severe infections); do not continue beyond 14 days.

src.q: In patients with renal impairment with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min, the dosage of clarithromycin should be reduced by one-half, i.e. 250 mg once daily, or 250 mg twice daily in more severe infections. Treatment should not be continued beyond 14 days in these patients.

items.t: Suspension (children): creatinine clearance < 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 - halve to 7.5 mg/kg per day; not beyond 14 days.

src.q: In children with creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min/1.73 m2, the dosage of clarithromycin should be reduced by half to 7.5 mg/kg per day. Dosage should not be continued beyond 14 days in these patients.

items.t: Prolonged-release: contraindicated if CrCl < 30 mL/min (use immediate-release); CrCl 30 to 60 mL/min - 50% dose reduction, maximum one 500 mg tablet per day.

src.q: Xetinin 500 mg Tablets are contraindicated in patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 mL/min.
For patients with moderate renal function (creatinine clearance 30 to 60 ml/min), a 50% dosage reduction should be implemented resulting in a maximum dose of one Xetinin 500 mg Tablets per day.

items.t: With ritonavir or other boosted HIV protease inhibitors: reduce clarithromycin by 50% if CrCl 30-60 mL/min and by 75% if CrCl < 30 mL/min.

src.q: For patients with CLCR 30 to 60 mL/min the dose of clarithromycin should be reduced by 50%. For patients with CLCR <30 mL/min the dose of clarithromycin should be decreased by 75%.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe hepatic failure combined with renal impairment (SmPC section 4.3). Otherwise use with caution in impaired hepatic function (mainly hepatically metabolised).

src.q: Clarithromycin should not be used in patients who suffer from severe hepatic failure in combination with renal impairment.
Clarithromycin is principally metabolised by the liver. Therefore, caution should be exercised in administering this antibiotic to patients with impaired hepatic function.

items.t: SmPC: safety not established; some studies show increased miscarriage risk after first/second-trimester exposure; malformation data conflicting. Use not advised without carefully weighing benefits against risks.

src.q: Some observational studies evaluating exposure to clarithromycin during the first and second trimester have reported an increased risk of miscarriage
Therefore, use during pregnancy is not advised without carefully weighing the benefits against risks

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS): clarithromycin can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; available data do not show effects on the baby's development; the higher miscarriage rate is likely partly due to underlying infection.

src.q: Clarithromycin can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
it is likely that the underlying infections in these women may have played a part

items.t: SmPC: safety in breastfeeding not established; small amounts in milk (about 1.7% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose).

src.q: The safety of clarithromycin for use during breast feeding of infants has not been established.
It has been estimated that an exclusively breastfed infant would receive about 1.7% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose of clarithromycin.

items.t: SPS: use with caution; all formulations can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring (GI upset, oral thrush, rash, sleep disturbance, irritability, sweating, poor feeding).

src.q: Use with caution All formulations of clarithromycin
All formulations of clarithromycin, including intravenous therapy can be used during breastfeeding with precautionary infant monitoring.
monitor for gastro-intestinal disturbances such as diarrhoea and vomiting, oral candida infection, rashes, sleep disturbances, irritability, sweating, and loss of appetite

items.t: SPS: data conflict on whether macrolide exposure via breast milk raises the risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; some studies found a higher risk in the first 90 days of life, especially the first 2 weeks.

src.q: There is conflicting data regarding whether there is an increased risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis from exposure to macrolides via breast milk.
Some studies have noted an increased risk during the first 90 days of life, and especially in the first 2 weeks after birth.

items.t: Rat fertility studies showed no harmful effects. Oral contraceptive users: diarrhoea, vomiting or breakthrough bleeding may mean contraceptive failure.

src.q: In the rat, fertility studies have not shown any evidence of harmful effects
Patients taking oral contraceptives should be warned that if diarrhoea, vomiting or breakthrough bleeding occur there is a possibility of contraceptive failure.

items.t: Most frequent: abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, taste disturbance (usually mild). Also common: insomnia, headache, dyspepsia, rash, hyperhidrosis, abnormal liver function tests.

src.q: The most frequent and common adverse reactions related to clarithromycin therapy for both adult and paediatric populations are abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting and taste perversion.
Psychiatric disorders Insomnia
Nervous system disorders Dysgeusia, headache
Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders Rash, hyperhidrosis

items.t: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation.

src.q: Torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia ventricular fibrillation

items.t: Hepatic failure, hepatocellular jaundice: stop and contact doctor if signs of liver disease.

src.q: Hepatic failure, jaundice hepatocellular
Patients should be advised to stop treatment and contact their doctor if signs and symptoms of hepatic disease develop

items.t: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, severe cutaneous reactions (AGEP, SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop immediately and treat urgently.

src.q: Anaphylactic reaction, angioedema
clarithromycin therapy should be discontinued immediately and appropriate treatment should be urgently initiated

items.t: Pseudomembranous colitis / C. difficile diarrhoea; rhabdomyolysis (often with statins, fibrates, colchicine or allopurinol); agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia; convulsions; deafness; acute pancreatitis; renal failure.

src.q: In some of the reports of rhabdomyolysis, clarithromycin was administered concomitantly with statins, fibrates, colchicine or allopurinol
Agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia

items.t: Before starting: check for QT prolongation history, ventricular arrhythmia, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, and interacting medicines (statins, anticoagulants, QT-prolonging drugs).

src.q: the use of clarithromycin is contraindicated in patients taking any of astemizole, cisapride, domperidone, pimozide and terfenadine; in patients who have electrolyte disturbances such as hypomagnesaemia or hypokalaemia

items.t: SPS: no ECG monitoring needed when used alone without risk factors; monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment if non-modifiable patient or medicine risk factors.

src.q: No ECG monitoring is required when used alone and in the absence of risk factors.
Monitor ECG, magnesium and potassium before and during treatment in people with non-modifiable patient and medicine risk factors.

items.t: On warfarin: monitor INR/prothrombin time frequently. On antidiabetic medicines: monitor glucose. With statins: monitor for myopathy symptoms.

src.q: INR and prothrombin times should be frequently monitored while patients are receiving clarithromycin and oral anticoagulants concurrently.
Patients should be monitored for signs and symptoms of myopathy.

items.t: Stop if signs of hepatic disease, severe hypersensitivity/SCAR; consider stopping if C. difficile diarrhoea.

src.q: Patients should be advised to stop treatment and contact their doctor if signs and symptoms of hepatic disease develop
discontinuation of clarithromycin therapy should be considered regardless of the indication

items.t: Immediate-release tablets and suspension can be taken with or without food.

src.q: Clarithromycin may be given without regard to meals as food does not affect the extent of bioavailability.
Clarithromycin may be given without regard to meals, as food does not affect the extent of bioavailability.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: take once daily with food; do not crush or chew.

src.q: one 500mg modified-release tablet daily to be taken with food
Do not crush or chew Xetinin XL 500 mg Tablets.

items.t: Suspension: reconstitute with water, shake well before each dose, give with an oral syringe at 12-hour intervals. Reconstituted suspension: shelf life 14 days; store below 30 °C; do not refrigerate or freeze.

src.q: The suspension should be shaken well before each use.
The doses should be given at 12-hour intervals.
Reconstituted suspension: 14 days
Store below 30°C. Do not refrigerate or freeze the reconstituted suspension.

items.t: Tell the prescriber/pharmacist about all other medicines (many serious interactions, e.g. simvastatin, colchicine, warfarin).

src.q: The use of clarithromycin is also contraindicated with ergot alkaloids, oral midazolam, HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors mainly metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g. lovastatin and simvastatin), colchicine, ticagrelor, ivabradine and ranolazine

items.t: Stop and seek advice if yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, itching, tender abdomen or loss of appetite; report palpitations or fainting.

src.q: Patients should be advised to stop treatment and contact their doctor if signs and symptoms of hepatic disease develop, such as anorexia, jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, or tender abdomen.

items.t: May cause dizziness, vertigo, confusion or disorientation; consider before driving.

src.q: The potential for dizziness, vertigo, confusion and disorientation, which may occur with the medication, should be taken into account before patients drive or use machines.

formulations.label: Film-coated tablets
formulations.strengths: 75 mg (300 mg tablets also exist for loading)

src.q: Each film-coated tablet contains 75 mg of clopidogrel (as hydrogen sulphate).

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Secondary prevention of atherothrombotic events in adults with recent myocardial infarction (a few days to under 35 days), ischaemic stroke (7 days to under 6 months) or established peripheral arterial disease.

src.q: Adult patients suffering from myocardial infarction (from a few days until less than 35 days), ischemic stroke (from 7 days until less than 6 months) or established peripheral arterial disease.

items.t: Acute coronary syndrome (with aspirin): NSTE-ACS including stenting after PCI; STEMI with PCI or in medically treated patients eligible for thrombolysis.

src.q: Non-ST segment elevation acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or non-Q-wave myocardial infarction), including patients undergoing a stent placement following percutaneous coronary intervention, in combination with acetylsalicylic acid (ASA).

items.t: With aspirin in adults with moderate to high-risk TIA (ABCD2 score ≥4) or minor ischaemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) within 24 hours of the event.

src.q: Adult patients with moderate to high-risk TIA (ABCD21 score ≥4) or minor IS (NIHSS2 ≤3) within 24 hours of either the TIA or IS event.

items.t: With aspirin in adults with atrial fibrillation, at least one vascular risk factor, unsuitable for vitamin K antagonists and with low bleeding risk.

src.q: are not suitable for treatment with Vitamin K antagonists (VKA) and who have a low bleeding risk

restrictions.note: No specialist-only or brand restriction found in the clopidogrel SmPC, MHRA or SPS pages checked.

items.t: Secondary prevention (MI, stroke, PAD) and atrial fibrillation: 75 mg once daily (with aspirin 75-100 mg daily in AF).

src.q: Clopidogrel should be given as a single daily dose of 75 mg.
In patients with atrial fibrillation, clopidogrel should be given as a single daily dose of 75 mg.

items.t: NSTE-ACS: loading dose 300 mg or 600 mg (600 mg may be considered under 75 years when PCI is intended), then 75 mg once daily with aspirin (aspirin not above 100 mg recommended). Trial data support up to 12 months.

src.q: clopidogrel treatment should be initiated with a single 300 mg or 600mg loading dose.
Clopidogrel treatment should be continued at 75 mg once a day
Clinical trial data support use up to 12 months

items.t: STEMI, medically treated and eligible for thrombolysis: 300 mg loading dose then 75 mg once daily with aspirin, for at least four weeks; over 75 years start without a loading dose.

src.q: clopidogrel should be given as a single daily dose of 75 mg initiated with a 300 mg loading dose
For medically treated patients over 75 years of age clopidogrel should be initiated without a loading dose.

items.t: STEMI with PCI: 600 mg loading dose for primary PCI or PCI more than 24 hours after fibrinolysis (caution if 75 years or older); 300 mg if PCI within 24 hours of fibrinolysis; then 75 mg daily with aspirin 75-100 mg, up to 12 months.

src.q: Clopidogrel should be initiated at a loading dose of 600 mg in patients undergoing primary PCI
Clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose should be given in patients undergoing PCI within 24 hours of receiving fibrinolytic therapy.

items.t: Moderate to high-risk TIA or minor ischaemic stroke: 300 mg loading dose then 75 mg once daily with aspirin 75-100 mg; start within 24 hours and continue 21 days, then single antiplatelet therapy.

src.q: should be given a loading dose of clopidogrel 300 mg followed by clopidogrel 75 mg once daily and ASA (75 mg -100 mg once daily)
be continued for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet therapy

items.t: Missed dose: within 12 hours, take it at once; after more than 12 hours, take the next dose at the usual time and do not double.

src.q: Within less than 12 hours after regular scheduled time: patients should take the dose immediately
should not double the dose

items.t: Should not be used in children because of efficacy concerns.

src.q: Clopidogrel should not be used in children because of efficacy concerns

items.t: Hypersensitivity to clopidogrel or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 2 or section 6.1.

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment.

items.t: Active pathological bleeding such as peptic ulcer or intracranial haemorrhage.

src.q: Active pathological bleeding such as peptic ulcer or intracranial hemorrhage.

items.t: Bleeding risk: use with caution with trauma, surgery or other conditions with increased bleeding risk, and with aspirin, heparin, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors, NSAIDs, SSRIs or other medicines that increase bleeding risk. Watch for signs of bleeding, especially in the first weeks.

src.q: clopidogrel should be used with caution in patients who may be at risk of increased bleeding from trauma, surgery or other pathological conditions
Patients should be followed carefully for any signs of bleeding including occult bleeding

items.t: Lesions with a tendency to bleed (particularly gastrointestinal and intraocular): use with caution.

src.q: should be used with caution in patients who have lesions with a propensity to bleed (particularly gastrointestinal and intraocular)

items.t: Elective surgery: if antiplatelet effect is not wanted, stop clopidogrel 7 days before.

src.q: clopidogrel should be discontinued 7 days prior to surgery

items.t: Age 75 or over: 600 mg loading dose not recommended in NSTE-ACS; in STEMI-PCI use only after individual bleeding-risk assessment.

src.q: The use of clopidogrel 600 mg loading dose is not recommended in patients with non-ST segment elevation acute coronary syndrome and ≥75 years of age due to increased bleeding risk

items.t: CYP2C19 poor metabolisers form less active metabolite and have a smaller antiplatelet effect; genotype tests are available.

src.q: In patients who are poor CYP2C19 metabolisers, clopidogrel at recommended doses forms less of the active metabolite of clopidogrel and has a smaller effect on platelet function.

items.t: Cross-reactivity with other thienopyridines (ticlopidine, prasugrel) has been reported; check history of thienopyridine allergy.

src.q: Patients should be evaluated for history of hypersensitivity to thienopyridines (such as clopidogrel, ticlopidine, prasugrel) since cross-reactivity among thienopyridines has been reported

items.t: Renal impairment and moderate hepatic disease: limited experience; use with caution.

src.q: Therefore clopidogrel should be used with caution in these patients
Clopidogrel should therefore be used with caution in this population

items.t: Non-minor ischaemic stroke (NIHSS >4) and patients planned for endarterectomy, thrombectomy, thrombolysis or anticoagulation: dual antiplatelet therapy not recommended.

src.q: In view of the lack of data, use of dual antiplatelet therapy is not recommended

items.t: Contains lactose and hydrogenated castor oil.

src.q: Plavix contains lactose.

items.t: Omeprazole (and esomeprazole): reduces active metabolite exposure and antiplatelet effect; concomitant use should be discouraged. SPS: avoid; use lansoprazole, pantoprazole or rabeprazole instead. Pantoprazole can be given with clopidogrel.

src.q: As a precaution, concomitant use of omeprazole or esomeprazole should be discouraged
For patients taking clopidogrel who require PPI therapy, avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole. Use lansoprazole, pantoprazole or rabeprazole in preference.
These results indicate that clopidogrel can be administered with pantoprazole.

items.t: MHRA: doctors should check whether patients on clopidogrel are buying omeprazole over the counter; pharmacists should check whether omeprazole buyers take clopidogrel.

src.q: Doctors should check whether patients who are taking clopidogrel are also buying over-the-counter omeprazole

items.t: Other CYP2C19 inhibitors: discourage concomitant use. MHRA lists ciprofloxacin among CYP2C19 inhibitors.

src.q: As a precaution concomitant use of strong or moderate CYP2C19 inhibitors should be discouraged
Discourage concomitant use of other known CYP2C19-inhibiting medicines with clopidogrel

items.t: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin): not recommended; increases bleeding intensity through independent effects on haemostasis.

src.q: the concomitant administration of clopidogrel with oral anticoagulants is not recommended since it may increase the intensity of bleedings

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors): co-administer with caution; naproxen increased occult GI blood loss.

src.q: NSAIDs including Cox-2 inhibitors and clopidogrel should be co-administered with caution

items.t: SSRIs: increase bleeding risk; use together with caution.

src.q: the concomitant administration of SSRIs with clopidogrel should be undertaken with caution

items.t: Opioid agonists (e.g. morphine) may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption; in ACS needing morphine or other opioids, consider a parenteral antiplatelet.

src.q: co-administration of opioid agonists has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel

items.t: Aspirin and heparin: possible increased bleeding; use with caution (combination with aspirin is standard in ACS for up to one year).

src.q: A pharmacodynamic interaction between clopidogrel and acetylsalicylic acid is possible, leading to increased risk of bleeding.

items.t: CYP2C8 substrates (e.g. repaglinide, paclitaxel): caution, clopidogrel raises their levels.

src.q: concomitant administration of clopidogrel and drugs primarily cleared by CYP2C8 metabolism (e.g., repaglinide, paclitaxel) should be undertaken with caution

items.t: Limited experience in renal impairment; use with caution. No eGFR/CrCl threshold or dose change is given.

src.q: Therapeutic experience with clopidogrel is limited in patients with renal impairment. Therefore clopidogrel should be used with caution in these patients

items.t: Severe hepatic impairment: contraindicated. Moderate hepatic disease (may have bleeding diatheses): limited experience; use with caution.

src.q: Severe hepatic impairment.
Experience is limited in patients with moderate hepatic disease who may have bleeding diatheses. Clopidogrel should therefore be used with caution in this population

items.t: SmPC: no clinical data; as a precaution it is preferable not to use clopidogrel in pregnancy.

src.q: it is preferable not to use clopidogrel during pregnancy as a precautionary measure

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor when benefits outweigh risks; limited data do not suggest harm; use at the end of pregnancy may increase postpartum haemorrhage risk; switching to low-molecular-weight heparin may be possible.

src.q: Clopidogrel can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor.
Taking clopidogrel at the end of pregnancy may increase the chance of heavy bleeding during childbirth (postpartum haemorrhage).

items.t: SmPC: as a precaution, breastfeeding should not be continued during treatment.

src.q: As a precautionary measure, breast-feeding should not be continued during treatment with Plavix.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPC): can be used with caution during breastfeeding with infant monitoring (diarrhoea, constipation, skin reactions, bruising or bleeding).

src.q: It can be used with caution during breastfeeding but monitoring is required. Monitoring As a precaution, monitor the infant for diarrhoea, constipation or skin reactions

items.t: No effect on fertility in animal studies.

src.q: Clopidogrel was not shown to alter fertility in animal studies.

items.t: Bleeding is the most common reaction (mostly in the first month). Common: haematoma, epistaxis, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, bruising, bleeding at puncture site.

src.q: Bleeding is the most common reaction reported both in clinical studies as well as in post-marketing experience where it was mostly reported during the first month of treatment.
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia

items.t: Serious bleeding including intracranial and gastrointestinal haemorrhage (some fatal): check blood count and other tests promptly if bleeding symptoms occur. Platelet transfusion may reverse the effect; there is no antidote.

src.q: blood cell count determination and/or other appropriate testing should be promptly considered whenever clinical symptoms suggestive of bleeding arise
platelet transfusion may reverse the effects of clopidogrel

items.t: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (very rare, sometimes after short exposure): potentially fatal; needs prompt treatment including plasmapheresis.

src.q: TTP is a potentially fatal condition requiring prompt treatment including plasmapheresis.

items.t: Acquired haemophilia: consider if isolated prolonged aPTT, with or without bleeding; refer to specialists and stop clopidogrel (MHRA: avoid invasive procedures).

src.q: Patients with a confirmed diagnosis of acquired haemophilia should be managed and treated by specialists, and clopidogrel should be discontinued.
Acquired haemophilia should be considered in the event of isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)

items.t: Very rare/not known: aplastic anaemia, agranulocytosis, severe neutropenia, angioedema, SJS/TEN, DRESS, anaphylactoid reactions, Kounis syndrome, acute liver failure.

src.q: Bullous dermatitis (toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens Johnson Syndrome, erythema multiforme, acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)), angioedema

items.t: No routine laboratory monitoring is stated. Promptly check blood count/other tests if symptoms suggest bleeding.

src.q: blood cell count determination and/or other appropriate testing should be promptly considered whenever clinical symptoms suggestive of bleeding arise

items.t: Watch carefully for bleeding, including occult bleeding, especially in the first weeks and after invasive procedures or surgery.

src.q: especially during the first weeks of treatment and/or after invasive cardiac procedures or surgery

items.t: Stop if acquired haemophilia is confirmed.

src.q: Patients with a confirmed diagnosis of acquired haemophilia should be managed and treated by specialists, and clopidogrel should be discontinued.

items.t: Oral, with or without food.

src.q: It may be given with or without food.

items.t: Bleeding may take longer to stop; report any unusual bleeding (site or duration).

src.q: Patients should be told that it might take longer than usual to stop bleeding when they take clopidogrel

items.t: Tell doctors and dentists about clopidogrel before any surgery and before starting any new medicine (including over-the-counter omeprazole).

src.q: Patients should inform physicians and dentists that they are taking clopidogrel before any surgery is scheduled and before any new medicinal product is taken.

higher dose - (particularly for infections such as otitis media, sinusitis, lower respiratory tract infections and urinary tract infections): 875 mg/125 mg three times a day.

items.t: 250 mg/125 mg tablets are not recommended in children < 40 kg.

src.q: Augmentin 250 mg/125 mg film-coated tablets are not recommended in children < 40 kg.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, to any penicillin or to any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substances, to any of the penicillins or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: History of a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) to another beta-lactam (e.g. a cephalosporin, carbapenem or monobactam).

src.q: History of a severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction (e.g. anaphylaxis) to another beta-lactam agent (e.g. a cephalosporin, carbapenem or monobactam).

src.q: History of jaundice/hepatic impairment due to amoxicillin/clavulanic acid

items.t: AGEP during treatment: stop and do not give amoxicillin again.

src.q: This reaction requires Augmentin discontinuation and contraindicates any subsequent administration of amoxicillin.

items.t: Hepatic events (cholestatic jaundice, hepatitis), mainly in males and elderly, may be linked to prolonged treatment; signs may appear several weeks after stopping. Can be severe, rarely fatal. Use with caution if there is evidence of hepatic impairment.

src.q: Hepatic events have been reported predominantly in males and elderly patients and may be associated with prolonged treatment.
in some cases may not become apparent until several weeks after treatment has ceased
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should be used with caution in patients with evidence of hepatic impairment

items.t: Ask about previous reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactams. Serious, occasionally fatal reactions more likely with penicillin allergy history and atopy. Stop if an allergic reaction occurs.

src.q: careful enquiry should be made concerning previous hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other beta-lactam agents
If an allergic reaction occurs, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy must be discontinued and appropriate alternative therapy instituted.

items.t: Avoid if infectious mononucleosis is suspected (morbilliform rash).

src.q: Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should be avoided if infectious mononucleosis is suspected

items.t: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)/macrophage activation syndrome: evaluate promptly if fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, high ferritin occur; stop unless another cause is found.

src.q: Patients who develop these signs and symptoms should be immediately evaluated and HLH/MAS diagnosis considered.
Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid therapy should be discontinued unless an alternative aetiology for HLH/MAS can be established.

items.t: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES), mainly in children: protracted vomiting 1-4 hours after a dose; severe cases can progress to shock.

src.q: Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES) has been reported mainly in children receiving amoxicillin/clavulanic acid
There have been severe cases including progression to shock.

items.t: Convulsions may occur with impaired renal function or high doses.

src.q: Convulsions may occur in patients with impaired renal function or in those receiving high doses

items.t: Antibiotic-associated colitis: stop immediately if it occurs; anti-peristaltic medicines are contraindicated.

src.q: Should antibiotic-associated colitis occur, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid should immediately be discontinued
Anti-peristaltic medicinal products are contraindicated in this situation.

items.t: Not suitable when the likely pathogen has beta-lactam resistance not mediated by clavulanate-sensitive beta-lactamases; do not use to treat penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.

src.q: This presentation should not be used to treat penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae .

items.t: High doses: maintain fluid intake and urine output (crystalluria risk).

src.q: During the administration of high doses of amoxicillin, it is advisable to maintain adequate fluid intake and urinary output in order to reduce the possibility of amoxicillin crystalluria.

items.t: May cause a false positive Coombs test and false positive Platelia Aspergillus EIA; use enzymatic glucose oxidase methods for urine glucose.

src.q: The presence of clavulanic acid in Augmentin may cause a non-specific binding of IgG and albumin by red cell membranes leading to a false positive Coombs test.
enzymatic glucose oxidase methods should be used whenever testing for the presence of glucose in urine

items.t: Suspensions contain aspartame (source of phenylalanine): use with caution in phenylketonuria; no data on aspartame use in infants below 12 weeks of age. They contain maltodextrin (glucose): patients with glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take them. Flavouring contains traces of benzyl alcohol (may cause allergic reactions).

src.q: This medicine should be used with caution in patients with phenylketonuria.
This medicine should be used with caution in patients with phenylketonuria.
Benzyl alcohol may cause allergic reactions.
Neither non-clinical nor clinical data are available to assess aspartame use in infants below 12 weeks of age.
Patients with rare glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Warfarin/acenocoumarol: raised INR reported. If used together, carefully monitor prothrombin time/INR when co-amoxiclav is added or stopped; anticoagulant dose may need adjusting.

src.q: in the literature there are cases of increased international normalised ratio in patients maintained on acenocoumarol or warfarin and prescribed a course of amoxicillin
If co-administration is necessary, the prothrombin time or international normalised ratio should be carefully monitored with the addition or withdrawal of amoxicillin.

items.t: Methotrexate: penicillins may reduce methotrexate excretion (toxicity). SPS: for short penicillin courses (up to 10 days) consider using with caution and monitor for toxicity.

src.q: Penicillins may reduce the excretion of methotrexate causing a potential increase in toxicity.
If the duration of penicillin is short (up to 10 days), consider using with caution and advise to monitor for signs of toxicity.

items.t: Probenecid: concomitant use not recommended.

src.q: Probenecid Concomitant use of probenecid is not recommended.

items.t: Mycophenolate mofetil: pre-dose mycophenolic acid levels fall by about 50%; dose change not normally needed without signs of graft dysfunction, but monitor closely during and shortly after the course.

src.q: However, close clinical monitoring should be performed during the combination and shortly after antibiotic treatment.

items.t: Allopurinol: increased likelihood of allergic skin reactions.

src.q: Concomitant use of allopurinol during treatment with amoxicillin can increase the likelihood of allergic skin reactions.

items.t: No adjustment if CrCl > 30 ml/min.

src.q: No adjustment in dose is required in patients with creatinine clearance (CrCl) greater than 30 ml/min.

items.t: 500 mg/125 mg tablets (adults/children ≥ 40 kg): CrCl 10-30 ml/min 500 mg/125 mg twice daily; CrCl < 10 ml/min 500 mg/125 mg once daily; haemodialysis 500 mg/125 mg every 24 hours plus a dose during dialysis, repeated at the end of dialysis.

src.q: CrCl: 10-30 ml/min 500 mg/125 mg twice daily CrCl < 10 ml /min 500 mg/125 mg once daily
Haemodialysis 500 mg/125 mg every 24 hours, plus 500 mg/125 mg during dialysis, to be repeated at the end of dialysis

items.t: 250 mg/125 mg tablets (adults/children ≥ 40 kg): CrCl 10-30 ml/min 250 mg/125 mg twice daily; CrCl < 10 ml/min 250 mg/125 mg once daily. In children < 40 kg with CrCl less than 30 ml/min, 2:1 presentations are not recommended (no dose adjustments available).

src.q: CrCl: 10-30 ml/min 250 mg/125 mg twice daily CrCl < 10 ml /min 250 mg/125 mg once daily
the use of Augmentin presentations with an amoxicillin to clavulanic acid ratio of 2:1 is not recommended, as no dose adjustments are available

items.t: Children < 40 kg (4:1 presentations): CrCl 10-30 ml/min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg/125 mg twice daily); CrCl < 10 ml/min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg once daily (maximum 500 mg/125 mg); haemodialysis 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg once daily plus a dose before and after dialysis.

src.q: Children < 40 kg CrCl: 10-30 ml/min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg twice daily (maximum 500 mg/125 mg twice daily). CrCl < 10 ml /min 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg as a single daily dose (maximum 500 mg/125 mg).
Haemodialysis 15 mg/3.75 mg/kg per day once daily.

items.t: 7:1 presentations (875 mg/125 mg tablets, 400/57 suspension): not recommended if CrCl < 30 ml/min (no dose-adjustment recommendations available).

In patients with creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min, the use of Augmentin presentations with an amoxicillin to clavulanic acid ratio of 7:1 is not recommended
