It is recommended to regularly monitor (every 3-6 months) the glycaemic status

items.t: Usual dose 1500 to 2000 mg once daily; maximum 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. Consider for at least 6 months.

src.q: The usual dose is 1,500-2000 mg once daily.
The maximum recommended dose is 2000 mg once daily with the evening meal. Glucophage SR should be considered for at least 6 months.

items.t: Elderly: adjust dose to renal function; assess renal function regularly.

src.q: Due to the potential for decreased renal function in elderly subjects, the metformin dosage should be adjusted based on renal function.

items.t: Children from 10 years and adolescents (type 2 diabetes): start 500 mg or 850 mg once daily during or after meals; adjust after 10 to 15 days. Maximum 2 g daily in 2 or 3 divided doses.

src.q: The usual starting dose is 500 mg or 850 mg metformin hydrochloride once daily, given during or after meals.
The maximum recommended dose of metformin hydrochloride is 2 g daily, taken as 2 or 3 divided doses.

items.t: Not licensed below 10 years (the SmPC licenses use from 10 years). Particular caution aged 10 to 12 years (few studied). Follow growth and puberty, especially before puberty. Confirm the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes before starting.

src.q: Glucophage can be used in children from 10 years of age and adolescents.
particular caution is recommended when prescribing to children aged between 10 and 12 years
a careful follow-up of the effect of metformin on these parameters in metformin-treated children, especially prepubescent children, is recommended
The diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus should be confirmed before treatment with metformin is initiated.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets should not be used in children (no data).

src.q: In the absence of available data, Glucophage SR should not be used in children.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to metformin or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to metformin or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Any acute metabolic acidosis (e.g. lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis); diabetic pre-coma.

src.q: Any type of acute metabolic acidosis (such as lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis). Diabetic pre-coma.

items.t: Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min).

src.q: Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min).

items.t: Acute conditions that may alter renal function: dehydration, severe infection, shock.

src.q: Acute conditions with the potential to alter renal function such as: dehydration, severe infection, shock.

items.t: Disease that may cause tissue hypoxia: decompensated heart failure, respiratory failure, recent myocardial infarction, shock.

src.q: Disease which may cause tissue hypoxia (especially acute disease, or worsening of chronic disease) such as: decompensated heart failure, respiratory failure, recent myocardial infarction, shock.

items.t: Hepatic insufficiency, acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism.

src.q: Hepatic insufficiency, acute alcohol intoxication, alcoholism.

items.t: Lactic acidosis (very rare, serious): risk rises with acute worsening of renal function, cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis. Temporarily stop metformin in dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever, reduced fluid intake). Other risk factors: excess alcohol, hepatic insufficiency, poorly controlled diabetes, ketosis, prolonged fasting, hypoxia.

src.q: Lactic acidosis, a very rare, but serious metabolic complication, most often occurs at acute worsening of renal function or cardiorespiratory illness or sepsis.
In case of dehydration (severe diarrhoea or vomiting, fever or reduced fluid intake), metformin should be temporarily discontinued and contact with a health care professional is recommended.
Other risk factors for lactic acidosis are excessive alcohol intake, hepatic insufficiency, inadequately controlled diabetes, ketosis, prolonged fasting and any conditions associated with hypoxia

items.t: Iodinated contrast (intravascular): stop metformin before or at the time of imaging; do not restart until at least 48 hours after, and only when renal function has been re-checked and is stable.

src.q: Metformin should be discontinued prior to or at the time of the imaging procedure and not restarted until at least 48 hours after, provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable

items.t: Surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia: stop metformin at the time of surgery; restart no earlier than 48 hours after surgery or resumption of oral nutrition, once renal function is re-checked and stable.

src.q: Metformin must be discontinued at the time of surgery under general, spinal or epidural anaesthesia.
Therapy may be restarted no earlier than 48 hours following surgery or resumption of oral nutrition and provided that renal function has been re-evaluated and found to be stable.

items.t: Heart failure: stable chronic heart failure - may be used with regular monitoring of cardiac and renal function. Acute and unstable heart failure - contraindicated.

src.q: In patients with stable chronic heart failure, metformin may be used with a regular monitoring of cardiac and renal function.
For patients with acute and unstable heart failure, metformin is contraindicated

items.t: Mitochondrial disease (MELAS, MIDD): metformin is not recommended; withdraw immediately if suggestive signs appear.

src.q: metformin is not recommended due to the risk of lactic acidosis exacerbation and neurologic complications which may lead to worsening of the disease

items.t: Medicines that can acutely impair renal function (antihypertensives, diuretics, NSAIDs) should be started with caution.

src.q: Medicinal products that can acutely impair renal function (such as antihypertensives, diuretics and NSAIDs) should be initiated with caution in metformin-treated patients.

items.t: Metformin alone does not cause hypoglycaemia; caution when combined with insulin or other oral antidiabetics (e.g. sulfonylureas, meglitinides).

src.q: Metformin alone does not cause hypoglycaemia, but caution is advised when it is used in combination with insulin or other oral antidiabetics (e.g. sulfonylureas or meglitinides).

items.t: Prediabetes indication: initiation not recommended at 75 years and older (benefit not established).

src.q: Due to the limited therapeutic efficacy data in the reduction of risk or delay of type 2 diabetes in patients 75 years and older, metformin initiation is not recommended in these patients.

items.t: Prolonged-release: tablet shells may appear in the faeces; this is normal.

src.q: The tablet shells may be present in the faeces. Patients should be advised that this is normal.

items.t: Prolonged-release in PCOS/premenopausal women: may cause ovulation in anovulatory women, which may lead to unintended pregnancy.

src.q: In premenopausal women, treatment with Glucophage SR may result in ovulation in anovulatory women, which may lead to unintended pregnancy.

items.t: Iodinated contrast agents: concomitant use not recommended - stop metformin before/at imaging, restart at least 48 hours after once renal function is stable.

src.q: Iodinated contrast agents Metformin must be discontinued prior to or at the time of the imaging procedure

items.t: Alcohol: not recommended - alcohol intoxication increases lactic acidosis risk, especially with fasting, malnutrition or hepatic impairment.

src.q: Alcohol intoxication is associated with an increased risk of lactic acidosis, particularly in case of fasting, malnutrition or hepatic impairment.

items.t: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics (especially loop diuretics): may impair renal function and raise lactic acidosis risk - close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

src.q: Some medicinal products can adversely affect renal function which may increase the risk of lactic acidosis, e.g. NSAIDs, including selective cyclo-oxygenase (COX) II inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists and diuretics, especially loop diuretics.
When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Glucocorticoids (systemic and local) and sympathomimetics: more frequent blood glucose monitoring may be needed; adjust metformin dose if necessary.

src.q: Medicinal products with intrinsic hyperglycaemic activity (e.g. glucocorticoids (systemic and local routes) and sympathomimetics)
More frequent blood glucose monitoring may be required, especially at the beginning of treatment.

items.t: OCT2 inhibitors (e.g. trimethoprim, cimetidine, dolutegravir, ranolazine): may raise metformin levels - caution, especially in renal impairment; consider dose adjustment.

src.q: Inhibitors of OCT2 (such as cimetidine, dolutegravir, ranolazine, trimethoprim, vandetanib, isavuconazole) may decrease the renal elimination of metformin
Caution is therefore advised, especially in patients with renal impairment, when these drugs are co-administered with metformin, as metformin plasma concentration may increase.

items.t: Assess GFR before starting and at least annually; every 3 to 6 months in the elderly and those at risk of progression. The SmPC table uses GFR in mL/min.

renal function should be assessed more frequently, e.g. every 3-6 months

items.t: GFR 60-89 mL/min: maximum 2000 mg/day; dose reduction may be considered as renal function declines.

src.q: 60-89 2000 mg Dose reduction may be considered in relation to declining renal function.

items.t: GFR 30-44 mL/min: maximum 1000 mg/day (same lactic acidosis review and half starting dose apply).

src.q: 30-44 1000 mg <30 - Metformin is contraindicated.

indicates no increased risk of congenital abnormalities nor feto/neonatal toxicity after exposure to metformin in the periconceptional phase and/or during pregnancy

src.q: The first injection of Metoject PEN should be performed under direct medical supervision.

items.t: Oncology regimens may use different (sometimes daily) schedules - these are specialist protocols, not autoimmune dosing.

src.q: For the treatment of cancer in which regimens vary and can require daily administration of methotrexate

items.t: MAXIMUM WEEKLY DOSE - SOURCES DIFFER: one tablet SmPC (RA, psoriasis) and the pen SmPC: in general not more than 25 mg per WEEK (pen: exceptionally up to 30 mg per WEEK). Another tablet SmPC (RA): not more than 20 mg per WEEK. All three SmPCs say doses above 20 mg per WEEK markedly increase toxicity, especially bone marrow suppression. The dose is ONCE WEEKLY, never daily.

src.q: should not exceed a total weekly dose of 25 mg
A weekly dose of 25 mg should in general not be exceeded.
should not exceed a total weekly dose of 20 mg
Doses exceeding 20 mg week can be associated with a substantial increase in toxicity
Doses exceeding 20 mg/week are associated with significant increase in toxicity, especially bone marrow suppression
specifically, that it should not be taken daily

items.t: Rheumatoid arthritis, tablets: usual 7.5-15 mg ONCE WEEKLY (never daily). Adjust gradually; total weekly dose not more than 25 mg. Over 20 mg/week markedly increases toxicity. Then reduce to lowest effective dose (usually within 6 weeks).

src.q: Rheumatoid arthritis The usual dose is 7.5 - 15 mg once weekly. The dose may be adjusted gradually to achieve an optimal response but should not exceed a total weekly dose of 25 mg.
Doses exceeding 20 mg per week can be associated with significant increase in toxicity, especially bone marrow suppression.

items.t: Rheumatoid arthritis, tablets (another tablet SmPC - differs from the one above): test dose 5-10 mg one week before; start 7.5 mg ONCE WEEKLY; total weekly dose should NOT exceed 20 mg per WEEK.

src.q: It is recommended that a test dose of 5-10 mg should be administered, one week prior to therapy to detect idiosyncratic adverse reactions.
the recommended initial dose is 7.5 mg methotrexate once weekly. The schedule may be adjusted gradually to achieve an optimal response but should not exceed a total weekly dose of 20 mg.

items.t: Psoriasis / psoriatic arthritis, tablets. One tablet SmPC: test dose 2.5-5 mg, check labs one week later; then usual 7.5-15 mg ONCE WEEKLY, up to 25 mg per WEEK if needed; then reduce to the lowest effective dose. Another tablet SmPC (psoriasis): test dose 5-10 mg one week before; 10-25 mg ONCE A WEEK, adjusted to response.

src.q: Before starting treatment it is advisable to give the patient a test dose of 2.5-5.0 mg to exclude unexpected toxic effects.
The usual dose is 7.5-15 mg taken once weekly. As necessary, the total weekly dose can be increased up to 25 mg.
It is recommended that a test dose of 5-10 mg should be administered, one week prior to therapy to detect idiosyncratic adverse reactions.
10-25 mg orally once a week and adjusted by the patient's response is recommended

items.t: Rheumatoid arthritis, pen: start 7.5 mg ONCE WEEKLY subcutaneously; increase by 2.5 mg per week as needed; generally not more than 25 mg per WEEK. Response in about 4-8 weeks; then reduce to lowest effective maintenance dose.

src.q: The recommended initial dose is 7.5 mg of methotrexate once weekly , administered subcutaneously.
A weekly dose of 25 mg should in general not be exceeded.

items.t: Psoriasis / psoriatic arthritis, pen: test dose 5-10 mg one week before; start 7.5 mg ONCE WEEKLY; generally not more than 25 mg per WEEK. Exceptionally up to 30 mg per WEEK (toxicity rises markedly).

src.q: It is recommended that a test dose of 5-10 mg should be administered parenterally, one week prior to therapy to detect idiosyncratic adverse reactions.
In a few exceptional cases a higher dose might be clinically justified, but should not exceed a maximum weekly dose of 30 mg of methotrexate as toxicity will markedly increase.

items.t: Crohn's disease, pen: induction 25 mg per WEEK subcutaneously (response in 8-12 weeks); maintenance 15 mg per WEEK.

src.q: Induction treatment: 25 mg/week administered subcutaneously. Response to treatment can be expected after approximately 8 to 12 weeks. Maintenance treatment: 15 mg/week administered subcutaneously.

items.t: Switching oral to injection: a dose reduction may be needed (variable oral bioavailability).

src.q: If changing the oral application to parenteral administration a reduction of the dose may be required due to the variable bioavailability of methotrexate after oral administration.

items.t: Elderly: use with extreme caution; consider dose reduction (reduced liver/kidney function and folate stores).

src.q: Methotrexate should be used with extreme caution in elderly patients, a dose reduction should be considered due to reduced liver and kidney function as well as lower folate reserves which occur with increased age.

items.t: Folic acid (SPS, RA): 5 mg ONCE WEEKLY on a DIFFERENT day from methotrexate; can increase to 10 mg weekly if side effects; continue for as long as methotrexate. Off-label use.

src.q: Folic acid 5mg weekly, on a different day to the methotrexate dose, is the most commonly recommended regimen from clinical studies and national guidance.
The dose can be increased to 10mg if the person experiences any adverse effects to the methotrexate.
Use of folic acid to reduce adverse effects is off-label.

items.t: Under 3 years: not recommended (insufficient data).

src.q: The use in children below 3 years of age is not recommended as insufficient data on efficacy and safety are available for this population (see section 4.4).
Use in children <3 years of age is not recommended as insufficient data on efficacy and safety is available for this population (see section 4.4).

items.t: JIA (pen, under 16 years): 10-15 mg/m2 body surface area ONCE WEEKLY; up to 20 mg/m2 ONCE WEEKLY in refractory cases (monitor more often). Subcutaneous only; refer to a paediatric rheumatology specialist.

src.q: The recommended dose is 10-15 mg/m² body surface area (BSA)/ once weekly .
Patients with JIA should always be referred to a rheumatology specialist in the treatment of children/adolescents.

items.t: ALL maintenance (tablets, 3 years and over): within specialist protocols; usually 20-40 mg/m2 ONCE WEEKLY.

src.q: Common accepted single doses lie in the range of 20-40 mg/m² body surface area and are usually given once weekly.

items.t: Crohn's disease: not enough paediatric experience to recommend the pen.

src.q: There is not sufficient experience in the paediatric population to recommend Metoject PEN for the treatment of Crohn's disease in this population.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to methotrexate or excipients.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to methotrexate or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Significantly impaired hepatic function (pen: severe liver impairment; bilirubin over 5 mg/dl (85.5 µmol/l)).

src.q: Significantly impaired hepatic function
If bilirubin is >5 mg/dl (85.5 µmol/l), methotrexate is contraindicated.

items.t: Significantly impaired renal function: CrCl under 30 ml/min.

src.q: severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min., see section 4.2 and section 4.4)

items.t: Alcoholism / alcohol abuse.

src.q: Alcoholism
alcohol abuse

items.t: Pre-existing blood dyscrasias (bone marrow hypoplasia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, significant anaemia).

src.q: Pre-existing blood dyscrasias, such as bone marrow hypoplasia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or significant anaemia

items.t: Severe acute or chronic infections; immunodeficiency syndromes.

src.q: Severe acute or chronic infections and immunodeficiency syndromes

items.t: Stomatitis, oral ulcers, known active GI ulcer disease.

src.q: Stomatitis, ulcers of the oral cavity and known active gastrointestinal ulcer disease

items.t: Pregnancy (one tablet SmPC and the pen SmPC: non-oncological use; another tablet SmPC: any use) and breastfeeding.

src.q: Additionally for non-oncological indications - Pregnancy (see section 4.6).
Breast-feeding (see section 4.6)
Methotrexate is teratogenic and should not be given during pregnancy or to mothers who are breast-feeding

items.t: Live vaccines must not be given during treatment.

src.q: During methotrexate therapy concurrent vaccination with live vaccines must not be carried out.

items.t: One tablet SmPC 4.3 also lists: liver disease including fibrosis, cirrhosis, recent or active hepatitis; active infectious disease.

src.q: Liver disease including fibrosis, cirrhosis, recent or active hepatitis
Active infectious disease

items.t: One tablet SmPC 4.3: methotrexate tablets should not be used with drugs with antifolate properties (e.g. co-trimoxazole; trimethoprim is also a folate antagonist).

src.q: Methotrexate tablets should not be used concomitantly with drugs with antifolate properties (e.g. co-trimoxazole)

items.t: One tablet SmPC 4.3: after use by a man or a woman, conception must be avoided with effective contraception for at least 6 months (see reproductive).

src.q: Following administration to a man or woman conception should be avoided by using an effective contraceptive method for at least 6 months after using Methotrexate 2.5 mg tablets

items.t: Bone marrow suppression can occur suddenly even at apparently safe doses; stop immediately for a serious fall in white cells or platelets.

src.q: Methotrexate-induced haematopoietic suppression may occur abruptly and with apparently safe dosages. Any serious decrease in leucocyte or platelet counts indicates the immediate discontinuation of treatment

items.t: Liver toxicity: avoid alcohol; avoid other hepatotoxic medicines unless clearly needed. Fibrosis/cirrhosis may occur with normal LFTs.

src.q: Additional hepatotoxic medicinal products should not be given during treatment with methotrexate unless clearly necessary. Alcohol consumption should be avoided
Histological changes, fibrosis and more rarely liver cirrhosis may not be preceded by abnormal liver function tests.

items.t: Lung toxicity (pneumonitis) at any dose, even 7.5 mg/week: stop if dry cough, dyspnoea or fever; exclude infection; do not restart if methotrexate lung disease.

src.q: Methotrexate-induced lung diseases such as pneumonitis can occur acutely and at any time during treatment, are not always completely reversible and have already been observed at all doses (including low doses of 7.5 mg/week).
If methotrexate-induced lung disease is suspected, treatment with corticosteroids should be initiated and treatment with methotrexate should not be restarted.

items.t: Dehydration (vomiting, diarrhoea, stomatitis) raises toxicity: stop methotrexate until resolved. Diarrhoea/ulcerative stomatitis need stopping (risk of fatal perforation).

src.q: In this case, treatment with methotrexate must be discontinued until the symptoms have disappeared.
Diarrhoea and ulcerative stomatitis may be signs of toxic effects and require the discontinuation of treatment

items.t: Renal impairment and NSAIDs: with any renal impairment (including mild), combining with NSAIDs is not recommended; monitor more often.

src.q: If risk factors such as renal function disorders, including mild renal impairment, are present, combined administration with NSAIDs is not recommended.

items.t: Pleural effusion / ascites (third space): slower elimination; drain before starting; dose reduction or stopping may be needed.

src.q: Pleural effusions and ascites should be drained prior to initiation of methotrexate treatment (see section 4.2).

items.t: Insulin-dependent diabetes: increased caution (cirrhosis without raised transaminases reported).

src.q: Increased caution should be exercised in patients with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus

items.t: Impaired pulmonary function and inactive chronic infections (zoster, TB, hepatitis B/C): particular caution (reactivation).

src.q: Particular caution is required in patients with impaired pulmonary function.

items.t: Photosensitivity: avoid intense sun/UV; use sun protection.

src.q: Patients should use adequate sun-protection to protect themselves from intense sunlight.

items.t: Folate-containing vitamin products may reduce effectiveness. Check vitamin B12 before folic acid, especially over 50 years.

src.q: It is recommended to check levels of vitamin B12 prior to initiating folic acid supplementation, particularly in adults aged over 50 years, as folic acid intake may mask a vitamin B12 deficiency.

items.t: Folate deficiency may increase methotrexate toxicity: particular care if folic acid deficiency is present.

src.q: Particular care is therefore advisable in the presence of existing folic acid deficiency.
Folate deficiency may increase methotrexate toxicity

items.t: One tablet SmPC: extreme caution in peptic ulcer or ulcerative colitis, debility, very young or old age, and psychiatric disorders.

src.q: Extreme caution should be exercised if there is peptic ulcer or ulcerative colitis.
Methotrexate should be used with extreme caution in - debility - extreme youth (see section 4.2) - old age (see section 4.2) - psychiatric disorders

items.t: Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole: risk of severe bone marrow suppression (may be delayed). SPS: avoid; if unavoidable, counsel, frequent FBC and extra FBC monitoring for at least 2 months. One tablet SmPC lists use with antifolate drugs (e.g. co-trimoxazole) under 4.3 Contraindications ("should not be used concomitantly").

src.q: Avoid prescribing co-trimoxazole or trimethoprim with methotrexate, due to the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.
consider the additional FBC monitoring, above routine monitoring (SPS page) , for at least 2 months
Methotrexate tablets should not be used concomitantly with drugs with antifolate properties (e.g. co-trimoxazole)

items.t: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen): increased methotrexate and renal toxicity. SPS: use with caution on specialist advice; avoid OTC NSAIDs without advice. One tablet SmPC: not recommended if any renal impairment (including mild). Another tablet SmPC: monitor methotrexate dosage when an NSAID is started (fatal toxicity reported).

src.q: Use NSAIDs in combination with methotrexate with caution on the advice of the specialist (for example, rheumatologist).
There is also a possibility of increased toxicity when low dose methotrexate and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicinal products or salicylates are combined.

Methotrexate dosage should be monitored if concomitant treatment with aspirin, ibuprofen or indometacin (NSAIDs) is commenced, as concomitant use of NSAID's has been associated with fatal methotrexate toxicity.

items.t: Penicillins (e.g. amoxicillin): reduced renal clearance of methotrexate. SPS: short courses (up to 10 days) with caution; watch for toxicity.

src.q: If the duration of penicillin is short (up to 10 days), consider using with caution and advise to monitor for signs of toxicity.

items.t: PPIs (e.g. omeprazole): delayed methotrexate elimination reported. SPS (low-dose methotrexate): evidence limited; no additional action; H2-receptor antagonist if an alternative is needed. One tablet SmPC: avoid PPIs with HIGH-dose methotrexate, especially in renal impairment.

src.q: Concomitant administration of methotrexate and omeprazole has led to delayed renal elimination of methotrexate.
Evidence to support a clinically significant interaction is limited.
Concomitant use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and high dose methotrexate should be avoided, especially in patients with renal impairment.

items.t: Ciprofloxacin: reduced renal clearance of methotrexate (raised levels, toxicity). Ciprofloxacin SmPC: concomitant use not recommended.

src.q: Penicillins (e.g. amoxicillin), glycopeptides, sulfonamides, ciprofloxacin and cefalotin can, in individual cases, reduce the renal clearance of methotrexate
The concomitant use of ciprofloxacin with methotrexate is not recommended

items.t: Statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin): liver toxicity possible; SPS: no additional action beyond routine monitoring.

src.q: Taking methotrexate and statins (for example, atorvastatin or simvastatin) can increase the risk of liver toxicity.

items.t: Hydroxychloroquine: no increase in methotrexate toxicity generally expected (pen SmPC).

src.q: An increase in the toxic effects of methotrexate is, in general, not to be expected when Metoject PEN is administered simultaneously with other antirheumatic medicinal products (e.g. gold compounds, penicillamine, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, azathioprine).

items.t: Others (not in master list): live vaccines (must not), nitrous oxide (avoid), leflunomide, metamizole (avoid), levetiracetam, ciclosporin, retinoids, probenecid, caffeine/theophylline.

src.q: Concurrent administration of metamizole and methotrexate can increase the haematotoxic effect of methotrexate, especially in elderly patients. Therefore, coadministration should be avoided.

items.t: Dose by creatinine clearance (CrCl): 60 ml/min or more = 100% dose; 30-59 ml/min = 50% dose; under 30 ml/min = must NOT be used.

src.q: Creatinine clearance (ml/min) Dose ≥ 60 100 % 30-59 50 % < 30 Methotrexate must not be used
Creatinine clearance (ml/min) ≥60 30-59 <30 Dose 100% 50% Metoject PEN must not be used

items.t: If serum creatinine rises, reduce the dose; monitor renal function and urinalysis. Monitor more often if renal function may be compromised (e.g. elderly) or with NSAIDs.

src.q: Renal function should be monitored by renal function tests and urinalyses. If serum creatinine levels are increased, the dose should be reduced.

items.t: SPS action level: creatinine rise over 30% above baseline in 12 months, or calculated GFR under 60 ml/min/1.73m2 - repeat in 1 week; if still more than 30% from baseline, withhold and discuss with specialist.

src.q: Creatinine increase greater than 30% above baseline over 12 months Calculated GFR less than 60ml/min/1.73m2 (repeat in 1 week, if still more than 30% from baseline, withhold and discuss with specialist team)

items.t: One tablet SmPC (oncology-wide): contraindicated if CrCl under 30 ml/min for doses under 100 mg/m2, and under 60 ml/min for doses over 100 mg/m2.

src.q: Severe/significantly impaired renal function (creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/min) for methotrexate doses <100 mg/m2, and moderate renal impairment (creatinine clearance less than 60 ml/min) for methotrexate doses >100 mg/m2

items.t: Contraindicated in significantly impaired hepatic function. Otherwise use with great caution, if at all, in significant current or previous liver disease (especially alcohol-related).

src.q: Methotrexate should be administered with great caution, if at all, to patients with significant current or previous liver disease, especially if due to alcohol.

items.t: One tablet SmPC 4.3: contraindicated in liver disease including fibrosis, cirrhosis, recent or active hepatitis (stricter than the other tablet SmPC and the pen SmPC, which say "great caution, if at all" for significant liver disease and contraindicate significant/severe hepatic impairment).

src.q: Methotrexate is contra-indicated in the presence of:
Liver disease including fibrosis, cirrhosis, recent or active hepatitis

items.t: Pen SmPC: bilirubin over 5 mg/dl (85.5 µmol/l) = contraindicated.

src.q: If bilirubin is >5 mg/dl (85.5 µmol/l), methotrexate is contraindicated.

items.t: Persistent liver enzyme rise: consider dose reduction or stopping. SPS: consider stopping and contact specialist if AST and/or ALT over 100 units/L.

src.q: In the event of a persistent increase in liver enzymes, consideration should be given to reducing the dose or discontinuing therapy.
AST and/or ALT greater than 100units/L

items.t: Contraindicated in pregnancy for non-cancer indications (powerful teratogen; miscarriage 42.5% vs 22.5% at low doses). Exclude pregnancy before starting.

src.q: Methotrexate is contraindicated during pregnancy in non-oncological indications (see section 4.3).
In non-oncologic indications, the absence of pregnancy must be confirmed before methotrexate is used.

items.t: If pregnancy occurs during treatment or within 6 months after: give advice on risk and offer ultrasound checks.

src.q: If pregnancy occurs during treatment with methotrexate and up to six months thereafter, medical advice should be given regarding the risk of harmful effects on the child associated with treatment and ultrasonography examinations should be performed to confirm normal foetal development.

items.t: BUMPS: should not be used in pregnancy for autoimmune disease; usually advised to wait at least 3 months after stopping before trying to conceive (differs from the SmPC 6-month contraception period for women).

src.q: Methotrexate should not be used in pregnancy to treat autoimmune diseases.
You will usually be advised by your specialist to wait at least three months before trying to conceive.

items.t: Contraindicated; stop breastfeeding before treatment.

src.q: As methotrexate passes into breast milk and may cause toxicity in nursing infants, treatment is contraindicated during the lactation period (see section 4.3). Breast-feeding is therefore to be stopped prior to treatment.

items.t: WOMEN: effective contraception during treatment and for at least 6 MONTHS after stopping (all three SmPCs). Confirm absence of pregnancy before starting (non-oncological use); repeat pregnancy tests as clinically required.

src.q: Women must not get pregnant during methotrexate therapy and effective contraception must be used during treatment with methotrexate and at least 6 months thereafter (see section 4.4).
In non-oncologic indications, the absence of pregnancy must be confirmed before methotrexate is used.

items.t: MEN: patient or female partner should use reliable contraception during treatment and for at least 3 MONTHS after stopping; no semen donation during and for 3 months after (SmPC).

src.q: As precautionary measures, sexually active male patients or their female partners are recommended to use reliable contraception during treatment of the male patient and for at least 3 months after cessation of methotrexate.
Men should not donate semen during therapy or for 3 months following discontinuation of methotrexate.

items.t: SOURCES DIFFER for men: one tablet SmPC (sections 4.3 and 4.4) says avoid conception for at least 6 MONTHS after stopping, for BOTH men and women; its own section 4.6, and the other tablet SmPC and the pen SmPC, say 3 MONTHS for men. BUMPS: specialists usually advise waiting at least 3 months before trying to conceive.

src.q: Following administration to a man or woman conception should be avoided by using an effective contraceptive method for at least 6 months after using Methotrexate 2.5 mg tablets
Following administration to man or woman conception should be avoided by using an effective contraceptive method for at least 6 months after stopping methotrexate.

As precautionary measures, sexually active male patients or their female partners are recommended to use reliable contraception during treatment of the male patient and for at least 3 months after cessation of methotrexate.
You will usually be advised by your specialist to wait at least three months before trying to conceive.

items.t: Fertility: oligospermia, menstrual dysfunction, amenorrhoea; usually reversible after stopping.

src.q: These effects appear to be reversible after discontinuation of therapy in most cases.

items.t: Very common: stomatitis, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite; raised liver enzymes/bilirubin. Common: leukopenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, headache, tiredness, drowsiness, pneumonia, pneumonitis, oral ulcers, diarrhoea, rash, pruritus.

src.q: Most frequently observed (very common) adverse reactions of methotrexate include gastrointestinal disorders (e.g. stomatitis, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, loss of appetite) and abnormal liver function tests

Other frequently occurring (common) adverse reactions are leukopenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, headache, tiredness, drowsiness, pneumonia, interstitial alveolitis/pneumonitis often associated with eosinophilia, oral ulcers, diarrhoea, exanthema, erythema and pruritus.

items.t: Most serious: bone marrow suppression, lung toxicity, liver toxicity, kidney toxicity, neurotoxicity, thromboembolism, anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

src.q: Most serious adverse reactions of methotrexate include bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity, hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, neurotoxicity, thromboembolic events, anaphylactic shock and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

items.t: Overdose (e.g. daily instead of weekly): blood disorders and GI ulceration/bleeding; some fatal (sepsis, renal failure, aplastic anaemia). Patients must seek urgent help if they think they took too much.

src.q: Overdose of methotrexate can lead to serious adverse effects such as haematopoietic disorders (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia, and pancytopenia) and gastrointestinal reactions
Patients should be advised to seek urgent medical attention if they think they have taken too much methotrexate.

items.t: Ulcerative stomatitis and diarrhoea: stop methotrexate (risk of fatal perforation).

src.q: Ulcerative stomatitis and diarrhoea require discontinuation of methotrexate therapy because of the risk of ulcerative enteritis and fatal intestinal perforation.

items.t: SmPC baseline: FBC with differential and platelets, liver enzymes, bilirubin, serum albumin, chest X-ray, renal function. Exclude TB and hepatitis B and C if indicated.

src.q: Complete blood count with differential blood count and platelets, liver enzymes, bilirubin, serum albumin, chest X-ray and renal function tests.

items.t: SPS baseline also lists blood pressure, weight, height, HIV, hepatitis B and C; TB screening and VZV immunity to consider. (SPS page is being updated to the Nov 2025 BSR guideline.)

src.q: The British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) guideline for the prescription and monitoring of conventional synthetic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs was published in November 2025.

items.t: One tablet SmPC, ongoing: FBC, LFTs, renal tests and mouth/throat check WEEKLY for the first 2 weeks, then every 2 weeks for a month, then at least monthly for 6 months, then at least every 3 months. More often after dose increases and in elderly. Another tablet SmPC: FBC, liver and renal tests (with urinalysis) every week until stable, then every 2 to 3 months.

src.q: The tests below must be conducted weekly in the first two weeks, then every two weeks for a month; thereafter, depending on the leucocyte count and the stability of the patient, at least once a month during the next six months and then at least every three months.

Full blood count (including haematocrit), hepatic and renal function tests (including urinalysis) should be carried out every week until treatment is stabilized, thereafter every 2 to 3 months throughout treatment.

items.t: SPS (rheumatology): FBC, LFT, creatinine/eGFR and albumin every 2 weeks for at least 6 weeks, then monthly for 3-12 months; once stable at least every 12 weeks.

src.q: Rheumatology patients Every 2 weeks for at least 6 weeks; then every month for 3-12 months
Rheumatology patients At least every 12 weeks

items.t: SPS stop/contact specialist: WCC under 3.5 x 10^9/L; neutrophils under 1.6 x 10^9/L; unexplained eosinophilia over 0.5 x 10^9/L; platelets under 140 x 10^9/L; unexplained albumin under 30 g/L; MCV over 105 fL; AST/ALT over 100 units/L. Also watch falling trends.

src.q: WCC less than 3.5 x 10 9/L Neutrophils less than 1.6 x 109/L Unexplained eosinophilia more than 0.5x 10 9/L Platelets less than 140 x 109/L Unexplained fall in serum albumin less than 30g/L
A downward trend of FBC and neutrophil count or an upward trend in liver transaminases could be a sign of toxicity, even if the absolute levels are normal.

items.t: Stop for: serious fall in WBC or platelets; suspected pneumonitis; ulcerative stomatitis or diarrhoea; GI bleeding.

src.q: Following the occurrence of haematemesis, black-coloured stools or blood in the stools, treatment must be discontinued.

items.t: ONCE A WEEK on the SAME, agreed day of the week - never daily. Do not divide the weekly dose (MHRA removed advice on dividing the dose).

src.q: It must be explicitly pointed out to the patient that for the therapy of rheumatic diseases, psoriasis or severe psoriatic arthritis methotrexate is administered only once a week.
Advice on dividing the once-weekly dose is being removed from the product information since this was identified as a source of confusion that could lead to medication error.

items.t: Pen: subcutaneous only, single use, use all contents. Sites: upper thighs or abdomen (not around the navel). Fixed day each week.

src.q: It is advisable to determine an appropriate fixed day of the week for the injection.
The medicinal product is for single use only.

items.t: Folic acid on a different day from methotrexate (SPS).

src.q: Folic acid supplements are usually avoided on the day of oral or subcutaneous methotrexate.

items.t: Take methotrexate ONCE A WEEK only, on your set day. NEVER take it daily - this can be fatal. Seek urgent help if you think you took too much.

src.q: inform the patient and their caregivers of the potentially fatal risk of accidental overdose if methotrexate is taken more frequently than once a week; specifically, that it should not be taken daily

items.t: Carry the patient card; write your weekly day on it; show it to any health professional (e.g. hospital admission).

src.q: carry it with them to alert any healthcare professionals they consult who are not familiar with their methotrexate treatment about their dosing schedule

items.t: Report sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever, bruising or bleeding, shortness of breath or persistent cough at once.

src.q: Counsel the person to report signs of methotrexate toxicity, for example sore throat, mouth ulcers, unexplained bruising or bleeding.
Patients should be informed of the risks of pneumonia and advised to contact their doctor immediately if they develop a persistent cough or persistent dyspnoea.

items.t: Do not buy NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen) over the counter without asking the doctor or pharmacist. Ask before any new medicine.

src.q: Ensure you counsel people taking methotrexate to avoid buying NSAIDs over-the-counter (e.g. oral ibuprofen or analgesic doses of aspirin) without discussing with their doctor or pharmacist first.

items.t: Avoid alcohol; use sun protection; avoid excess caffeine drinks.

src.q: Consumption of alcohol should be avoided or minimised (see section 4.4).

items.t: Effective contraception: women during treatment and for at least 6 months after; men (or their female partner) during treatment and for at least 3 months after. One tablet SmPC says 6 months for men too.

src.q: Female patients of reproductive potential must be counselled regarding pregnancy prevention and planning.
If women of a sexually mature age are treated, effective contraception must be used during treatment and for at least six months after.
Following administration to a man or woman conception should be avoided by using an effective contraceptive method for at least 6 months after using Methotrexate 2.5 mg tablets
Naprosyn 500mg Tablets: Each tablet contains 500mg naproxen

formulations.label: Gastro-resistant tablets
formulations.note: Swallow whole; do not break or crush. Licensed in adults only (not recommended under 16).

src.q: Naproxen Gastro-Resistant tablets should be swallowed whole and not broken or crushed.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Adults: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthrosis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, acute musculoskeletal disorders, dysmenorrhoea. Children: juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.

src.q: Adults: Treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthrosis (degenerative arthritis), ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, acute musculoskeletal disorders and dysmenorrhoea. Children: Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis

items.t: Gastro-resistant (adults): rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthrosis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal disorders, dysmenorrhoea (acute gout not listed).

src.q: Naproxen is indicated in adults for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthrosis (degenerative arthritis), ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal disorders

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the SmPCs or the MHRA pages accessed.

items.t: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis: 500 mg-1 g daily in 2 doses 12 hours apart (or once daily). Loading dose of 750 mg or 1 g/day in the acute phase for severe night pain/morning stiffness, switching from high-dose anti-rheumatic, or pain-predominant osteoarthrosis.

src.q: Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis 500mg to 1g taken in 2 doses at 12-hour intervals or alternatively, as a single administration.
a loading dose of 750mg or 1g per day for the acute phase is recommended

items.t: Acute gout (tablets): 750 mg at once, then 250 mg every 8 hours until the attack has passed.

src.q: Acute gout 750mg at once then 250mg every 8 hours until the attack has passed.

items.t: Acute musculoskeletal disorders and dysmenorrhoea: 500 mg initially, then 250 mg every 6-8 hours as needed; maximum 1250 mg/day after the first day.

src.q: Acute musculoskeletal disorders and dysmenorrhoea 500mg initially followed by 250mg at 6 - 8 hour intervals as needed, with a maximum daily dose after the first day of 1250mg.

items.t: Older people: lowest effective dose for the shortest time; monitor regularly for GI bleeding. Gastro-resistant: start at the lowest recommended dose, especially in older people.

src.q: The patient should be monitored regularly for GI bleeding during NSAID therapy.
Therapy should be started at the lowest recommended dose, especially in older people.

items.t: Review treatment at regular intervals; stop if no benefit or intolerance.

src.q: Treatment should be reviewed at regular intervals and discontinued if no benefit is seen or intolerance occurs.

items.t: Tablets, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (over 5 years): 10 mg/kg/day in 2 doses 12 hours apart. Not recommended for any other indication under 16 years.

src.q: Paediatric population (over 5 years) For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis: 10mg/kg/day taken in 2 doses at 12-hour intervals. Naprosyn is not recommended for use in any other indication in children under 16 years of age.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets: not recommended under 16 years.

src.q: Naproxen is not recommended for use in children under 16 years of age.

items.t: Active or history of peptic ulceration or active GI bleeding; history of GI bleeding or perforation related to previous NSAIDs.

src.q: Active or history of peptic ulceration or active gastrointestinal bleeding (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding). History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, related to previous NSAIDs therapy.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to naproxen or naproxen sodium. Should not be given if aspirin or other NSAIDs induce asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps or urticaria (potentially fatal).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to naproxen, naproxen sodium, or any of the excipients.
Naprosyn should not be given to patients in whom aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory/analgesic drugs induce the syndrome of asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps or urticaria.

items.t: Severe renal, hepatic or heart failure; baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute; last trimester of pregnancy.

src.q: Severe renal, hepatic or heart failure
Naprosyn is contraindicated in patients with baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute
Naproxen is contraindicated during the last trimester of pregnancy

items.t: GI bleeding, ulceration or perforation can occur at any time and can be fatal; risk rises with dose, ulcer history and age. Start at the lowest dose; consider misoprostol or a PPI in at-risk patients and with low-dose aspirin. Withdraw if GI bleeding or ulceration occurs.

src.q: Combination therapy with protective agents (e.g. misoprostol or proton pump inhibitors) should be considered for these patients
When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving Naprosyn, the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Cardiovascular: naproxen 1000 mg daily may carry a lower thrombotic risk but some risk cannot be excluded. Uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease: only after careful consideration.

src.q: Although data suggest that the use of naproxen (1000mg daily) may be associated with a lower risk, some risk cannot be excluded.

Patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure, established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, and/or cerebrovascular disease should only be treated with naproxen after careful consideration.

items.t: Renal: use with great caution in impaired renal function; monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance and keep hydrated. Assess renal function before and during treatment when renal blood flow is compromised (volume depletion, cirrhosis, sodium restriction, heart failure, renal disease, diuretics, older people).

src.q: it should be used with great caution in patients with impaired renal function and the monitoring of serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance is advised and patients should be adequately hydrated
should have renal function assessed before and during Naprosyn therapy

items.t: Coagulation disorders or drugs affecting haemostasis: observe carefully; naproxen prolongs bleeding time.

src.q: Patients who have coagulation disorders or are receiving drug therapy that interferes with haemostasis should be carefully observed if naproxen- containing products are administered.

items.t: Asthma or allergic disease: bronchospasm may be precipitated. Ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease: give with care. SLE / mixed connective tissue disease: aseptic meningitis risk.

src.q: Bronchospasm may be precipitated in patients suffering from, or with a history of, bronchial asthma or allergic disease.
NSAIDs should be given with care to patients with a history of gastrointestinal disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease)

items.t: Liver: LFT elevations and severe hepatic reactions (including fatal hepatitis) reported. Visual disturbance: ophthalmological examination.

src.q: Severe hepatic reactions, including jaundice and hepatitis (some cases of hepatitis have been fatal) have been reported
patients who develop visual disturbances during treatment with naproxen-containing products should have an ophthalmological examination

items.t: Serious skin reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop at the first rash, mucosal lesion or sign of hypersensitivity; never restart after SJS/TEN/DRESS.

src.q: Naprosyn should be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions, or any other sign of hypersensitivity.
treatment with Naprosyn must not be restarted and should be permanently discontinued

items.t: Long-term use: regular medical supervision; prolonged use in older or debilitated patients is not recommended.

src.q: Patients treated with NSAIDs long-term should undergo regular medical supervision to monitor for adverse events.
Prolonged use of NSAIDs in these patients is not recommended.

items.t: If steroids are reduced or stopped during therapy, taper slowly and watch for adrenal insufficiency.

src.q: If steroid dosage is reduced or eliminated during therapy, the steroid dosage should be reduced slowly

items.t: Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin, heparin): considered unsafe unless under direct medical supervision (NSAIDs may enhance anticoagulant effects).

src.q: It is considered unsafe to take NSAIDs in combination with anti-coagulants such as warfarin or heparin unless under direct medical supervision

items.t: Other NSAIDs including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors: avoid. Regular naproxen for more than one day may inhibit the antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin.

src.q: Avoid concomitant use of two or more NSAIDs (including aspirin) as this may increase the risk of adverse effects
concomitant naproxen usage for more than one day consecutively may inhibit the effect of low-dose acetylsalicylic acid on platelet activity

items.t: Antiplatelets and SSRIs: increased GI bleeding risk. Corticosteroids: increased GI ulceration or bleeding (caution).

src.q: There is an increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding (see Section 4.4) when anti-platelet agents and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are combined with NSAIDs.
caution should be taken when co-administering with cortico-steroids because of the increased risk of gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding

items.t: Diuretics: decreased diuretic effect and higher nephrotoxicity risk (caution). Antihypertensives: reduced effect. ACE inhibitors / ARBs: increased risk of renal impairment, especially with poor renal function.

src.q: Caution is advised when Naprosyn is co-administered with diuretics as there can be a decreased diuretic effect.
Concomitant use of NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin-II receptor antagonists may increase the risk of renal impairment, especially in patients with pre-existing poor renal function

items.t: Methotrexate: caution (possible enhanced toxicity from reduced tubular secretion).

src.q: Caution is advised where methotrexate is given concurrently because of possible enhancement of its toxicity

items.t: Highly protein-bound drugs (hydantoins, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas, anticoagulants): observe for overdosage; adjust dose if needed. Quinolones: possible increased convulsion risk. Lithium, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, cardiac glycosides, probenecid, mifepristone, zidovudine also interact.

src.q: Patients simultaneously receiving Naprosyn and a hydantoin, sulfonamide or sulfonylurea should be observed for adjustment of dose if required.
Patients taking quinolones may have an increased risk of developing convulsions.

items.t: Antacids or colestyramine may delay (not reduce) absorption.

src.q: Concomitant administration of antacid or colestyramine can delay the absorption of naproxen but does not affect its extent.

items.t: Warfarin (warfarin SmPC): NSAIDs should be avoided if possible, or given with caution and increased clinical and laboratory monitoring.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring

items.t: Spironolactone (spironolactone SmPC): use with NSAIDs may lead to severe hyperkalaemia. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril SmPC): worsening renal function and raised serum potassium; caution, keep hydrated, monitor renal function.

src.q: may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Metformin (metformin SmPC): close monitoring of renal function is necessary when an NSAID is started or used with metformin.

src.q: When starting or using such products in combination with metformin, close monitoring of renal function is necessary.

items.t: Methotrexate (SPS, methotrexate SmPC): increased risk of methotrexate toxicity; use with caution on specialist advice; not recommended if renal impairment (even mild) is present.

src.q: Use NSAIDs in combination with methotrexate with caution on the advice of the specialist (for example, rheumatologist).
If risk factors such as renal function disorders, including mild renal impairment, are present, combined administration with NSAIDs is not recommended.

items.t: Contraindicated if baseline creatinine clearance (CrCl) is less than 30 ml/minute (metabolites accumulate; haemodialysis does not lower naproxen levels).

src.q: Naprosyn is contraindicated in patients with baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute because accumulation of naproxen metabolites has been seen in patients with severe renal failure or those on dialysis
Haemodialysis does not decrease the plasma concentration of naproxen because of the high degree of protein binding.

items.t: Renal impairment (CrCl 30 ml/minute or more): consider a lower dose; use with great caution; monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance.

src.q: A lower dose should be considered in patients with renal or hepatic impairment.
it should be used with great caution in patients with impaired renal function

items.t: MHRA: patients at risk of renal impairment or failure (particularly elderly) should avoid NSAIDs if possible.

src.q: patients at risk of renal impairment or renal failure (particularly elderly people) should avoid NSAIDs if possible

items.t: Severe hepatic failure: contraindicated. Other hepatic impairment or cirrhosis: consider a lower dose; use the lowest effective dose (unbound naproxen increased).

src.q: Severe renal, hepatic or heart failure
The implication of this finding for Naprosyn dosing is unknown but it is prudent to use the lowest effective dose.

items.t: Last trimester: contraindicated (SmPC 4.3).

src.q: Naproxen is contraindicated during the last trimester of pregnancy
Use of Naproxen in the last trimester of pregnancy is contraindicated

items.t: First and second trimesters: do not give unless clearly necessary; lowest dose, shortest time. From week 20: oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction reported; consider antenatal monitoring after several days of use; stop if found.

src.q: Therefore, during the first and second trimester of pregnancy, naproxen should not be given unless clearly necessary.
Antenatal monitoring for oligohydramnios and ductus arteriosus constriction should be considered after exposure to naproxen for several days from gestational week 20 onward.

items.t: Note: the 500 mg tablet SmPC section 4.6 ends with 'contraindicated during pregnancy' (whole pregnancy), which conflicts with its own section 4.3 (last trimester only) and with the gastro-resistant SmPC (third trimester).

src.q: Consequently, Naproxen is contraindicated during pregnancy.
Consequently, Naproxen is contraindicated during the third trimester of pregnancy

items.t: MHRA: avoid systemic NSAIDs from week 20 unless clinically required; contraindicated after 28 weeks. BUMPS: not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially from 20 weeks; paracetamol usually recommended instead.

src.q: avoid prescribing systemic NSAIDs from week 20 of pregnancy unless clinically required and prescribe the lowest dose for the shortest time in these circumstances
Use of naproxen during pregnancy is not advised unless prescribed by a doctor, especially if you are 20 or more weeks pregnant.

items.t: SmPC: found in breast milk; avoid in breastfeeding.

src.q: Naproxen has been found in the milk of lactating women. The use of Naprosyn should be avoided in patients who are breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: short-term use only, with caution, because its long half-life risks accumulation; monitor infant for vomiting, diarrhoea, drowsiness, bruising or bleeding. Ibuprofen or diclofenac are preferred.

src.q: Naproxen can be used during breastfeeding for short-term use only, due to the risk of accumulation in breastfed infants. Infant monitoring is required.
Monitor infants for vomiting and diarrhoea, drowsiness, or signs of bruising or bleeding.

items.t: May impair fertility; not recommended in women attempting to conceive; consider stopping if difficulty conceiving or under investigation.

src.q: may impair fertility and is not recommended in women attempting to conceive

items.t: Most common are gastrointestinal: heartburn, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort (SmPC gives no frequency table).

src.q: The most commonly observed adverse events are gastrointestinal in nature. Heartburn, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhoea, flatulence, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort and epigastric distress.

items.t: GI bleeding (sometimes fatal, especially older people), ulceration, perforation: stop treatment.

src.q: More serious reactions which may occur are gastro-intestinal bleeding, which is sometimes fatal, particularly in older people

items.t: Anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reactions (may be fatal); serious skin reactions including SJS, TEN, DRESS.

src.q: Anaphylactoid reactions, like anaphylaxis, may have a fatal outcome.

items.t: Renal failure, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome; hyperkalaemia; heart failure; fatal hepatitis; blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic and haemolytic anaemia); aseptic meningitis.

src.q: glomerular nephritis, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, haematuria, raised serum creatinine, renal papillary necrosis and renal failure
Metabolic and nutrition disorders: hyperkalaemia.

items.t: SPS baseline: blood pressure, eGFR, full blood count, serum creatinine; LFTs if hepatic impairment. SmPC: assess renal function before treatment if renal blood flow compromised.

src.q: Estimated glomerular filtration rate Full blood count Serum creatinine Liver function tests
should have renal function assessed before and during Naprosyn therapy

items.t: SPS after starting or dose change: eGFR or serum creatinine and FBC within 2 weeks; blood pressure within 4 weeks; then periodically.

src.q: After started or dose changed Consider Within 2 weeks Estimated glomerular filtration rate or Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) Full blood count

items.t: SmPC: monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance in renal impairment; regular supervision for long-term use; monitor older people for GI bleeding.

src.q: the monitoring of serum creatinine and/or creatinine clearance is advised

items.t: Stop if GI bleeding or ulceration, at the first skin rash or sign of hypersensitivity, or if no benefit.

src.q: When GI bleeding or ulceration occurs in patients receiving Naprosyn, the treatment should be withdrawn.

items.t: Take preferably with or after food.

src.q: To be taken preferably with or after food.

items.t: Gastro-resistant tablets: swallow whole; do not break or crush.

src.q: Naproxen Gastro-Resistant tablets should be swallowed whole and not broken or crushed.

items.t: Report any unusual abdominal symptoms, especially bleeding, particularly early in treatment.

src.q: should report any unusual abdominal symptoms (especially GI bleeding) particularly in the initial stages of treatment

items.t: May cause drowsiness, dizziness, vertigo, visual disturbance; do not drive if affected.

src.q: If patients experience these or similar undesirable effects, they should not drive or operate machinery.
Losec 20 mg hard gastro-resistant capsules

formulations.label: Dispersible gastro-resistant tablets
formulations.note: Tablets can be dispersed in non-carbonated water for swallowing difficulties or children; do not use milk or carbonated water.

src.q: Losec MUPS 20 mg gastro-resistant tablets
DO NOT USE milk or carbonated water.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Adults: duodenal and gastric ulcer (treatment and prevention of relapse); H. pylori eradication with antibiotics; treatment and prevention of NSAID-associated ulcers; reflux oesophagitis (treatment and long-term management); symptomatic GORD; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

src.q: Treatment of duodenal ulcers Prevention of relapse of duodenal ulcers Treatment of gastric ulcers Prevention of relapse of gastric ulcers
Treatment of NSAID-associated gastric and duodenal ulcers Prevention of NSAID-associated gastric and duodenal ulcers in patients at risk
Treatment of symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Treatment of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

items.t: Children over 1 year and ≥ 10 kg: reflux oesophagitis; heartburn and acid regurgitation in GORD. Children and adolescents over 4 years: H. pylori duodenal ulcer (with antibiotics).

src.q: Children over 1 year of age and ≥ 10 kg Treatment of reflux oesophagitis Symptomatic treatment of heartburn and acid regurgitation in gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Children and adolescents over 4 years of age

items.t: Children's H. pylori treatment should be supervised by a specialist.

src.q: The treatment should be supervised by a specialist.

items.t: 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks (a further 2 weeks if not healed). Poorly responsive: 40 mg once daily, usually healed within 4 weeks.

src.q: The recommended dose in patients with an active duodenal ulcer is Losec 20 mg once daily. In most patients healing occurs within two weeks.
In patients with poorly responsive duodenal ulcer Losec 40 mg once daily is recommended and healing is usually achieved within four weeks.

items.t: Prevention of duodenal ulcer relapse (H. pylori negative or eradication not possible): 20 mg once daily (10 mg may suffice; up to 40 mg if needed).

src.q: the recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily. In some patients a daily dose of 10 mg may be sufficient. In case of therapy failure, the dose can be increased to 40 mg.

items.t: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks (a further 4 weeks if not healed). Poorly responsive: 40 mg once daily, usually healed within 8 weeks. Relapse prevention: 20 mg once daily, up to 40 mg.

src.q: Treatment of gastric ulcers The recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily. In most patients healing occurs within four weeks.
In patients with poorly responsive gastric ulcer Losec 40 mg once daily is recommended and healing is usually achieved within eight weeks.

items.t: H. pylori eradication (one week, choose antibiotics by local guidance): omeprazole 20 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg + amoxicillin 1 g, each twice daily; or omeprazole 20 mg + clarithromycin 250-500 mg + metronidazole 400-500 mg (or tinidazole 500 mg), each twice daily; or omeprazole 40 mg once daily + amoxicillin 500 mg and metronidazole 400 mg three times daily.

src.q: Losec 20 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg + amoxicillin 1 000 mg, each twice daily for one week

items.t: NSAID-associated ulcers: treatment 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks (further 4 weeks if needed). Prevention in at-risk patients (age > 60, previous ulcer or upper GI bleed): 20 mg once daily.

src.q: For the treatment of NSAID - associated gastric and duodenal ulcers, the recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily.
(age > 60, previous history of gastric and duodenal ulcers, previous history of upper GI bleeding) the recommended dose is Losec 20 mg once daily

items.t: Reflux oesophagitis: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks (further 4 weeks if needed); severe oesophagitis 40 mg once daily for 8 weeks. Long-term management of healed oesophagitis: 10 mg once daily, up to 20-40 mg.

src.q: In patients with severe oesophagitis Losec 40 mg once daily is recommended and healing is usually achieved within eight weeks.
For the long-term management of patients with healed reflux oesophagitis the recommended dose is Losec 10 mg once daily. If needed, the dose can be increased to Losec 20 mg to 40 mg once daily.

items.t: Symptomatic GORD: 20 mg daily (10 mg may be enough). If no control after 4 weeks, investigate further.

src.q: Treatment of symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease The recommended dose is Losec 20 mg daily.
If symptom control has not been achieved after four weeks treatment with Losec 20 mg daily, further investigation is recommended.

items.t: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: start 60 mg daily, adjust individually (20 to 120 mg daily). Doses above 80 mg daily: divide and give twice daily.

src.q: The recommended initial dose is Losec 60 mg daily.
When dose exceed Losec 80 mg daily, the dose should be divided and given twice daily.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment needed.

src.q: Elderly Dose adjustment is not needed in the elderly

items.t: Reflux oesophagitis / GORD symptoms: ≥ 1 year and 10-20 kg: 10 mg once daily (up to 20 mg). ≥ 2 years and > 20 kg: 20 mg once daily (up to 40 mg). Duration: oesophagitis 4 to 8 weeks; GORD symptoms 2 to 4 weeks (investigate if not controlled).

src.q: ≥ 1 year of age 10 to 20 kg 10 mg once daily. The dose can be increased to 20 mg once daily if needed ≥ 2 years of age > 20 kg 20 mg once daily. The dose can be increased to 40 mg once daily if needed
Reflux oesophagitis : The treatment time is 4 to 8 weeks.

items.t: H. pylori duodenal ulcer, over 4 years (specialist supervised, one week, all twice daily): 15-30 kg: omeprazole 10 mg + amoxicillin 25 mg/kg + clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg; 31-40 kg: omeprazole 20 mg + amoxicillin 750 mg + clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg; > 40 kg: omeprazole 20 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg.

src.q: 15 to 30 kg Combination with two antibiotics: Losec 10 mg, amoxicillin 25 mg/kg body weight and clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg body weight are all administered together two times daily for one week.

items.t: Not licensed under 1 year (capsule and dispersible tablet SmPCs). Long-term treatment in children is not recommended, although some with chronic illness may need it.

src.q: Children over 1 year of age and ≥ 10 kg
Some children with chronic illnesses may require long-term treatment although it is not recommended.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to omeprazole, substituted benzimidazoles or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance, substituted benzimidazoles or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Must not be used with nelfinavir.

src.q: Omeprazole like other proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) must not be used concomitantly with nelfinavir

items.t: Alarm symptoms (unintended weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena) or suspected gastric ulcer: exclude malignancy first - treatment may mask symptoms.

src.q: In the presence of any alarm symptom (e.g. significant unintentional weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis or melena) and when gastric ulcer is suspected or present, malignancy should be excluded

items.t: Hypomagnesaemia (severe; usually after ≥ 3 months, mostly after 1 year): fatigue, tetany, delirium, convulsions, dizziness, ventricular arrhythmia. Consider measuring magnesium before and during prolonged treatment, especially with digoxin or diuretics.

src.q: Severe hypomagnesaemia has been reported in patients treated with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole for at least three months, and in most cases for a year.

consider measurement of magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during prolonged treatment, especially in those who will take a PPI concomitantly with digoxin or drugs that may cause hypomagnesaemia (eg, diuretics)

items.t: Fractures: high doses and long use (> 1 year) may modestly increase hip, wrist and spine fracture risk (10-40%), mainly in the elderly. Patients at risk of osteoporosis need guideline care with adequate vitamin D and calcium.

src.q: Proton pump inhibitors, especially if used in high doses and over long durations (> 1 year), may modestly increase the risk of hip, wrist and spine fracture, predominantly in the elderly or in presence of other recognised risk factors.
treat patients at risk of osteoporosis according to current clinical guidelines and ensure they have an adequate intake of vitamin D and calcium

items.t: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE): if lesions (especially sun-exposed) with arthralgia, seek help promptly and consider stopping. SCLE with one PPI may raise risk with others.

src.q: If lesions occur, especially in sun-exposed areas of the skin, and if accompanied by arthralgia, the patient should seek medical help promptly and the health care professional should consider stopping Losec.
a patient who develops SCLE with a particular PPI may be at risk of the same reaction with another

items.t: GI infections: slightly increased risk of Salmonella and Campylobacter, and possibly Clostridioides difficile in hospital.

src.q: Treatment with proton pump inhibitors may lead to slightly increased risk of gastrointestinal infections such as Salmonella and Campylobacter and, in hospitalised patients, possibly also Clostridioides difficile

items.t: Vitamin B12: absorption may fall on long-term therapy - consider in those with low stores or risk factors.

src.q: This should be considered in patients with reduced body stores or risk factors for reduced vitamin B12 absorption on long-term therapy.

items.t: Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur at any time and may progress to renal failure: stop omeprazole if suspected.

src.q: Omeprazole should be discontinued in case of suspected TIN, and appropriate treatment should be promptly initiated.

items.t: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP) reported rarely/very rarely.

src.q: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), which can be life-threatening or fatal

items.t: Chromogranin A tests: stop omeprazole at least 5 days before CgA measurement.

src.q: omeprazole treatment should be stopped for at least 5 days before CgA measurements

items.t: Long-term use (especially > 1 year): keep patients under regular surveillance.

src.q: As in all long-term treatments, especially when exceeding a treatment period of 1 year, patients should be kept under regular surveillance.

items.t: Excipients: capsules contain lactose; dispersible tablets contain sucrose.

src.q: Each capsule contains 8 mg lactose.
Losec gastro-resistant tablets contain sucrose.

items.t: Clopidogrel: omeprazole reduces exposure to clopidogrel's active metabolite. SmPC and MHRA: concomitant use should be discouraged (MHRA: unless considered essential). SPS: avoid this combination; other PPIs are considered safe with clopidogrel.

src.q: As a precaution, concomitant use of omeprazole and clopidogrel should be discouraged
Concomitant use of clopidogrel and omeprazole or esomeprazole is to be discouraged unless considered essential.
Avoid the combined use of clopidogrel with omeprazole or esomeprazole due to a significant interaction. Other PPIs are considered safe with clopidogrel.

items.t: Nelfinavir: contraindicated. Atazanavir: not recommended (if unavoidable, monitor closely, raise atazanavir dose, do not exceed omeprazole 20 mg). Posaconazole, erlotinib: avoid. Ketoconazole/itraconazole absorption reduced.

src.q: Concomitant administration of omeprazole with nelfinavir is contraindicated
Concomitant administration of omeprazole with atazanavir is not recommended
For posaconazole and erlotinib concomitant use should be avoided.

items.t: CYP2C19 substrates: omeprazole (moderate CYP2C19 inhibitor) may raise levels of R-warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, cilostazol, diazepam and phenytoin (monitor phenytoin for the first 2 weeks).

src.q: Examples of such drugs are R-warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, cilostazol, diazepam and phenytoin.
Monitoring phenytoin plasma concentration is recommended during the first two weeks after initiating omeprazole treatment

items.t: Methotrexate: levels may rise with PPIs; with high-dose methotrexate consider temporarily stopping omeprazole.

src.q: In high-dose methotrexate administration a temporary withdrawal of omeprazole may need to be considered.

items.t: Digoxin: bioavailability increased ~10%; caution with high omeprazole doses in the elderly - reinforce digoxin monitoring. Tacrolimus: levels may rise - monitor.

src.q: caution should be exercised when omeprazole is given at high doses in elderly patients. Therapeutic drug monitoring of digoxin should then be reinforced.

items.t: CYP2C19/CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. clarithromycin, voriconazole) raise omeprazole levels - dose change not usually needed (consider in severe hepatic impairment with long-term use). Inducers (rifampicin, St John's wort) lower omeprazole levels.

src.q: active substances known to inhibit CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 (such as clarithromycin and voriconazole) may lead to increased omeprazole serum levels
Active substances known to induce CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 or both (such as rifampicin and St John's wort) may lead to decreased omeprazole serum levels

items.t: Diuretics (and digoxin): consider magnesium monitoring with long-term PPI use (hypomagnesaemia).

src.q: For patients expected to be on prolonged treatment or who take PPIs with digoxin or drugs that may cause hypomagnesaemia (e.g. diuretics), healthcare professionals should consider measuring magnesium levels before starting PPI treatment and periodically during treatment.

items.t: No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can occur - stop if suspected.

src.q: Dose adjustment is not needed in patients with impaired renal function
Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis can progress to renal failure.

items.t: Hepatic impairment: a daily dose of 10 mg to 20 mg may be sufficient. Very rarely, encephalopathy in pre-existing liver disease.

src.q: In patients with impaired hepatic function a daily dose of 10 mg to 20 mg may be sufficient
Very rare: Hepatic failure, encephalopathy in patients with pre-existing liver disease

items.t: SmPC: omeprazole can be used in pregnancy (> 1000 exposed outcomes, no adverse effects on pregnancy or fetus/newborn).

src.q: indicate no adverse effects of omeprazole on pregnancy or on the health of the foetus/newborn child
Omeprazole can be used during pregnancy.

items.t: BUMPS: omeprazole is the preferred PPI in pregnancy (most safety information); no good evidence linking PPIs to miscarriage, birth defects, stillbirth, preterm delivery or low birth weight.

src.q: Omeprazole is the PPI that is preferred for use in pregnancy as there is more information about its safety.
There is no good evidence that omeprazole or other PPIs are linked to miscarriage, birth defects, stillbirth, preterm delivery, or low infant birth weight.

items.t: Excreted in breast milk but not likely to affect the child at therapeutic doses.

src.q: Omeprazole is excreted in breast milk but is not likely to influence the child when therapeutic doses are used.

src.q: Caution is also necessary in patients receiving potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE-inhibitors, and in patients with myotonia congenita or severe haemolysis.

src.q: This is particularly important in patients with cardiac disease and in those receiving digitalis.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: caution with a history of peptic ulcer. Potassium chloride can cause GI ulceration, haemorrhage or stricture (lower oesophagus, small bowel), more likely with local GI disorders, cardiovascular disease or prolonged therapy.

src.q: Oral potassium should be prescribed with caution in patients with a history of peptic ulcer.
may induce ulceration, haemorrhage or stricture formation in the gastrointestinal tract, in particular the lower oesophagus and the small bowel

src.q: Ingestion of potassium chloride may induce hyperkalaemia in patients with familial hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis.

src.q: In patients with acidosis, the acid-base balance should be monitored.
In patients with hypertension, it should be remembered that correction of hypokalaemia may lower blood pressure.

items.t: Excipients: the effervescent tablets (sucrose) and the oral solution (sorbitol) should not be taken in hereditary fructose intolerance; the oral solution contains E122 and parabens (may cause allergic reactions).

Patients with hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) should not take/be given this medicine.

items.t: ACE inhibitors (e.g. lisinopril): risk of hyperkalaemia; use with caution. Lisinopril SmPC: combination with potassium supplements is not recommended; if needed, use with caution and frequent serum potassium monitoring.

src.q: If co-administered with potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE-inhibitors, the risk of hyperkalaemia must be considered.
Therefore, the combination of Lisinopril tablet with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended.
If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics and aldosterone antagonists (e.g. spironolactone): risk of hyperkalaemia. Spironolactone SmPC: potassium supplements should not be given routinely with spironolactone.

src.q: Hyperkalaemia can result from the concurrent use of potassium supplements with ACE inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, ciclosporin, potassium sparing diuretics and tacrolimus.
potassium supplements should not be given routinely with Aldactone as hyperkalaemia may be induced

items.t: Trimethoprim SmPC: potassium supplements with trimethoprim may significantly raise serum potassium; monitor potassium as appropriate.

src.q: Concomitant use of drugs that may increase serum potassium levels may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.
Monitoring of potassium should be undertaken as appropriate

items.t: Co-trimoxazole SmPC: co-trimoxazole may cause clinically relevant hyperkalaemia; use caution with other drugs that can cause hyperkalaemia. Oral solution SmPC: use potassium supplements with caution with medicines that may raise plasma potassium.

Concomitant use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) may result in clinically relevant hyperkalaemia.
Potassium supplements should be used with caution in patients who are receiving medications that may increase plasma potassium levels.

Dose changes should be made in steps of 50 mg at intervals of at least one week, up to a maximum of 200 mg/day.

items.t: Start 25 mg once daily; after 1 week increase to 50 mg once daily. Then 50 mg steps at least weekly; maximum 200 mg/day.
