Renal and urinary disorders Common Acute kidney injury Reproductive system and breast disorders Common Gynaecomastia*, Breast pain**

items.t: Gynaecomastia is related to dose and duration and is usually reversible on stopping; rarely some breast enlargement persists.

src.q: Development appears to be related to both dosage level and duration of therapy and is normally reversible when the drug is discontinued.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia can be fatal (arrhythmia). Stop if hyperkalaemia develops and take measures to lower potassium.

src.q: Hyperkalaemia may be fatal.
Should hyperkalaemia develop Aldactone should be discontinued, and if necessary, active measures taken to reduce the serum potassium to normal

items.t: Acute kidney injury (common). Frequency not known: agranulocytosis, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia; toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS, pemphigoid.

src.q: Not known Leukopenia, Agranulocytosis, Thrombocytopenia
Not known Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), Pemphigoid

items.t: SPS (heart failure) baseline: renal function (creatinine/eGFR) and electrolytes; contraindicated if potassium > 5.0 mmol/L or severe renal impairment.

src.q: Electrolytes Serum potassium · contraindicated if greater than 5.0 mmol/L
contraindicated in severe renal impairment or acute renal insufficiency

items.t: Potassium and creatinine 1 week after starting or any dose increase, monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months for a year, then every 6 months (SmPC, severe heart failure; SPS the same). Blood pressure before and after each dose change (SPS).

src.q: The recommended monitoring for potassium and creatinine is 1 week after initiation or increase in dose of spironolactone, monthly for the first 3 months, then quarterly for a year, and then every 6 months.
After 1 week; then monthly for first 3 months, then every 3 months for one year
Every 6 months Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) or Estimated glomerular filtration rate Electrolytes

items.t: SPS: reduce dose and recheck if potassium is > 5.5 and < 6 mmol/L; stop and seek specialist advice if potassium > 6 mmol/L. SmPC (severe heart failure): stop or interrupt if potassium > 5 mEq/L.

src.q: Potassium is greater than 5.5 mmol/L and less than 6 mmol/L
Stop and seek specialist advice if any of the following occur: Potassium Potassium is greater than 6 mmol/L
Discontinue or interrupt treatment for serum potassium >5 mEq/L

items.t: MHRA: with ACE inhibitors/ARBs in heart failure, monitor potassium and renal function regularly.

src.q: regularly monitor serum potassium levels and renal function

items.t: Tablets: once daily with a meal is recommended.

src.q: Administration of Aldactone once daily with a meal is recommended.

items.t: Suspension: take with a meal; shake well; use the 1 ml syringe for doses up to 10 mg and the 5 ml syringe for larger doses; follow with water. Can be given via nasogastric tube.

src.q: Spironolactone should be taken together with a meal.
The smaller 1 ml syringe is for measuring doses of less than or equal to 10 mg.
water should be taken after each dose of spironolactone
Suitable for administration via nasogastric (NG) feeding tubes.

items.t: Avoid NSAIDs unless prescribed and avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes. Contact the prescriber if diarrhoea, vomiting, or infection with fever and sweating occurs.

src.q: Avoid NSAIDs unless prescribed Avoid salt substitutes containing potassium Contact prescriber if diarrhoea, vomiting, or infection with fever and sweating occurs

items.t: Drowsiness and dizziness can occur; take care driving until the response is known.

src.q: Caution is advised when driving or operating machinery until the response to initial treatment has been determined.

items.t: Breast enlargement or pain can occur in men; usually reversible.

src.q: Gynaecomastia may develop in association with the use of spironolactone.

formulations.label: Tablets, 66 mg dry extract (e.g. THR 13668/0014)
formulations.strengths: 66 mg extract from fresh flowering herb (equivalent to 170-305 mg dried herb)
formulations.note: Herbal products differ in extract and dose; check the specific product's THR SPC.

src.q: One tablet contains 66 mg of extract (as dry extract) from fresh St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum L.) flowering herb (equivalent to 170-305 mg of dried St John's wort flowering herb).

formulations.label: Film-coated tablets, 450 mg dry extract (e.g. THR 43546/0001)
formulations.strengths: 450 mg extract from aerial parts (equivalent to 1350-2700 mg herb)
formulations.note: Contains soya: must not be used in peanut or soya allergy (this product's SPC).

src.q: Each film-coated tablet contains: 450mg of extract (as dry extract) from St. John's Wort aerial parts (Hypericum perforatum L.)
Patients who are allergic to peanut or soya must not use this medicinal product.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Traditional herbal medicine to relieve symptoms of slightly low mood and mild anxiety, based on traditional use only.

src.q: A traditional herbal medicinal product used to relieve the symptoms of slightly low mood and mild anxiety, based on traditional use only.

items.t: Registered under the Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) scheme - efficacy based on traditional use only. Not intended for depression: people with signs of depression should get medical advice. Some unlicensed St John's wort products sold in the UK or online lack interaction warnings (MHRA).

src.q: Patients with signs and symptoms of depression should seek medical advice for appropriate treatment.
Some unlicensed products on the UK market or available online do not include the appropriate warnings regarding possible interactions.

items.t: Adults and elderly: one tablet three times a day; short-term use only. See a doctor if symptoms worsen or do not improve after 6 weeks.

src.q: For oral short term use only. Adults and the elderly: Take one tablet three times a day.
A doctor or qualified healthcare practitioner should be consulted if symptoms worsen, or do not improve after 6 weeks.

items.t: Adults and elderly: one tablet daily, swallowed whole. See a doctor if symptoms worsen or do not improve after 6 weeks.

src.q: For adults and the elderly, take 1 tablet daily.
The patient should consult a doctor or a qualified healthcare practitioner if symptoms worsen or do not improve after 6 weeks.

items.t: Not recommended under 18 years (insufficient data).

src.q: This product is not recommended for use in children or adolescents under 18 years
Kira LowMood relief tablets are not for use in children and adolescents under 18 years old.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to St John's wort or excipients (450 mg-extract product: also peanut or soya allergy).

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active ingredient or any of the excipients.
Hypersensitivity to the active ingredient, soya, peanut or any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Known skin photosensitivity, or phototherapy/photodiagnostic procedures.

src.q: Patients with known dermal photosensitivity or patients undergoing phototherapy or any photodiagnostic procedures.

items.t: Contraindicated with ciclosporin, systemic tacrolimus, amprenavir, indinavir and other protease inhibitors, irinotecan and warfarin (CYP and P-glycoprotein induction).

src.q: Concomitant use with ciclosporin, tacrolimus for systemic use, amprenavir, indinavir and other protease inhibitors, irinotecan and warfarin
The concominant use of ciclosporin, tacrolimus for systemic use, amprenavir, indinavir and other protease inhibitors, irinotecan and warfarin is contraindicated.

items.t: 450 mg-extract product SPC 4.3: should not be taken with any of the medicines listed in its section 4.5.

src.q: This product should not be taken concomitantly with the medicines included in section 4.5.

items.t: Many interactions: St John's wort induces CYP1A2, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, lowering levels and effect of many medicines; pharmacodynamic interactions with SSRIs and triptans.

src.q: This results in pharmacokinetic interactions with a large number of medicines leading to a potential decrease in the effectiveness of those medicines.
Clinically significant pharmacodynamic interactions have also been identified with SSRI antidepressants, and the triptan group of medicines used to treat migraines.

items.t: Photosensitivity (very rare, especially fair skin): avoid excessive sunbathing, sunbeds and solariums.

src.q: Persons using this product should avoid excessive sunbathing or the use of sunbeds or solariums.

items.t: Stop at least 10 days before elective surgery (interactions with anaesthetic medicines).

src.q: This product should be discontinued at least 10 days prior to elective surgery due to the potential for interactions with medicinal products used during general and regional anaesthesia

items.t: Hormonal contraception: women using hormonal contraception to prevent pregnancy should not take St John's wort (unplanned pregnancies and breakthrough bleeding reported).

src.q: women taking hormonal contraception for pregnancy prevention should not take herbal products that contain St John's wort

items.t: Epilepsy: concomitant use with any antiepileptic is not recommended; advise patients with epilepsy not to use St John's wort.

src.q: concomitant use of St John's wort and antiepileptic medicine is not recommended: healthcare professionals should advise patients with epilepsy not to use products that contain St John's wort

items.t: Do not exceed the stated dose.

src.q: Do not exceed the stated dose.

items.t: THR SPC: should not be taken with the medicines in its interaction table, including: tramadol; clarithromycin (and erythromycin); warfarin (contraindicated); SSRIs (e.g. sertraline) and other antidepressants; triptans; antiepileptics; calcium-channel blockers (e.g. amlodipine); simvastatin and atorvastatin; PPIs (omeprazole, lansoprazole); thyroxine; digoxin; HIV antivirals; hormonal contraceptives and HRT; immunosuppressants.

src.q: Therefore this product should not be taken concomitantly with the medicines included in the table below
Analgesics Tramadol Reduced blood levels with risk Do not take with this product.
Calcium channel blockers Amlodipine
Lipid regulating drugs Simvastatin Reduced blood levels with risk of Atorvastatin therapeutic failure.
Proton pump inhibitors Lansoprazole Reduced blood levels with risk of Omeprazole therapeutic failure.
Thyroid hormones Thyroxine Reduced blood levels with risk of therapeutic failure.

items.t: MHRA: CYP3A4 inducers such as St John's wort may reduce simvastatin and atorvastatin levels.

src.q: Inducers of CYP3A4 (eg, efavirenz, rifampicin, St John's wort) may reduce plasma concentrations of simvastatin and atorvastatin.

items.t: Other UK SmPCs: St John's wort speeds levothyroxine metabolism (levothyroxine dose may need increasing); may lower omeprazole levels; sertraline SmPC - use with caution and avoid whenever possible.

src.q: or the herbal medicine, St John's Wort ( hypericum perforatum ), should be undertaken with caution and avoided whenever possible due to the potential for a pharmacodynamic interaction
Metabolism of levothyroxine (thyroxine) is accelerated by rifampicin, barbituarates, products containing St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum L.) and primidone.
Active substances known to induce CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 or both (such as rifampicin and St John's wort) may lead to decreased omeprazole serum levels

renal.note: No renal impairment information in the two THR SPCs accessed (THR 13668/0014, THR 43546/0001).

hepatic.note: No hepatic impairment information in the two THR SPCs accessed (THR 13668/0014, THR 43546/0001).

items.t: Safety not established; use in pregnancy is not recommended.

src.q: In the absence of sufficient data, the use during pregnancy and lactation is not recommended.

items.t: Safety not established; use during breastfeeding is not recommended.

src.q: Safety of the product during pregnancy and lactation has not been established.
In the absence of sufficient data, the use during pregnancy and lactation is not recommended.

items.t: Reduces the effect of hormonal contraceptives (pills, implants, injections, patches; emergency contraception): risk of unintended pregnancy and breakthrough bleeding. No fertility studies.

src.q: Users of oral contraceptives taking St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) may experience intracyclic menstrual bleeding and risk of contraception failure is increased.
herbal products containing St John's wort can decrease the effect of this contraceptive cover
No studies on the effects on fertility have been performed.

items.t: Frequency not known: GI upset (dyspepsia, anorexia, nausea, diarrhoea, constipation), allergic skin reactions (rash, urticaria, itch), fatigue, restlessness; sunburn-like reactions in strong sunlight. Also reported: headache, neuropathy, anxiety, dizziness, mania.

src.q: Gastrointestinal disorders including dyspepsia, anorexia, nausea, diarrhoea or constipation; allergic skin reactions such as rash, urticaria, pruritis; fatigue and restlessness have been reported. The frequency is not known.
Other adverse reactions that have been reported include headaches, neuropathy, anxiety, dizziness, and mania.

items.t: Serotonergic adverse reactions with SSRIs/triptans; loss of effect of critical medicines (e.g. transplant rejection with ciclosporin/tacrolimus, loss of HIV suppression, reduced anticoagulation, unintended pregnancy). Mania reported.

src.q: Due to increased risk of undesirable effects associated with these interactions this product should not be used concomitantly with these types of medicines.
Reduced blood levels with risk of Sirolimus transplant rejection.
Reduced blood levels with risk of therapeutic failure.

items.t: Overdose (5 to 17-fold doses): seizures and confusion reported; protect from sunlight for 1 to 2 weeks after massive overdose.

src.q: After ingestion of massive overdoses, the patient should be protected from sunlight and other UV-light sources for 1-2 weeks.

items.t: Review all current medicines (including contraception) for interactions before use.

src.q: Therefore this product should not be taken concomitantly with the medicines included in the table below

items.t: Seek medical advice if symptoms worsen or last more than 6 weeks.

src.q: If the condition worsens, or if symptoms persist for more than six weeks medical advice should be sought.

items.t: Stop at least 10 days before elective surgery.

src.q: This product should be discontinued at least 10 days prior to elective surgery

items.t: Oral; 66 mg-extract tablets three times a day (short-term use).

src.q: Take one tablet three times a day.

items.t: 450 mg-extract tablets once daily, swallowed whole with a little liquid; do not chew.

src.q: The tablets should be swallowed whole with a little liquid. The tablets should not be chewed.

items.t: Tell your doctor/pharmacist you take St John's wort - it interacts with many medicines.

src.q: This results in pharmacokinetic interactions with a large number of medicines leading to a potential decrease in the effectiveness of those medicines.

src.q: Advise women taking hormonal contraceptives for pregnancy prevention not to take herbal products containing St John's wort

src.q: healthcare professionals should advise patients with epilepsy not to use products that contain St John's wort

src.q: Persons using this product should avoid excessive sunbathing or the use of sunbeds or solariums.

Each hard capsule contains 50 mg tramadol hydrochloride.

formulations.strengths: 100 mg (also 150 mg, 200 mg in the same range)
formulations.note: Twice-daily dosing at least 8 hours apart; swallow whole. Dosing differs from immediate-release capsules.

src.q: Each prolonged-release tablet contains 100 mg tramadol hydrochloride
The dose interval must not be less than 8 hours.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Moderate to severe pain.

src.q: Treatment of moderate to severe pain.

items.t: MHRA (2025): prolonged-release opioids should not be used for acute pain after surgery; use immediate-release opioids for short-term post-operative pain.

src.q: prolonged-release opioids provide relief from chronic severe pain, however, they should not be used for the treatment of acute pain following surgery

items.t: Not for use in narcotic withdrawal treatment; not a substitute in opioid-dependent patients.

src.q: for use in narcotic withdrawal treatment
Tramadol is not suitable as a substitute in opioid-dependent patients.

items.t: Acute pain (adults and 12 years and over): initial 100 mg, then 50 or 100 mg every 4-6 hours; match duration to clinical need. Maximum 400 mg/day except in special circumstances.

src.q: Acute pain: An initial dose of 100 mg is usually necessary. This can be followed by doses of 50 or 100 mg 4-6 hourly intervals
The total daily dose of 400 mg active substance should not be exceeded, except in special circumstances.

items.t: Pain with chronic conditions: start 50 mg, then titrate to pain severity; reassess need regularly (dependence and withdrawal reported). Maximum 400 mg/day.

src.q: Pain associated with chronic conditions: An initial dose of 50 mg is advised and then titration according to pain severity.

items.t: Prolonged-release (adults and over 12 years): usually 100 mg twice daily (morning and evening); increase to 150 mg or 200 mg twice daily if needed. Interval at least 8 hours. Maximum 400 mg/day except in special clinical circumstances.

src.q: The starting dose is usually 100 mg tramadol hydrochloride as prolonged-release tablet twice daily, in the morning and in the evening. If the pain relief is not sufficient, the dose may be increased to 150 mg twice daily or 200 mg twice daily.
A total daily dose of 400 mg of tramadol hydrochloride should not be exceeded except in special clinical circumstances.
The dose interval must not be less than 8 hours.

items.t: Elderly: no adjustment usually needed up to 75 years without hepatic or renal insufficiency; over 75 years extend the dosing interval if necessary.

src.q: A dose adjustment is not usually necessary in patients up to 75 years without clinically manifest hepatic or renal insufficiency.
Therefore, if necessary the dosage interval is to be extended according to the patient's requirements.

items.t: Use the lowest effective dose; never longer than absolutely necessary. Agree goals and an end-of-treatment plan; taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: Tramadol should under no circumstances be administered for longer than absolutely necessary.
When a patient no longer requires therapy with tramadol, it may be advisable to taper the dose gradually to prevent symptoms of withdrawal.

items.t: Not suitable for children under 12 years (capsules and prolonged-release tablets).

src.q: Tramadol capsules are not suitable for children below the age of 12 years.
Tramadol prolonged-release tablets are not suitable for children under 12 years of age.

items.t: Post-operative use after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea: rare life-threatening events; extreme caution and close monitoring. Not recommended where respiratory function may be compromised.

src.q: Extreme caution should be exercised when tramadol is administered to children for post-operative pain relief
Tramadol is not recommended for use in children in whom respiratory function might be compromised

items.t: Hypersensitivity; acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids or other psychotropic medicines; MAOI now or within 14 days; epilepsy not adequately controlled; narcotic withdrawal treatment.

src.q: in acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids, or other psychotropic medicinal products
in patients who are receiving MAO inhibitors or who have taken them within the last 14 days
in patients with epilepsy not adequately controlled by treatment

items.t: Particular caution: opioid dependence, head injury, shock, reduced consciousness of uncertain origin, respiratory centre or function disorders, raised intracranial pressure (MR SmPC also: renal and hepatic impairment).

src.q: Tramadol may only be used with particular caution in opioid-dependent patients, patients with head injury, shock, a reduced level of consciousness of uncertain origin, disorders of the respiratory centre or function, increased intracranial pressure.

items.t: Seizures reported at recommended doses; higher risk above 400 mg/day or with other seizure-threshold-lowering medicines. Epilepsy or seizure susceptibility: only if compelling circumstances.

src.q: Convulsions have been reported in patients receiving tramadol at the recommended dose levels.
Patients with epilepsy or those susceptible to seizures should be only treated with tramadol if there are compelling circumstances.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (alone or with serotonergic medicines): observe carefully at start and dose increases; reduce or stop if suspected.

src.q: Serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition, has been reported in patients receiving tramadol in combination with other serotonergic agents or tramadol alone
If serotonin syndrome is suspected, a dose reduction or discontinuation of therapy should be considered depending on the severity of the symptoms.

items.t: Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder can develop even at therapeutic doses; higher risk with personal/family history of substance use disorder, tobacco use or mental health disorders. Monitor for drug-seeking behaviour.

src.q: Repeated use of Tramadol can lead to opioid use disorder (OUD).
Patients will require monitoring for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. too early requests for refills).

items.t: CYP2D6: poor metabolisers may get inadequate analgesia; ultra-rapid metabolisers risk opioid toxicity even at usual doses.

src.q: If a patient has a deficiency or is completely lacking this enzyme an adequate analgesic effect may not be obtained.
if the patient is an ultra-rapid metaboliser there is a risk of developing <side effects> of opioid toxicity even at commonly prescribed doses

items.t: Opioids may occasionally cause reversible adrenal insufficiency requiring monitoring and glucocorticoid replacement.

src.q: Opioid analgesics may occasionally cause reversible adrenal insufficiency requiring monitoring and glucocorticoid replacement therapy.

items.t: Sleep-related breathing disorders (central sleep apnoea): consider reducing the opioid dose.

src.q: In patients who present with CSA, consider decreasing the total opioid dosage.

items.t: SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, mirtazapine and MAOIs: serotonin syndrome risk. SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, antipsychotics and other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs: convulsion risk.

src.q: Concomitant therapeutic use of tramadol and serotonergic medicinal products, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), MAO inhibitors (see section 4.3), tricyclic antidepressants and mirtazapine may cause serotonin syndrome
Tramadol can induce convulsions and increase the potential for selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: increased INR with major bleeding and bruising reported. Use caution; MHRA advises considering extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol and warning patients about bleeding signs.

src.q: Caution should be exercised during concomitant treatment with tramadol and coumarin derivatives (e.g. warfarin) due to reports of increased INR with major bleeding and ecchymoses in some patients.
consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: Benzodiazepines, other opioids, other CNS depressants and alcohol: sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death; lowest dose, shortest duration if combined.

src.q: if a decision is made to prescribe tramadol concomitantly with respiratory or CNS depressants, the lowest effective dose of tramadol should be used, and the duration of the concomitant treatment should be as short as possible

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin) might inhibit tramadol metabolism; clinical importance not studied.

src.q: Other medicinal products known to inhibit CYP3A4, such as ketoconazole, ritonavir and erythromycin, might inhibit the metabolism of tramadol
The clinical importance of such an interaction has not been studied

items.t: Carbamazepine may reduce the analgesic effect; ondansetron may increase tramadol requirement; gabapentin/pregabalin increase respiratory depression risk.

src.q: Simultaneous or previous administration of carbamazepine (enzyme inducer) may reduce the analgesic effect and shorten the duration of action.
The concomitant use of Tramadol with gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) may result in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

items.t: St John's wort (THR SPC): reduced tramadol blood levels with risk of therapeutic failure; do not take together.

src.q: Analgesics Tramadol Reduced blood levels with risk Do not take with this product.

items.t: Ciprofloxacin (ciprofloxacin SmPC): avoid combining with tramadol, which lowers the seizure threshold (risk of seizures, including status epilepticus).

src.q: concomitant treatment of ciprofloxacin with drugs known to trigger seizures or lower the seizure threshold, such as but not limited to tramadol, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, should be avoided

items.t: Clopidogrel (clopidogrel SmPC): opioid agonists may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption (clinical relevance unknown); in acute coronary syndrome consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent.

src.q: co-administration of opioid agonists has the potential to delay and reduce the absorption of clopidogrel presumably because of slowed gastric emptying. The clinical relevance is unknown.
Consider the use of a parenteral antiplatelet agent in acute coronary syndrome patients requiring co-administration of morphine or other opioid agonists.

items.t: Renal insufficiency or dialysis: elimination delayed; carefully consider prolonging the dosing interval (no numeric threshold stated).

src.q: In patients with renal and/or hepatic insufficiency the elimination of tramadol is delayed. In these patients prolongation of the dosage intervals should be carefully considered according to the patient's requirements.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: not recommended in severe renal insufficiency.

src.q: In cases of severe renal and/or severe hepatic insufficiency tramadol hydrochloride prolonged-release tablets are not recommended.

items.t: Hepatic insufficiency: elimination delayed; carefully consider prolonging the dosing interval.

src.q: In patients with renal and/or hepatic insufficiency the elimination of tramadol is delayed.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: not recommended in severe hepatic insufficiency.

src.q: In cases of severe renal and/or severe hepatic insufficiency tramadol hydrochloride prolonged-release tablets are not recommended.

items.t: SmPCs: inadequate human safety evidence, so tramadol should not be used in pregnant women. Regular use may cause neonatal withdrawal; use in labour may depress neonatal breathing.

src.q: There is inadequate evidence available on the safety of tramadol in human pregnancy. Therefore tramadol should not be used in pregnant women.
Administration during labour may depress respiration in the neonate

items.t: BUMPS (differs from SmPC): take only if recommended by a doctor; studies overall do not show miscarriage or birth defects; use near delivery can cause neonatal withdrawal.

src.q: Tramadol should only be taken during pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
Studies of pregnant women using tramadol do not, overall, show that it causes miscarriage or birth defects in the baby.

items.t: SPS: reserve tramadol in pregnancy for when other analgesics have been ineffective.

src.q: Reserve tramadol use in pregnancy where other alternative analgesics have been ineffective.

items.t: Capsule SmPC: not recommended (may cause infant respiratory depression).

src.q: Administration to nursing women is not recommended as tramadol may be secreted in breast milk and may cause respiratory depression in the infant.

items.t: Prolonged-release SmPC: should not be used during lactation, or stop breastfeeding during treatment; a single dose usually does not require stopping breastfeeding.

src.q: For this reason tramadol should not be used during lactation or alternatively, breast-feeding should be discontinued during treatment with tramadol.
Discontinuation of breast-feeding is generally not necessary following a single dose of tramadol.

items.t: SPS (differs from SmPCs): can be used short term with caution at the lowest effective dose; monitor the infant (sedation, breathing difficulties, feeding, weight gain); extra caution under 2 months; regular use beyond 3 days under close supervision.

src.q: Tramadol (both oral and intravenous) can be used short-term during breastfeeding with caution and infant monitoring.
Regular use of any opioid in a breastfeeding mother beyond 3 days should be under close medical supervision.

items.t: Post-marketing surveillance does not suggest an effect on fertility.

src.q: Post marketing surveillance does not suggest an effect of tramadol on fertility.

items.t: Very common: nausea, dizziness. Common: headache, somnolence, vomiting, constipation, dry mouth, sweating (hyperhidrosis), fatigue.

src.q: The most commonly reported adverse reactions are nausea and dizziness, both occurring in more than 10% of patients.
Common: vomiting, constipation, dry mouth
Common: headache, somnolence

items.t: Respiratory depression (rare), especially if doses are considerably exceeded or with other CNS depressants.

src.q: Rare: respiratory depression, dyspnoea If the recommended doses are considerably exceeded and other centrally depressant substances are administered concomitantly (see section 4.5), respiratory depression may occur.

items.t: Convulsions (rare), mainly at high doses or with seizure-threshold-lowering drugs.

src.q: Epileptiform convulsions occurred mainly after administration of high doses of tramadol or after concomitant treatment with medicinal products which can lower the seizure threshold

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (frequency not known): reduce dose or stop.

src.q: Frequency not known: serotonin syndrome

items.t: Anaphylaxis and allergic reactions (rare); hypoglycaemia (not known); dependence and withdrawal syndrome.

src.q: Rare: allergic reactions (e.g. dyspnoea, bronchospasm, wheezing, angioneurotic oedema) and anaphylaxis
Frequency not known: hypoglycaemia

items.t: Long-term treatment: careful and regular monitoring (with breaks if needed) to decide whether to continue.

src.q: then careful and regular monitoring should be carried out (if necessary with breaks in treatment) to establish whether and to what extent further treatment is necessary

items.t: With serotonergic medicines: careful observation especially at start and dose increases.

src.q: careful observation of the patient is advised, particularly during treatment initiation and dose escalations

items.t: With warfarin: consider extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol (MHRA).

src.q: consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: Capsules: swallow whole, not divided or chewed, with enough liquid, with or without food.

src.q: The capsules are to be taken whole, not divided or chewed, with sufficient liquid, with or without food.

items.t: Prolonged-release tablets: swallow whole, not divided or chewed, with enough liquid, regardless of meals.

src.q: The prolonged-release tablets must be swallowed whole, not divided or chewed, with sufficient liquid, irrespective of mealtimes.

items.t: May cause drowsiness and dizziness; may affect driving, especially with alcohol.

src.q: Tramadol may cause effects such as somnolence and dizziness and therefore may impair the reactions of drivers and machine operators.

items.t: MHRA: risk of dependence and addiction even at therapeutic doses; learn signs of overdose; do not stop suddenly after long-term use.

src.q: discuss with patients that prolonged use of opioids may lead to drug dependence and addiction, even at therapeutic doses

items.t: If taking warfarin: seek urgent INR test for signs of bleeding (e.g. nosebleed over 10 minutes, blood in urine/stool, severe bruising).

src.q: you should seek medical treatment and have an urgent International Normalised Ratio test should you experience any of the following symptoms
Each tablet contains 200 mg of trimethoprim.
Each 5 ml contains 50 mg of Trimethoprim

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Treatment of infections caused by trimethoprim-sensitive organisms, including urinary and respiratory tract infections.

src.q: Trimethoprim is indicated for the treatment of susceptible infections caused by trimethoprim - sensitive organisms including urinary tract and respiratory tract infections.

items.t: Prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections.

src.q: Trimethoprim is also indicated for the prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections.

items.t: Prevention and treatment of UTI, and treatment of other susceptible infections, in adults and children.

src.q: Trimethoprim is indicated for the prevention and treatment of urinary tract infections in adults and children

restrictions.note: No specialist-only, shared-care or brand restrictions found in the tablet SmPC, the suspension SmPC, SPS or MHRA pages checked. Dialysis use is specialist-supervised (see renal).

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 200 mg TWICE DAILY. Duration 3 days (e.g. uncomplicated cystitis in women) up to 2 weeks, by type and severity of infection. The first dose can be doubled.

src.q: Adults and children over 12 years of age: 200 mg twice daily

Treatment should continue for a period of between 3 days (e.g. uncomplicated bacterial cystitis in women) to 2 weeks depending on the nature and severity of the infection. The first dose can be doubled.

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 100 mg ONCE daily AT NIGHT.

src.q: Long-term treatment and prophylactic therapy: Adults and children over 12 years: 100 mg at night

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 200 mg (20 ml) TWICE DAILY.

src.q: Treatment of urinary tract infections and all other susceptible infections: 200 mg (20 ml) twice daily.

items.t: Adults and children over 12 years: 100 mg (10 ml) at night.

src.q: Long-term prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections: 100 mg (10 ml) at night.

items.t: Elderly: dose depends on kidney function (see renal).

src.q: Elderly Depending on kidney function, see special dosage schedule.

items.t: Tablets, children 6 to 12 years: 100 mg twice daily for acute infections; 50 mg at night for long-term/prophylaxis.

src.q: Children 6 years to 12 years: 100 mg twice daily
Children 6 years to 12 years of age: 50 mg at night.

items.t: Tablets are not suitable under 6 years; use a suspension. The same SmPC's prophylaxis section also says the tablet is not suitable under 12 years (internal inconsistency in the source).

src.q: This dosage form is not suitable for use in children younger than 6 years; a more suitable dosage form (such as a suspension) should be used in this age group.
This dosage form is not suitable for use in children younger than 12 years; a more suitable dosage form (such as a suspension) should be used in this age group.

items.t: Suspension, children 6 weeks to 12 years, UTI treatment: 8 mg/kg daily in two equal doses. Suggested: 6 weeks-5 months 25 mg (2.5 ml) twice daily; 6 months-5 years 50 mg (5 ml) twice daily; 6-12 years 100 mg (10 ml) twice daily.

src.q: Children 6 weeks to 12 years of age Treatment of urinary tract infections is based on a dosage of 8 mg/kg body weight daily, subdivided into two equal doses.
25 mg (2.5 ml) twice daily 50 mg (5 ml) twice daily 100 mg (10 ml) twice daily

items.t: Suspension, long-term prevention of recurrent UTI: 2 mg/kg daily as a single dose at night. Suggested: 6 months-5 years 25 mg (2.5 ml); 6-12 years 50 mg (5 ml) at night.

src.q: Long-term prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection is based on 2 mg/kg body weight daily given as a single dose at night.
25 mg (2.5 ml) at night 50 mg (5 ml) at night

items.t: Lower age limit differs by SmPC: tablet SmPC says do not give to premature infants or children under 4 months; suspension SmPC says do not give to premature infants and neonates under 6 weeks.

src.q: Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age
premature infants and neonates under 6 weeks

items.t: Take particular care with blood monitoring in children on long-term therapy.

src.q: Particular care should be exercised in the haematological monitoring of children on long term therapy.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to trimethoprim or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: Severe hepatic insufficiency.

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in severe hepatic insufficiency.

items.t: Megaloblastic anaemia and other blood dyscrasias.

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in megaloblastic anaemia and other blood dyscrasias.

items.t: First trimester of pregnancy (the tablet SmPC 4.3 also says it should not be given to pregnant women, without naming a trimester).

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in first trimester of pregnancy
Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age

items.t: Premature infants and young infants - SmPCs differ: tablet SmPC 4.3 says under 4 months; suspension SmPC 4.3 says neonates under 6 weeks.

src.q: Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age
Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women (first trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.6)), premature infants and neonates under 6 weeks.

items.t: Hyperkalaemia: closely monitor electrolytes in patients at risk (renal insufficiency, poorly controlled diabetes, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or salt substitutes, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, heparin).

src.q: Close monitoring of serum electrolytes is advised in patients at risk for hyperkalaemia (see section 4.8).
Patients at risk for the development of hyperkalaemia include those with renal insufficiency, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus

items.t: Folate deficiency (actual or potential, e.g. elderly): use with caution; consider a folate supplement. Trimethoprim may depress haemopoiesis.

src.q: Caution should be exercised in the administration of trimethoprim to patients with actual or potential folate deficiency (e.g. the elderly). Administration of a folate supplement should be considered.
Trimethoprim may cause depression of haemopoiesis.

items.t: Marked renal impairment: avoid accumulation and haematological toxicity; dialysis patients only under specialist (infection + renal) supervision.

src.q: In patients with marked impairment of renal function, care should be taken to avoid accumulation and resulting adverse haematological effects.
Trimethoprim should only be initiated and used in dialysis patients under close supervision from specialists in both infectious disease and renal medicine.

items.t: Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS): stop immediately if signs appear; never restart after SJS/TEN/DRESS.

src.q: If signs and symptoms suggestive of these reactions appear, trimethoprim should be withdrawn immediately
If the patient has developed a serious reaction such as SJS, TEN or DRESS with the use of trimethoprim, the treatment must not be restarted in this patient at any time.

items.t: Acute porphyria: tablet SmPC says use with caution; suspension SmPC says avoid if known or suspected risk.

src.q: Caution should be used in patients with acute porphyria.
If a patient has a known or suspected risk of acute prophyria, treatment with trimethoprim should be avoided.

items.t: Neonates: use only under careful medical supervision (tablet SmPC).

src.q: Trimethoprim should be used under careful medical supervision in neonates.

items.t: Tablets contain lactose; suspension: patients with hereditary fructose intolerance should not take it.

src.q: Each tablet contains 50 mg lactose
Patients with rare hereditary problems of fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.

items.t: Methotrexate: tablet SmPC says avoid (increased antifolate effect); suspension SmPC says risk of haematological toxicity. SPS: avoid; if unavoidable, frequent FBC.

src.q: Trimethoprim increases the antifolate effect of methotrexate therefore use should be avoided.
Avoid prescribing co-trimoxazole or trimethoprim with methotrexate, due to the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.

items.t: Potassium-raising medicines (potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, heparin): risk of significant hyperkalaemia; monitor potassium.

src.q: Concomitant use of drugs that may increase serum potassium levels may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.
Monitoring of potassium should be undertaken as appropriate (see section 4.4).

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: trimethoprim may increase the anticoagulant effect.

src.q: Trimethoprim may potentiate the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and other coumarins.

items.t: Dapsone: plasma levels of both drugs may rise.

src.q: Dapsone: Plasma concentrations of trimethoprim and dapsone may increase when taken together.

items.t: Other folate antagonists: may cause folate deficiency in predisposed patients.

src.q: Trimethoprim may induce folate deficiency in patients predisposed to folate deficiency such as those receiving concomitant folate antagonists or anticonvulsants.

items.t: Diuretics (mainly thiazides) in elderly: more thrombocytopenia with purpura.

src.q: In elderly patients concurrently taking diuretics, primarily thiazides, there is an increased incidence of thrombocytopenia with purpura.

items.t: Digoxin, phenytoin (careful monitoring), procainamide, ciclosporin (nephrotoxicity), repaglinide (hypoglycaemia; monitor glucose), rifampicin, pyrimethamine.

src.q: Careful monitoring of patients treated with digoxin or phenytoin is advised
Monitoring of blood glucose is advised if co-administered with repaglinide (see section 4.5).

items.t: eGFR over 30: normal dose. eGFR 15 to 30: normal dose for 3 days, then half dose. eGFR under 15: half the normal dose. Measure: both the tablet and suspension SmPCs name the measure eGFR, but print the unit as "ml/min" (not ml/min/1.73 m2); the thresholds are kept as eGFR because that is the measure the sources name. If only CrCl is known, treat the bands as approximate.

src.q: Dosage advised where there is reduced kidney function: eGFR (ml/min) Dosage advised Over 30 Normal 15- 30 Normal for 3 days then half dose Under 15 Half the normal dose
Dosage advised eGFR (ml/min)

items.t: Consider monitoring renal function and electrolytes, especially with longer use. Dialysis: start and use only under close specialist supervision (infection + renal); trimethoprim is removed by dialysis.

src.q: Monitoring of renal function and serum electrolytes should be considered particularly with longer term use, in patients with impaired renal function.
Trimethoprim is removed by dialysis.

items.t: Contraindicated in severe hepatic insufficiency. Fatal haematological effects have been reported especially in elderly or those with renal or hepatic impairment.

src.q: Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in severe hepatic insufficiency.
Fatalities have been reported (especially in the elderly, or those with impairment of renal or hepatic function in whom careful monitoring is advised

items.t: First trimester: contraindicated (increased risk of miscarriage and malformations, including neural tube defects, oral clefts and heart defects; folate interference).

src.q: Trimethoprim is contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy (see section 4.3).
in particular neural tube defects, oral clefts and cardiovascular defects

items.t: Second and third trimesters: avoid unless clinically necessary. Note: both SmPCs also contain a broader line in 4.6 ("contra-indicated in pregnant women"), and the tablet SmPC 4.3 says it should not be given to pregnant women without naming a trimester; the trimester-specific advice is shown here.

src.q: In the second and third trimesters, use should be avoided, unless clinically necessary.
Trimethoprim is contra-indicated in pregnant women, premature infants or infants during the first few weeks of life.
Trimethoprim should not be administered to pregnant women, premature infants or children under 4 months of age

items.t: BUMPS (UKTIS patient leaflet): usually avoided in early pregnancy because it can lower folate; if needed in early pregnancy it is usually given with high-dose folic acid. Other antibiotics are usually used first for UTI.

src.q: Trimethoprim is usually avoided in early pregnancy because it can lower folate levels in your body.
If trimethoprim is needed in early pregnancy, it is usually prescribed with a high-dose folic acid supplement to help maintain folate levels.

items.t: Tablet SmPC: excreted in breast milk but not contraindicated for short-term use.

src.q: Trimethoprim is excreted in breast milk but is not contra-indicated for short term use in lactating mothers.

items.t: Suspension SmPC: effects on the suckling child are likely; contraindicated if the breastfed infant is under 4 months. (The two SmPCs differ; both statements concern trimethoprim in milk, so both are shown whatever the formulation.)

src.q: Effects on the suckling child are likely if therapeutic doses are administered to breast-feeding mothers.
Trimethoprim is contraindicated if the breast fed infant is less than 4 months of age.

items.t: Usual caution when prescribing for women of child-bearing age.

src.q: The usual caution in prescribing any drug for women of child bearing age should be exercised with trimethoprim.

items.t: BUMPS: no evidence that use by the father around conception affects the baby.

src.q: There is no evidence that trimethoprim taken by the father before or around the time of conception affects the baby.

items.t: Very common: hyperkalaemia. Common: headache, nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, rash, urticaria, candida (monilial) overgrowth.

src.q: Very common: Hyperkalaemia
Common: Nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting.
Common: Skin rashes, urticaria
Common: Monilial overgrowth

items.t: Blood disorders (very rare: neutropenia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, pancytopenia; megaloblastic anaemia; methaemoglobinaemia). Tell patients to seek immediate help for fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, purpura, bruising or bleeding.

src.q: Very rare: Leucopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopaenia, bone marrow depression, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia
advised to seek immediate medical attention if symptoms such as fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, purpura, bruising or bleeding develop.

items.t: SJS, TEN, DRESS: stop at once; never restart.

src.q: the treatment must not be restarted in this patient at any time.

items.t: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatic necrosis (very rare, may be fatal); aseptic meningitis (recurs on re-exposure); anaphylaxis, angioedema.

src.q: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatic necrosis may be fatal.
Very rare: Hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, angioedema

items.t: Long-term treatment or folate-deficiency risk (e.g. elderly): regular blood counts for pancytopenia.

src.q: Regular haematological tests should be undertaken in patients receiving long term treatment and those predisposed to folate deficiency, (e.g. the elderly), to check for possible pancytopaenia.

items.t: Serum potassium if at risk of hyperkalaemia or taking potassium-raising medicines.

src.q: If concomitant use of the above-mentioned agents is deemed appropriate, monitoring of serum potassium is recommended (see section 4.5).

items.t: Folic acid deficiency: give calcium folinate, check response; stopping trimethoprim may be needed.

src.q: If there is evidence of folic acid deficiency, calcium folinate should be administered and response checked by haematologic monitoring. It may be necessary to discontinue trimethoprim.

items.t: Oral. Where a single daily dose is used, taking it at bedtime may maximise urinary concentrations.

src.q: Where a single dose is required, dosage at bedtime may maximise urinary concentrations.

items.t: Tablet breakline is for ease of swallowing only, not for dividing into equal doses.

src.q: The breakline is only to facilitate breaking for ease of swallowing and not to divide into equal doses.

items.t: Seek immediate medical help for fever, sore throat, rash, mouth ulcers, purpura, bruising or bleeding.

src.q: Patients and their carers should be told how to recognise signs of blood disorders

items.t: Know the signs of severe skin reactions and report them.

src.q: Patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for skin reactions.

formulations.label: Tablets
formulations.strengths: 0.5 mg; 5 mg (each from its own UK SmPC)

src.q: Each tablet contains 0.5mg Warfarin Sodium.
Each tablet contains warfarin sodium 5 mg.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Prophylaxis of systemic embolism in rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation; prophylaxis after prosthetic heart valve insertion; prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; transient cerebral ischaemic attacks.

src.q: Prophylaxis of systemic embolism in patients with rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation. Prophylaxis after insertion of prosthetic heart valves. Prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
Transient attacks of cerebral ischaemia.

items.t: Give every patient a patient-held information booklet ('warfarin card') and explain which symptoms need medical attention.

src.q: Patients should be given a patient-held information booklet ('warfarin card') and informed of symptoms for which they should seek medical attention.

items.t: Adults (all indications): typical induction 10 mg daily for 2 days, tailored to the individual; usual maintenance 3 to 9 mg once daily at the same time each day, adjusted to prothrombin time/INR.

src.q: The typical induction dose is 10mg daily for 2 days but this should be tailored to individual requirements.
The daily maintenance dose is usually 3 to 9mg taken at the same time each day.

items.t: Emergencies: start heparin and warfarin together; stop heparin at least six hours before the first control test.

src.q: In emergencies, anticoagulant therapy should be initiated with heparin and warfarin together.
should be discontinued at least six hours before the first test is carried out

items.t: Elderly: as for adults but the dose may need to be lower.

src.q: Elderly: As for adults, but dosage may need to be lowered.

items.t: Protein C deficiency: start without a loading dose (even with heparin); protein S deficiency: start slowly.

src.q: In patients with protein C deficiency, therapy should be introduced without a loading dose of warfarin even if heparin is given.

items.t: Dose may need reducing with weight loss, acute illness or stopping smoking; may need increasing with weight gain, diarrhoea or vomiting.

src.q: Loss of weight Acute illness Cessation of smoking
Weight gain Diarrhoea Vomiting

items.t: No paediatric data are available in the SmPC.

src.q: Paediatric population: No data are available.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to warfarin or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Haemorrhagic stroke

items.t: Haemorrhagic stroke; clinically significant bleeding.

src.q: Haemorrhagic stroke (see section 4.4 for further details) Clinically significant bleeding

items.t: Within 72 hours of major surgery with risk of severe bleeding; within 48 hours postpartum.

src.q: Within 72 hours of major surgery with risk of severe bleeding
Within 48 hours postpartum

items.t: Pregnancy (first and third trimesters).

src.q: Pregnancy (first and third trimesters, see section 4.6)

items.t: Drugs whose interaction may significantly increase bleeding risk (e.g. fibrinolytics such as streptokinase and alteplase).

src.q: Drugs where interactions may lead to a significantly increased risk of bleeding
Fibrinolytic drugs such as streptokinase and alteplase are contraindicated in patients receiving warfarin.

items.t: Any condition where bleeding risk may outweigh the benefit of anticoagulation.

src.q: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in any physical condition in which the risk of haemorrhage might be greater that the potential clinical benefits of anticoagulation

items.t: Bleeding is the most frequent adverse effect. Give with caution where there is a risk of serious haemorrhage (e.g. NSAID use, recent ischaemic stroke, bacterial endocarditis, previous GI bleeding). Risk factors include INR >4.0, age ≥65, variable INRs, uncontrolled hypertension, cerebrovascular disease, falls risk, anaemia, malignancy, renal insufficiency, interacting drugs.

src.q: Warfarin should be given with caution to patients where there is a risk of serious haemorrhage (e.g. concomitant NSAID use, recent ischaemic stroke, bacterial endocarditis, previous gastrointestinal bleeding)
Risk factors for bleeding include high intensity of anticoagulation (INR >4.0), age ≥65, highly variable INRs

items.t: Active peptic ulcer: treat with caution, review regularly and teach how to recognise bleeding.

src.q: Due to a high risk of bleeding, patients with active peptic ulcers should be treated with caution.

items.t: Ischaemic stroke: a break is justified; restart 2-14 days after, depending on infarct size and blood pressure; stop for 14 days with large embolic stroke or uncontrolled hypertension.

src.q: Warfarin treatment should be re-started 2-14 days following ischaemic stroke, depending on the size of the infarct and blood pressure.

items.t: Surgery: no severe bleeding risk - operate with INR <2.5. Severe bleeding risk - stop warfarin 3 days before. If warfarin cannot be stopped 3 days before, reverse with low-dose vitamin K. Routine dental surgery (e.g. extraction) does not need warfarin stopped.

src.q: For surgery where there is a risk of severe bleeding, warfarin should be stopped 3 days prior to surgery.
anticoagulation should be reversed with low-dose vitamin K
Warfarin need not be stopped before routine dental surgery, eg, tooth extraction.

items.t: Thyroid disorders: hyper- or hypothyroidism changes warfarin metabolism; monitor closely when starting.

src.q: patients with hyper- or hypo-thyroidism should be closely monitored on starting warfarin therapy

items.t: Protein C deficiency: risk of skin necrosis on starting; start without loading dose.

src.q: Patients with protein C deficiency are at risk of developing skin necrosis when starting warfarin treatment.

items.t: Calciphylaxis (rare): consider stopping warfarin if diagnosed; reported also with normal renal function.

src.q: In case calciphylaxis is diagnosed, appropriate treatment should be started and consideration should be given to stopping treatment with warfarin.
cases have been reported in patients taking warfarin, including those with normal renal function

items.t: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy: acute kidney injury possible, linked to excessive anticoagulation and haematuria; close monitoring including renal function if supratherapeutic INR with haematuria.

src.q: Close monitoring including renal function evaluation is advised in patients with a supratherapeutic INR and hematuria (including microscopic).

items.t: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genetic variability can significantly affect dose needs.

src.q: Genetic variability particularly in relation to CYP2C9 and VKORC1 can significantly affect dose requirements for warfarin.

items.t: Contains lactose.

src.q: contains 48.350 mg lactose per tablet

items.t: Narrow therapeutic range: care with all concomitant therapy. Any change to medication, including OTC products, warrants more INR monitoring.

src.q: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic range and care is required with all concomitant therapy.
Any change to medication, including self-medication with OTC products, warrants increased monitoring of the INR.

items.t: Avoid if possible (or give with caution and more clinical and laboratory monitoring): clopidogrel, NSAIDs (including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors), SSRI and SNRI antidepressants, heparins, other anticoagulants and antiplatelets.

src.q: The following examples should be avoided, or administered with caution with increased clinical and laboratory monitoring: Clopidogrel NSAIDs (including aspirin and cox-2 specific NSAIDS)
SSRI and SNRI antidepressants

items.t: Potentiate warfarin (dose may need reducing, more monitoring): omeprazole, paracetamol (prolonged regular use), statins (not pravastatin; mainly fluvastatin), sulfamethoxazole, erythromycin, metronidazole, azole antifungals, amiodarone, allopurinol and others.

src.q: omeprazole, paracetamol (prolonged regular use)
statins (not pravastatin; predominantly associated with fluvastatin) erythromycin, sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole
When these drugs are co-administered, warfarin dosage may need to be reduced and the level of monitoring increased.

items.t: Broad-spectrum antibiotics may potentiate warfarin by reducing vitamin K-producing gut flora (no specific antibiotic is named in this statement).

src.q: Broad spectrum antibiotics may potentiate the effect of warfarin by reducing the gut flora which produce vitamin K.

items.t: St John's wort: must not be used with warfarin (proven reduced warfarin levels and effect).

src.q: Herbal preparations containing St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) must not be used whilst taking warfarin

items.t: Tramadol (MHRA 2024): can raise INR with severe, possibly fatal bleeding; be aware, consider dose adjustment and extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol.

src.q: Taking warfarin and tramadol together can cause harmful drug interactions, which can raise the International Normalised Ratio (INR)
consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: 0.5 mg tablet SmPC only (not in the 5 mg tablet SmPC): oral anti-diabetic agents and diuretics are also listed as potentiating warfarin.

src.q: methylphenidate, diuretics, oral anti-diabetic agents, anabolic steroids

items.t: Corticosteroids: variable effect on INR; increase monitoring when starting and stopping.

src.q: Examples of drugs with variable effect Corticosteroids, nevirapine, ritonavir
in these cases increased monitoring on starting and stopping therapy is advised

items.t: Drugs that reduce warfarin effect include barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, oral contraceptives, oestrogens.

src.q: Examples of drugs which antagonise the effect of warfarin Barbiturates, primidone, carbamazepine, griseofulvin, oral contraceptives, rifampicin

items.t: Miconazole (including oral gel) inhibits CYP2C9: monitor anticoagulant effect; warfarin dose reduction may be needed.

src.q: Miconazole inhibits CYP2C9, caution should be exercised in patients on oral anticoagulants, such as warfarin

items.t: Foods and alcohol: avoid cranberry products; large or sudden diet changes in vitamin K-rich foods (liver, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, green leafy vegetables) can affect control; acute heavy alcohol raises INR; moderate alcohol permitted; avoid herbal medicines/food supplements.

src.q: Patients should be advised to avoid cranberry products.
Moderate alcohol intake can be permitted.
Patients should generally avoid taking any herbal medicines or food supplements whilst taking warfarin

items.t: No dose threshold given. Monitor INR more often in renal disease; renal insufficiency is a bleeding risk factor.

src.q: INR should be monitored more frequently in patients at an increased risk of over coagulation e.g. patients with severe hypertension, liver or renal disease.

items.t: No dose threshold given. Monitor INR more often in liver disease (risk of over-coagulation).

src.q: INR should be monitored more frequently in patients at an increased risk of over coagulation e.g. patients with severe hypertension, liver or renal disease.

items.t: Contraindicated in the first and third trimesters (warfarin embryopathy; fatal bleeding and stillbirth). Rarely prescribed in pregnancy; switch to other anticoagulants during pregnancy or after conception.

src.q: Warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy in the first and third trimester
patients should be switched on to other anticoagulants during pregnancy or after conception

items.t: BUMPS: avoided in pregnancy where possible (birth defects); may sometimes be recommended with mechanical heart valves. Do not stop without specialist advice; people with a metal valve need urgent specialist advice within a day or two of a positive test.

src.q: Warfarin is avoided in pregnancy where possible as it can cause birth defects.
If you have a metal heart valve you should seek urgent advice from your specialist or GP within a day or two of a positive pregnancy test.

items.t: SmPC: can be used during breastfeeding; no effects expected at therapeutic doses.

src.q: Warfarin can be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: SPS: preferred oral anticoagulant in breastfeeding; monitor the infant for bruising and blood in urine, vomit or stools.

src.q: Warfarin can be used during breastfeeding, although infant monitoring is required.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for bruising on the skin, blood in urine, vomit, or stools.

items.t: Women of child-bearing age should use effective contraception. No fertility data.

src.q: Women of child-bearing age who are taking warfarin tablets should use effective contraception during treatment.
Fertility No data available

adverseCommon.note: One warfarin SmPC (section 4.8) gives all adverse reactions as frequency 'not known'; haemorrhage is the most frequently reported adverse effect (SmPC 4.4). Sources checked: both warfarin SmPCs.

items.t: Haemorrhage (including cerebral haemorrhage, subdural haematoma, GI bleeding): the most frequent adverse effect. Unexpected bleeding at therapeutic INR should be investigated.

src.q: The most frequently reported adverse effect of all oral anticoagulants is haemorrhage.
Unexpected bleeding at therapeutic levels should always be investigated and INR monitored.

items.t: Life-threatening haemorrhage: stop warfarin, give prothrombin complex concentrate 30-50 units/kg (or FFP 15 mL/kg if none); discuss with haematologist/NPIS. Non-life-threatening: slow IV phytomenadione 10-20 mg (adults).

src.q: Stop warfarin treatment, give prothrombin complex concentrate (factors II, VII, IX, and X) 30-50 units/kg
give slow intravenous injection of phytomenadione (vitamin K1) 10-20 mg for adults

items.t: Skin necrosis (rare, mainly with loading doses over 10 mg, within 3-5 days, often obese elderly women); calciphylaxis; 'purple toes'. Discontinuation usually advised.

src.q: Skin necrosis is a rare but potentially serious effect. It is associated with loading doses of over 10mg
Advice on management usually includes discontinuing the warfarin.

items.t: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy (acute kidney injury).

src.q: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy (see section 4.4), haematuria

items.t: Baseline prothrombin time or INR before starting (5 mg tablet SmPC). SPS baseline: clotting screen, FBC, LFTs, serum creatinine or eGFR (ORBIT score); consider TFTs and blood pressure.

src.q: Baseline prothrombin (PT) or INR measurements should be made before beginning therapy with warfarin tablets.
Required Baseline Clotting screening Full blood count Liver function tests

items.t: INR daily or on alternate days early in treatment, then at longer intervals once stable in range. SPS: daily/alternate days, then twice weekly for 1-2 weeks, then weekly; once stable every 12 weeks (more often if high risk, poor control or interacting medicine).

src.q: the INR should be determined daily or on alternate days in the early days of treatment
Daily or on alternate days; then twice weekly for 1-2 weeks; then weekly, depending on local protocol
